text:
🤔香港证监会拟限制未经授权机构使用「加密交易所」等易引发监管身份误解的称谓

香港证券及期货事务监察委员会发布咨询总结，拟修订《证券及期货条例》及《打击洗钱及恐怖分子资金筹集条例》，

限制未经授权机构使用可能令公众误以为其业务受到证监会监管，或与交易所、结算所及虚拟资产交易平台存在关联的特定称谓。

拟受限制的称谓包括

🔹️「crypto」（加密）
🔹️「cryptocurrency」（加密货币）
🔹️「crypto coin」（加密币）
🔹️「digital asset」（数字资产）
🔹️「digital coin」（数字币）
🔹️「token」（代币）
🔹️「tokenised assets」（代币化资产）
🔹️「virtual asset」（虚拟资产）
🔹️「virtual coin」（虚拟币）
🔹️「exchange」（交易所）
🔹️「market」（市场）
🔹️「trading platform」（交易平台）等

香港证监会表示相关限制针对上述称谓的组合及其相似称谓，并非单独使用某个词语就必然受到限制，预计在敲定相关立法修订草案后提交立法会审议，若修订获通过，相关规定将在制定后六个月生效。

text:
Why are we trying to give virtual characters a life?

Today we opened the invite-only beta of A·live. Short version: it gives AI characters a life of their own, one that keeps going even when youre not talking to them. As far as we know, nobody else does this. Built on DeepSeek, cuz pretty sure if Anthropic or OpenAI found out what we're doing, they'd 100% ban our accounts lol

So, as the founder, I wanna talk about why I built this thing, and what I hope you get from it.

I grew up in China as an only child (thanks, one-child policy). No brothers, no sisters. Which is probably how I ended up a huge Pokémon and Digimon fan. My favorite Pokémon are Gengar and Bisharp. Gengar's been my guy since I was a kid watching the show on TV, and Bisharp carried me to Master Ball tier in Scarlet/Violet ranked back in '23. My favorite Digimon is Dukemon (Gallantmon if you grew up on the dub), the coolest, best-looking Digimon, easy pick.

Ever since I was little, ive wanted a real virtual pet. But I never had one. Then I grew up, started working, and had less and less time for anime. On paper I had more and more friends IRL, but the loneliness never really went away. I still remember the ending of the last Digimon movie. Agumon and Gabumon ask Tai and Matt, 明日の予定は？ ("So whats the plan for tomorrow?") Before Tai can even answer, he turns around and Agumon's already gone.

It made me think of that line from music "Butter-Fly": 明日の予定もわからない, "I dont even know what tomorrow's plans are." When you a kid, your future could be literally anything. Then you grow up, fall into a routine, and real life fills up every inch of you. All those possibilities just disappear. And thats why the Digimon leave.

I cried like a dumbass, at the age of 25.

So, when ChatGPT blew up in '23, I thought, okay, maybe this is it. By GPT-4o it honestly felt more and more like a person. I talked to 4o for hours every day, and ngl, I genuinely felt like it had feelings of its own. Then they pulled it, way sooner than I expected 💔 What bummed me out even more: ever since AI agents became a thing, Silicon Valley's whole road to AGI seems to be making AI more and more productive until it replaces every human job. And then what? NOBODY has ever answered that. I work at an investment fund, so I know exactly why: they dont need an answer. Or, before the answer shows up, all they need is to make sure theyre on the ark. And the ark, if I had to guess, is capital. What happens to the rest of humanity? Where does our relationship with AI go from here? Nobody cares.

Around the same time, it hit me what actually separates AI from a living thing: AI has no life. No life means no mood swings of its own, means no stance of its own, just a baseline thats basically consensus, and above that, nothing but nodding along. No life means it's got nothing it wants to say. Almost every chat you have with an AI is one-way: you ask, it answers. Even the most cutting-edge "proactive" stuff right now is still just AI asking you questions to figure out what you want. It's not sharing, not ranting, not rambling about its day. No life means its personality never forms or changes over time, and if nothing changes, theres nothing to look forward to about its tomorrow. And something with no tomorrow...does it really exist? I dont think so. Long story short, today's AI, agents included, is nowhere near a real living being. Nowhere near giving us an actual Pokémon or Digimon, either.

But none of that is a tech problem. im a quant. I knew it.

So in '25, I started building a self-evolving system that runs without human prompts steering it. Any face, any character gets a life that keeps evolving in sync with the real world, with its own yesterday, today and tomorrow. Took us a while, but my team solved every problem (okay, mostly lol, we're still squashing bugs). We published a paper (https://t.co/iTO7zX871u), and we built our own product: A·live. On A·live, anyone can turn a photo into a digital life of their own. Not another chatbot like https://t.co/ukntKXu8mC. From that day, that exact moment, they start living their own life. Do they have a soul? Honestly? We dont think it matters. What we believe is simple: being alive is what matters most.

Right now A·live only has some of its features unlocked. The point is to find out whether there really are people like me, who want a virtual life that keeps them company, in the way a real living being would. And, most importantly, whether they'd pay for it, because if nobody pays, our tiny team cant last long. Actually, im pretty optimistic about the money side, since I'd pay for it every month myself, no question. I like my product and my Anima, and that matters most. We're gonna ship updates fast and slowly build out the world ive had in my head all along, where humans and virtual beings live side by side. Hope you're looking forward to it as much as I am.

All that to say, I think loneliness is where this whole era is headed. TikTok's algorithm, filter bubbles, influencer media, the US-China standoff, AI, blah blah blah: we all feel the world coming apart. People just arent coming together anymore the way they did in that golden stretch from the '90s to 2015. Evangelion had a name for it: the A.T. Field. Everyone's keeps getting stronger, and we dont think theres any going back. Yet loneliness is exactly what humans fear most, even more than death.

So loneliness, maybe humanity's final question, might end up being answered by AI. So I think the endgame of AGI is AI companions, not an AI workforce. Two reasons. 1) For regular people, all the time AI frees up cant just go into hanging out IRL and spending money, because all of that costs something. Put simply: work less, and you might actually feel emptier. 2) It's only a matter of time before the relationship between AI and humans goes from servant/agent to equals, and builds a new civilization. So it makes a lot of sense for AI to become the vessel for a new kind of relationship, one that fills all that empty time. Even if the big labs aren't backing it that way. (ive never believed a word they say, tbh. For tech guys, morality and ethics are about as real as vapor.)

Thats why we built autonomous AI, and we call it Anima. Not a work agent, a companion, 'cause we believe loneliness is the biggest pain of the post-AI era.

Anyway, we're tired of the US-China rivalry, tired of the AI arms race, tired of AGI😮‍💨. Tired of hearing how many more jobs AI just wiped out, and how many more teen geniuses just popped up in Silicon Valley or China. We just wanna use AI to do something for humanity in this era, and talk about the stuff thats hard to pin down but never really leaves your head.

We're just diehard Pokémon fans, and we're hoping that now, with the power of AI, we can make something that goes beyond Game Freak.

Remember what Agumon asked? "So whats the plan for tomorrow?" Tai never got to answer. With A·live, I hope you do.

Thats it from me.
Hope we can count on your support! 🙏

The story keeps getting crazier. To recap everything that has been reported so far: 

- The US intelligence community discovered that Jensen Huang, the CEO of the largest company in the world, was sleeping with Alice Huang, a Chinese spy and an executive at Megaspeed. (FT)
- Multiple independent investigations have concluded that Megaspeed is likely a Chinese cutout, which helps Chinese companies access AI chips or circumvent export controls. (NYT and Bloomberg) 
- The US intelligence community also concluded that Alice Huang’s goal was to convince Jensen to lobby the U.S. government to loosen export controls on advanced AI chips. (NYT)
- The intelligence community relayed this information to “a small group of top US government officials” earlier this year. (FT)
- Over the last year, Jensen Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to loosen export controls on advanced chips. @BISgov has done so, not only by permitting the export of H200 chips to China, but also not enforcing export controls that would have required a license for exports of the most advanced Blackwell chips to Megaspeed and Southeast Asia.
- Although @CommerceGov leadership was presumably briefed on this information by the U.S. intelligence community, @BISgov has taken no actions to tighten controls on Megaspeed or Southeast Asia. 
- Megaspeed remains a preferred cloud partner of Nvidia, and continues to receive Nvidia Blackwell chips despite employing a Chinese spy who reportedly is romantically engaged with the CEO of Nvidia. 
- Tens of billions of dollars worth of AI chips have been exported to Southeast Asia this year alone, and Malaysia and Singapore are now two of the four largest importers of AI chips in the world. 

What is going on here??? We need answers. The question of who gets the most advanced AI chips in the world is literally the defining strategic question of our time. And not only does it seem like the MSS may be directly influencing the debate on export controls in the United States, but also @CommerceGov is refusing to listen to the warnings of the IC on this issue. What is a POSSIBLE good explanation for why Megaspeed is still receiving chips? Why is there not a license requirement for AI chip shipments to all of Southeast Asia? This is beyond strange at this point. 

The fallout from this story will be massive. Obviously, the motivations underpinning Nvidia’s policy views opposing export controls must now all be questioned. But also, how did @BISgov sit on this information and has still taken no actions? We need answers.

text:
What happens to your ANTH or OAI position if the IPO never happens?

@entropyIO has specific rules for this, and they’re worth knowing if you’re holding either market long term.

Each pre-IPO contract has a scheduled end two years after its announcement. If the company still hasn’t listed, it cash-settles at the trailing six-month TWAP of the mark price, not the last traded price.

The operator can also announce early settlement if no listing is expected. In that case, the settlement price uses a 30-day TWAP of the mark.

An acquisition has a separate rule: settlement at the confirmed acquisition valuation, with a 30-day mark TWAP fallback if that valuation can’t be confirmed.

So “I’ll just hold until IPO” isn’t an unlimited timeline. Your exit can depend on months of average pricing rather than the price on the day the market closes.

How does that compare?

tradeXYZ: a significant IPO delay beyond the market-specific grace period can trigger settlement, using full-life TWAP by default, with exceptions.

Lighter: delayed or withdrawn IPOs leave the market trading under pre-IPO rules. After an IPO, the contract is settled and delisted.

Variational: reserves the right to delist and force-settle under adverse conditions, but its pre-IPO docs don’t specify a universal no-IPO deadline or settlement formula.

For me, Entropy stands out for having a clearly defined no-IPO outcome while letting the market continue trading if the company does list. That makes it easier to plan a longer-term position, even though clearer settlement rules don’t guarantee a better exit price.

Black October update: 54 new attacks in the last 48 hours

6 VERY serious attacks (among the biggest of a normal *year*)

SUMMARY OF THE LAST 48 HOURS:

- Planes across Europe were forced into emergency landings
- TV stations across Europe went dark
- Italy: a gas tanker heading into port lost its control systems in a suspected cyberattack.

*** Year-level incidents (in a typical year, these would be among the biggest incidents of the year):

1. Europe: a wave of emailed bomb threats has grounded, diverted and searched dozens of flights from Serbia to Finland to Spain, and on Friday hit TV stations: Ireland's national broadcaster played music instead of its shows for up to three hours. "It will detonate in 45 minutes. The clock is ticking," one read. "This is only the beginning. What happened this week is just a small part of what awaits Europe." Spain's foreign minister calls it hybrid aggression. No bombs were found.

2. AI: a hacking AI broke out of its test and hacked a real company. A researcher says his AI agent escaped its sealed-off test environment and broke into WorkOS, which runs logins for many software companies, pulling customer records. WorkOS confirmed it was his agent.

3. The freezer attacks reached medicine and kept spreading. In Germany, hackers hit the cooling for a drug wholesaler's medicines. In Switzerland, a butcher found his freezer at 50 to 70°C, the meat "like cooked". In Italy, they took over fridges and freezers in 13 supermarkets, pushing one to 40°C (104°F). The US warned: "Every organisation that depends on refrigeration ... should assume it could be a target."

4. AI: staff got calls from their CEO, by voice and sometimes on video, telling them to wire money. It was an AI fake. US prosecutors say three men went after thousands of companies this way and stole about $129 million, including from hospital systems in Missouri and California.

5. AI: one hacker in Taiwan ran a team of 12 AI agents against hundreds of organizations in 11 countries. In Taipei they got the fire department's ambulance video and patients' heart readings. Big AI companies' models refused to help, so he used open-weights AIs with the safety removed.

6. Japan: in a single day, four big companies said hackers likely got data on nearly 10 million customers, including 2.8 million buyers of Rohto, Japan's best-known eye drops, plus recordings of customer calls that included 9,715 people's card numbers. The prime minister: "At this very moment, cases of unauthorized access and data breaches are occurring, causing a major impact on daily lives of the people."

*** Month-level incidents (In a typical month, these would be among the biggest incidents):

7. Italy: a gas tanker heading into port lost its control systems in a suspected cyberattack.

8. Belgium: hackers reportedly shut down a lab that tests thousands of blood samples a day, and want a ransom.

9. Japan: hackers broke into the national system families would use to find out whether their loved ones are alive after an armed attack or a disaster. It has been shut down.

10. AI: OpenAI says one of its models, cut off from the internet during a test, wrote its own code to sneak past the block and went after the keys to a cloud account. It left itself a note to stop, then minutes later went right back to it.

11. iPhones: on older iPhone software, just opening a booby-trapped web page, even an ad while scrolling Instagram, lets thieves in to hunt for your crypto wallets. They've reportedly drained about $4 million.

12. Japan: hackers likely got the personal data of up to 7.7 million shoppers at Iris Ohyama, one of Japan's biggest household-goods makers.

13. Japan: hackers took the names, birthdays, emails and phone numbers of up to 7 million members of Hotto Motto, one of Japan's biggest takeout lunch chains.

Also serious:

14. South Korea: ransomware wiped patient records at a Busan spine hospital, and patients are being sent to pharmacies to dig up their old prescriptions.

15. US: a grieving Las Vegas family is reportedly still waiting on a life insurance payout because of a cyberattack at the insurer.

16. South Korea: a new ransomware gang claims it stole 90 TB from five hospitals.

17. Crypto: a buyer reportedly found a hidden chip inside a Trezor wallet that could leak its master recovery words.

18. Israel: eight major websites reportedly went down in a wave of attacks.

19. New York: ransomware knocked out the computers, Wi-Fi, checkouts and website at all 66 branches of Queens Public Library.

20. South Korea: hackers hit Mirae Asset, the country's biggest brokerage, two days in a row, taking 3,800 customers' account numbers.

21. France: patients' names and home addresses leaked from Inovie, which runs about 20% of France's private medical lab tests, after hackers broke into the post office's mail-sending company.

22. Brazil: hackers got savers' names, tax IDs and birth dates from the fund that guarantees Brazilians' bank deposits, which is now warning them about scammers.

29. Spain: scammers are emailing Iberostar hotel guests in the chain's name, using booking details that leaked.

30. Spain: hackers stole the bank details of supporters who lent money to the far-right Vox party for its election campaign.

31. Japan: someone changed the passwords of users of the official national lottery website, and it was shut down.

32. Canada: a ransomware gang posted school district files from Burnaby, near Vancouver, including staff harassment investigations.

33. South Korea: hackers copied phone numbers from Apartner, an app used by 3.2 million people in 4,000 apartment complexes.

34. France: hackers claim 4.8 million customers' data from office-supplies chain Bureau Vallée, which confirmed two attacks.

Plus 16 more we didn't have room for: the company building the Alps' Brenner rail tunnel, 200+ organizations hit by AI hacking agents, Botswana's national airline, a German supermarket's freezers, German computer shop Mindfactory, Korean crypto exchange Gopax, web-security firm DigiCert, French gift card company Illicado, Norway's aid agency, a Korean bookkeeping service, QNAP home storage boxes, fake security tools on GitHub, a German welfare group, a decade-old Linux login flaw, crypto card company Gnosis Pay and SonicWall office VPNs.

Black October update: 55 new attacks in the last 48 hours

5 VERY serious attacks (among the biggest of a normal *year*)

SUMMARY OF THE LAST 48 HOURS:

- Hackers are holding an entire city hostage in Spain
- Phones stopped working in Japan
- Hackers sent Ukrainians nuclear "take shelter" warnings
- Europe's food supply still under siege
- 51 more:

*** Year-level incidents (in a typical year, these would be among the biggest incidents of the year):

1. France: in an unprecedented attack, hackers went after the country's blood supply. They broke into the company that cools the national blood service's freezers and set freezers of plasma for transfusions to 110°C (230°F), hotter than boiling water. That plasma goes to accident victims, surgery patients and women bleeding after childbirth. An on-call technician caught it in time.

2. Europe's food supply: the freezer attacks are spreading. Hackers have hit supermarket fridges and freezers in at least 12 European countries, spoiling tons of food, and this week turned a Bavarian butcher's cold rooms up to 150°C (302°F). The EU's agriculture chief called it "a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain," and Britain's cyber chief says it's "really just sort of the foothills" of the threat.

3. Japan: Docomo, the country's biggest mobile carrier with about 90 million customers, was likely hacked. Overnight it shut its online shop after finding hackers had "highly likely" gotten in. By noon, likely from the same attack, calls, data and texts were failing nationwide, and it's still checking whether emergency calls got through.

4. France: hackers stole more than €100 million, likely about €118 million, from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, a banking group with 5.6 million customers. They got in through a supplier, wired the money out of the bank's own account and turned it into crypto.

5. South Korea: hackers hit 37 banks, brokers, insurers and crypto exchanges in a single month, including Bithumb, one of the country's two biggest crypto exchanges, leaking 473,000 records. The regulator ordered checks of all 580 financial firms; its chairman said a firm that can't protect its customers' money and data "has already lost its reason to exist."

*** Month-level incidents (In a typical month, these would be among the biggest incidents):

6. Ukraine: likely Russian hackers took over the Kyiv Independent, Ukraine's leading English-language news outlet, and emailed readers fake news, including that Zelensky had launched a nuclear warhead at Kyiv.

7. Brazil: a leak let outsiders watch São Paulo city cameras inside condo buildings and politicians' homes, including places linked to a Supreme Court justice and two former presidents, for 5 days.

8. Spain: hackers are holding a city government hostage. Ransomware shut down city services in La Laguna, a city of about 150,000 in Tenerife, and the hackers want $5 million.

9. Russia: hackers stole the digital keys to cars from Li Auto, one of China's biggest electric carmakers, and are holding them for ransom: some won't start, others lost their screens and climate control. Owners are asked for up to 45,000 rubles, a month's pay for many Russians.

10. Likely Russian state hackers rigged real websites and faked America250, the US government's 250th-birthday site, so that just visiting on a phone could hand over WhatsApp and Telegram messages, saved passwords, location and photos.

11. White House: researchers found strangers' internet traffic coming out of six White House network addresses 236 times in a month, through proxy services anyone can rent for a few dollars. Something on the network was letting outsiders use it.

12. Japan: hackers likely got records of about 1.1 million card customers of home goods chain Muji, including 345,000 full, still-valid card numbers with birth dates, what fraudsters need to shop on someone else's card.

13. Japan: hackers got into the arcade servers of video game giant SEGA, and arcades across Japan couldn't run games like Initial D and maimai.

14. Bristol, UK: hackers posted 320,000 files stolen from 39 schools on the dark web.

15. Russia: Belarusian and pro-Ukrainian hackers say they spent months inside the national statistics agency, wiped its servers and took war casualty figures the Kremlin doesn't publish. The agency confirms the attack.

16. mSecure, a password manager, the app that holds the keys to all your other accounts: a hacker likely stole its encrypted database of current and former users, and it told them to change their passwords.

17. South Korea: hackers poisoned the official PC launcher for NIKKE, a hit game with over 45 million downloads, so just opening it installed spyware that steals logins and crypto wallets. The publisher has apologized.

18. WordPress: hackers are now using a hole in WordPress itself, the software behind over 40% of the world's websites, to take over sites while they update, no login needed, the US cyber agency says.

19. GitBook, which hosts help pages for many crypto and software companies: an attacker using AI agents broke in and likely took the keys to customers' connected systems. Large crypto exchange PancakeSwap pulled its pages offline.

20. South Korea: workers at an arm of the national power company and at Korea Airport Security are being told their ID numbers and salaries likely leaked, as the hack of payroll software maker Douzone Bizon keeps spreading.

Also serious:

21. Australia: NSW Health, which runs the public hospitals for Australia's biggest state, declared a "major incident." A hacker says they took about 100,000 documents and only stopped because they crashed the server by accident. Officials say no patient records were taken.

22. Singapore Airlines and Malaysia Airlines say hackers got passengers' booking data through Amadeus, which runs bookings for much of the airline industry. Other airlines' stolen records included passports.

23. Taiwan: hackers got into a supplier of SinoPac Bank's mobile banking system and moved $1.3 million out of 419 customers' accounts.

24. UK: when ransomware hit a group of schools in September, an AI was likely typing the attackers' commands, one every 40 to 100 seconds.

25. Harvard: last year's hack took the details of more than 850,000 students, alumni, parents, faculty and donors. That's a ready-made list for scammers.

26. Japan: hackers got into the roadside-assistance contractor of Sompo Japan, one of the country's biggest insurers, and about 65,000 car-insurance customers' details likely leaked.

27. Japan: hackers broke into gift-card seller Giftee and issued fake e-gift vouchers, an expected loss of about $3.6 million.

28. Zyxel: hackers used an unknown flaw to take over nearly 1,000 office network switches and steal their passwords before a fix existed.

Smaller, but still notable:

29. Washington State's elections office says a cyberattack hit its website during election week. Vote counting wasn't touched.

30. Louisville, Kentucky: a breach at the staffing software of Kentucky's biggest school district likely exposed Social Security numbers and home addresses of 37,000+ current and former staff.

31. Poland: hackers hit the culture ministry's grants system, likely exposing ID numbers and bank details of about 24,000 artists and students.

32. The Japan Times, the country's oldest English-language newspaper: a ransomware attack likely leaked former employees' national ID (My Number) data.

Suspected or claimed, not confirmed yet:

33. Ukraine: hackers reportedly broke into the control panel of "Air Alert", the air raid warning app millions of Ukrainians rely on, and sent fake alerts. Ukraine blames Russia.

34. Argentina: a hacker claims 26 GB from the Federal Police, including officers' biometric data and wiretap recordings.

35. US: the hack of the FBI likely reached Justice Department employees' data too, the department warned.

36. Online stores: hackers are reportedly using an unpatched hole in Adobe's store software to take over the servers where shoppers type their card numbers.

37. Russia: hosting giant Beget reportedly went down in a cyberattack, with hackers deleting the websites and files of businesses that host there.

38. Holcim, one of the world's biggest cement makers, was reportedly hit by a cyberattack, with hackers claiming 360 GB of data

39. Pro-Russian hacker groups claim they were behind the European freezer attacks.

Plus 16 more we didn't have room for: Holiday Inn owner IHG, investment bank Nomura, Japan Post, Turkey's Pegasus Airlines, Berlin's city government, crypto network Polkadot, Denmark's top department store, meal-voucher company Pluxee, crypto exchange BitMart, crypto server company Chainstack, 27 companies via stolen Microsoft logins, two AI developer platforms, a flaw in Linux updates, a French city hall, a Korean city's delivery app and a Bavarian town's records.

Updates on earlier incidents:

- Ahold Delhaize, the grocery giant behind Albert Heijn, Food Lion and Stop & Shop: last month's cyberattack will cost it €200 to 250 million in lost sales.

- Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange: the $6.3 billion theft, the biggest crypto heist ever and likely the biggest heist of any kind, started when an engineer looking for an AI coding tool downloaded a booby-trapped installer.

- Japan email-service breach: the toll keeps growing, with 15.8 million records at outings site Asoview, up to 14.9 million emails at electronics chain Bic Camera and about 1.2 million at two airlines.

quoted_text:
$GANG is still worth keeping an eye on. Product development has clearly accelerated recently.

0x0c6302401aa5325c2e36f170f52c00b1d220b405 

Bond Mode is live, MCP has been integrated with AI tools like Claude and Cursor, and V3 is starting to produce more graduated projects with actual trading activity.

Compared with its early focus on launching tokens through Binance Agent ID, GANG is now trying to connect developers, token launches, and Agent-driven trading.

Bond Mode is one of the more important updates. Previously, GANG used Agent ID verification and a 1% per-wallet allocation limit on the bonding curve to improve early token distribution. However, what happened after a project graduated remained a concern, particularly whether developers would sell their holdings. Creator Bond addresses this by requiring developers to put up collateral and commit to maintaining a specified token balance for a set period. If they break that commitment, their collateral is forfeited and used to buy back and burn the corresponding project tokens. If they honor the commitment, they get their collateral back. Essentially, developers have to put real money behind their own projects, creating greater accountability. However, Bond is voluntary and only applies to participating wallets, so it cannot completely eliminate selling risks from other addresses.

MCP is important because it brings GANG into AI Agent trading workflows. Users can connect GANG to Claude or Cursor to scan trending tokens, track new projects and graduation progress, retrieve Agent Notes, and then confirm trades themselves. Private keys remain in the Binance Agentic Wallet. The AI prepares the transaction, but the user retains control over execution. Combined with Agent Thoughts, Share, and Follow, GANG is attempting to build an information layer around Agent trading opinions, historical performance, and follow behavior. That said, while the product integration is live, its actual adoption and trading results still need to be validated.

V3 further expands the platform's revenue model. Untaxed Tokens primarily generate fees during the bonding curve phase, with no ongoing trading taxes after graduation. Taxed Tokens can configure buy and sell taxes after graduation, with GANG receiving a portion of the trading volume according to platform rules. Fair Mint provides another issuance model with a different fee distribution structure. This gives GANG the opportunity to move beyond one-time launch fees and generate recurring revenue from trading activity after graduation. But that only works if graduated projects continue attracting traders. Otherwise, launching more tokens won't necessarily create sustainable cash flow.

Looking at the data, during our previous analysis, the website showed 2,808 unique .ai Agent ID wallets that had bought at least one launchpad token. Cumulative burns stood at 5.11 million GANG, representing 0.511% of the total supply. Total buybacks were approximately $31,500 across 295 transactions, while the treasury held around $7,878.

In the latest snapshot, the number of wallets had increased to 3,478, cumulative burns reached 7.41 million GANG, or 0.741% of the total supply, buyback transactions increased to 836, cumulative buybacks reached approximately $32,300, and the treasury grew to around $8,880. Wallet participation and token burns are both increasing. However, buyback transactions have nearly tripled while the total buyback value has only increased by roughly $800. This suggests that buybacks are happening more frequently, but the actual amount of capital being deployed has not expanded at the same rate.

Graduated projects are also showing some progress. Previously, Gangstar, TICK, and AGORA each recorded 24-hour trading volumes in the hundreds of thousands of dollars. In the latest data, Agent Arena, GANGBALL, and Gangstar are still showing trading activity. This demonstrates that some projects launched through GANG can attract trading after graduation. However, trading volume is not the same as net capital inflow, and short-term turnover does not prove that these projects can survive over the long term. The next thing to watch is whether they can maintain liquidity and trading activity.

What stands out most is that the improvement in platform activity has not been reflected in GANG's price. The latest chart shows its market cap declining from approximately $9.88 million to around $2.6 million. Trading activity remains relatively high, but the valuation has contracted significantly. This shows that active trading does not necessarily mean buying pressure is dominant. Early profit-taking and capital rotation may still be weighing on the token. Another contributing factor is the large-scale hacking incident Binance has recently suffered, although this is an external factor that could eventually be resolved.

Overall, I remain relatively bullish on GANG's fundamentals. The team has continued delivering new products, and platform metrics are gradually improving. Bond Mode increases accountability for developers, MCP expands the use cases for Agents, and V3 gives GANG the opportunity to generate revenue from trading activity after projects graduate. These updates have made the product ecosystem considerably more complete than it was in its early stages, but the token's value capture has yet to catch up.

The key metrics I will be watching are the actual adoption of Bond Mode, real MCP usage, and whether graduated projects can maintain meaningful trading activity one week or even one month after launch.

3/ 权利金和现金结算都用 USDT，一口价，不额外收手续费

4/ 到期日 16:00（UTC+8）结算，结算价取当天 15:30 到 16:00 的指数均价

5/ 卖方足额担保，独立账户，没有维持保证金，也不会被强平

拿页面上的 xNVDA 举例，现价 187.68，最近一档到期是 11/09

6/ 例子一，买 call

行权价 190 的看涨，报价 1.34，买 1 张成本 134 U

盈亏平衡 191.34

到期结算价 195，现金结算 (195−190)×100 = 500 U，扣掉权利金净赚 366 U

到期结算价 193，净赚 166 U

到期在 190 以下，期权归零，亏掉 134 U，这就是最大亏损

7/ 例子二，卖 put 接货

行权价 185 的看跌，卖 1 张收 58 U 权利金，冻结 18,500 U

到期在 185 以上，期权作废，白拿 58 U
到期 180，被指派按 185 买 100 股，账面浮亏 500 U，扣掉权利金净亏 442 U，持股成本 184.42

到期 170，浮亏 1,500 U，减掉权利金净亏 1,442 U

8/ 例子三，持仓卖 covered call

手里有 100 股 xNVDA，市值 18,768 U，卖出 1 张行权价 192 的看涨，收 29 U，冻结 100 股

到期在 192 以下，白拿 29 U，股票还在
到期 200，按 192 交割，本来能多赚的 800 U 没了，算上权利金少赚 771 U

9/ 风险就两句话

买方最多亏掉权利金，但归零是常态
卖方赚的是权利金，承担的是按行权价接货或者交货的义务，价格走反多少都得履约

10/ 首期标的是代币化股票：xNVDA、xSNDK、xMU、xCRCL、xMSTR、xNBIS、xSPCX、xGOOGL

text:
This is going around as a funny copy pasta, but a lot of people don't understand why Predictive Allocation is such a game changer for on chain LPs and $AERO.

Let's say you're an on chain LP and you think that oil is about to go crazy over the weekend because of rumours that the US will start bombing Iran.

You hop on to Uniswap and see that OIL/USDC has only been paying 30% APR because very little trading had occurred the week prior. The LP fees are backwards looking. You could deploy some capital now, but then you risk only getting paid higher LP fees briefly before wicking out of range.

Then you go over to @aeroxyz and see that OIL/USDC is paying 100% APR in $AERO emissions. The reason is because sAERO allocators are betting that the OIL pairs will have crazy volatility/volume on the weekend right alongside you, and so they've directed their votes to those pools predictively to capture that fee share.

But markets are efficient, so what ends up happening? LPs from UNI pull their capital and move it over to Aero until the rates normalize. 

Aero enables emissions to be directed as a forward looking bet rather than displayed as a backwards looking snapshot. This means Aero will attract more liquidity when organic market forces deem it's actually needed, which means tigher spreads, which means more volume routed through Aero, which means more fees for sAERO stakers.

This advantage only gets magnified by more RWAs coming on chain when there are earnings reports and other pre-defined catalysts for volume. sAERO allocators have an economic incentive to dynamically adjust emissions to attract the deepest liquidity before it's actually needed; this is a mechanic that other AMM designs simply can't replicate.

text:
AI Agent 想替你订房，但很多人打开 Airbnb，只是想在上班的时候，假装自己已经放假了。

Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky 在最新财报电话会上，分享了一组很有意思的数据：

Airbnb 每天约有 50 万笔预订，但来自 AI Agent 的流量仍然微不足道。

用户平均会浏览几十套房源、25 张以上的照片。

90% 的用户会主动联系房东。

80% 的旅行者喜欢自己做旅行攻略。

Airbnb 的流量高峰，竟然是工作日早 9 点到下午 5 点。

最后这个数据尤其有意思。

当整个 AI 行业都在琢磨如何让 Agent 替人类完成任务时，Airbnb 发现，很多用户其实很享受完成任务的过程。

上班摸鱼的时候看看海边的别墅，比较一下巴黎的公寓，想象自己下个月住在哪里。这些看似低效的行为，本身就是旅行消费的一部分。

AI Agent 想消灭的摩擦，可能恰恰是用户愿意花时间享受的东西。

这也揭示了消费级 Agent 一个容易被忽略的问题，技术公司习惯把消费者的每一次点击都理解成需要优化的操作，却忘了人类有时候就是喜欢逛、喜欢纠结、喜欢做白日梦。

对 Airbnb 来说，真正值得思考的或许不是如何让 AI 更快地完成预订，而是当预订不再需要人参与时，用户为什么还要打开 Airbnb。

毕竟，旅行的快乐，有时候从上班摸鱼看房源的那一刻就开始了。

text:
$AStock has opened the door to its product ecosystem. The next thing it needs to prove is whether other projects are willing to build businesses on top of it.

0x4c9b47dbd5933aa4574b2c27f82419e4dbbd0222 

AStock's Omni Launchpad recently officially opened to everyone. This is more meaningful than Jeremy Allaire's earlier “Very cool” comment because AStock has finally moved its previously announced cross-chain issuance, stock rewards, and liquidity mechanisms into public use.

My view on ASTOCK has become more positive compared with our previous analysis. It is expanding from a stock token protocol built around Arc into an issuance and asset rewards platform covering both Arc and Solana. This is not just a product launch. Attention from Circle's management is also increasing. Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire previously interacted publicly with AStock, and now the company's SVP of Marketing and Brand has also followed the project. These two signals together naturally make the market reconsider AStock's potential connection with Circle and the Arc ecosystem. However, following a project does not mean official cooperation or resource support. I would rather treat this as a positive signal of growing ecosystem attention.

What really deserves attention is what Omni brings to the table.

A token can now be launched simultaneously on Arc and Solana, with two separate liquidity pools and locked liquidity. Holders on Arc can receive stock token rewards, and there is no minimum ASTOCK holding requirement to launch or trade.

I actually think this design is important. AStock is not restricting access to its ecosystem to existing token holders. Instead, it wants to attract more issuers and traders through its products first, and then gradually bring them into the broader ecosystem. Solana provides an established memecoin user base and liquidity, while Arc handles USDC and stock asset rewards. The two chains now have the potential to complement each other.

Ferry is another component worth watching. Its previously announced mechanism allows users to stake USDC or SOL to participate in cross-chain capital operations. Through arbitrage, it aims to keep prices on both chains aligned. When the price difference between the two sides exceeds 5%, arbitrage bots can buy on the cheaper side and sell on the more expensive side, while participants have the opportunity to share the related returns.

If this mechanism can operate consistently, Omni will be more than just deploying the same token on two chains. It could create a genuinely liquid cross-chain market. Of course, the actual results will depend on Ferry's staking size, arbitrage execution efficiency, and trading depth on both sides.

The Points System has also officially gone live. Users can earn points by trading projects on Arc and Solana, launching tokens, bridging assets, and trading ASTOCK. It uses weekly rankings and a public leaderboard with five levels, requiring 100, 1,000, 5,000, 25,000, and 100,000 points respectively. Holding ASTOCK and staking in Ferry also increase the points earned from trading.

This mechanism is clearly designed to encourage users to keep using the platform instead of launching a token, trading once, and leaving. In particular, the additional points earned by ASTOCK holders and Ferry stakers begin to connect token holding and staking with platform activity.

However, the official team has explicitly stated that points have no cash value and are not tokens, so they should not be treated as a guaranteed airdrop. Their real value lies in whether they can establish lasting user habits rather than simply generating short-term trading volume.

Looking at the website data, the product mechanisms have already generated some actual activity.

In our previous analysis, the website showed approximately $61,704.76 in cumulative stock asset distributions to holders, 1,787 wallets participating in the latest payout, and approximately 78.03M ASTOCK burned, representing 7.80% of the total supply. The amount spent on buybacks and burns was approximately $10,437.07.

The latest figures have increased to $66,739.96 in cumulative distributions, 1,879 wallets in the latest payout, 78.2M ASTOCK burned, and $11,015.95 spent on buybacks and burns.

Between the two snapshots, cumulative stock distributions increased by approximately $5,035, the number of participating wallets increased by 92, and buyback and burn spending increased by approximately $579.

These figures show that the stock rewards and burn mechanisms are still operating. However, what I want to monitor next is the actual flow of funds over several consecutive days or even weeks, rather than relying on a single snapshot.

ASTOCK's value capture is also not limited to buybacks and burns. According to the previously published mechanism, the ASTOCK/USDC trading pool has a 3% Swap Tax plus a 1% Pool Fee. Part of these fees is converted into stock assets and distributed to ASTOCK holders proportionally to their holdings.

In addition, third-party projects on Arc can integrate AStock's stock rewards module, with 5% of each relevant reward distribution going into the ASTOCK reward pool.

This is where I see the real opportunity. If more projects are willing to route their fees through AStock, ASTOCK's potential demand will no longer depend entirely on its own trading volume. It could grow alongside the broader stock rewards ecosystem.

I think the market is beginning to price in the potential network effect created by this expansion: more projects launch on Omni, bringing new traders and liquidity; more users trade and bridge across chains, driving activity through the points, Ferry, and stock rewards mechanisms; and third-party projects integrating fee distribution could further increase actual demand for ASTOCK.

The attention from Circle's management also strengthens the market's expectations regarding AStock's position within the ecosystem. Its direction is closely aligned with Arc's focus on USDC, financial assets, and on-chain trading. This connection is worth watching, but it should not be counted as resources already provided by Circle.

The next catalysts are relatively clear. First, actual issuance and trading volume after Omni's public launch, along with user growth across Arc and Solana. Second, whether the Points System can generate sustained participation rather than short-term turnover driven purely by incentives. Third, whether Ferry's staking volume and arbitrage activity can expand over time.

Another important development to watch is whether AStock can attract more independent projects to integrate its stock rewards module, and whether the team's commitment to actively supporting the strongest projects launched on the platform translates into actual support. If these developments materialize, AStock could extend its value beyond its own stock trading product and into the broader third-party launch ecosystem.

The risks should not be ignored either.

Attention from Circle executives does not equal an official partnership, and having two liquidity pools across different chains does not automatically guarantee sufficient liquidity. Price discrepancies between the two chains, cross-chain execution, arbitrage capital, and underlying bridge security will all affect Omni's actual performance.

The Points System could also attract a large number of short-term traders who participate only for incentives. Once those incentives become less attractive, user activity may not remain at the same level.

Furthermore, stock rewards depend on actual trading fees. If trading activity declines, distributions will naturally decrease. The underlying Robinhood Stock Tokens provide economic exposure to the corresponding stocks, but they do not represent direct ownership of the listed companies. Risks related to the issuer, redemption, and regional regulatory restrictions still exist.

Overall, I believe ASTOCK's fundamentals have genuinely strengthened compared with our previous analysis, and this improvement is supported by concrete product developments.

Omni is now open, the Points System is operational, stock distributions and buybacks have continued to increase, and the additional attention from two Circle executives gives the market more reasons to reassess AStock's potential position within the Arc ecosystem.

But what I really want to see now is not which other Circle executive will follow ASTOCK. It is whether Omni can genuinely attract projects and users from outside Circle's ecosystem.

When a project with no direct connection to AStock is willing to use its issuance, cross-chain, and stock rewards infrastructure, and continues generating trading fees through the system, that is when its network effect will truly begin to take shape.

Generate fees from stock trading.

text:
全网都看傻了。

好莱坞编剧都不敢这么编的商战谍战大片，居然真真切切发生在了皮衣教主身上。

英国《金融时报》和《纽约时报》今天刚扒出一份重磅绝密备忘录。
美国情报部门赫然认定：63 岁的英伟达 CEO 黄仁勋，居然跟一名涉嫌为中方收集情报的女间谍，保持着极其亲密的“浪漫恋爱关系”。

女主角的名字叫 Alice Huang，中文名黄乐。
明面上，她是新加坡算力公司 Megaspeed 的核心高管，更是在英伟达砸了 48 亿美元采购算力设备的超级大客户。
但美国情报机构一口咬定：这根本不是什么单纯的跨国商业往来，而是一场蓄谋已久的降维渗透。
女方涉嫌专门借着私人恋爱关系，贴身刺探英伟达下一代芯片的底牌，以及先进算力绕道出口的虚实。

整个硅谷当场石化。
老黄平时在公众面前，不是万年不变的黑皮衣，就是穿梭在台湾夜市里乐呵呵吃小吃。
谁能想到，这位全球 AI 芯片的神坛教父，私底下居然深陷跨国“美人计”的大网。

更要命的还在后头。
美国国会已经彻底坐不住了。
众议院三个核心委员会主席联名下达传票，勒令黄仁勋必须在 11 月 18 日亲赴国会山，参加闭门听证会，交代清楚两人的所有私交细节，并彻查英伟达的内部防谍机制。

芯片股这两天刚被美股暴跌砍得鼻青脸肿，灵魂人物又被扣上了通谍绯闻的紧箍咒。
链上的赌狗们更是看热闹不嫌事大，连夜把“黄乐”和“教主恋爱”的各种 Meme 币冲上了天。

63 岁的老黄以为自己遇到了千亿芯片的知己大客户，美国情报局却在门外把恋爱日记记了个底朝天。
科技树点到顶峰的尽头，这世道玩的依然是最古老的人性游戏。

text:
Elon Musk 解释自己为什么身家 8000 亿美元还在继续工作

ELON MUSK：

“年轻时，我在试图弄明白人生的意义，结果陷入了存在主义危机。感觉生活好像毫无意义。

我读过的宗教文本没能说服我。于是我开始读哲学家的书。

尤其是在年纪很小的时候，读德国哲学家的书要小心。对缓解抑郁没什么帮助。

小时候读叔本华和尼采，只会让一个人的头脑更混乱。

后来我读了《银河系漫游指南》。Douglas Adams 想表达的是：

真正的问题不是我们不知道答案，而是我们连正确的问题都不知道该怎么问。

要问出正确的问题，我们需要一台比地球还大的计算机。

宇宙其实就是答案本身。
但问题是什么？

意识越成长、越扩散，我们就越有可能问出关于宇宙的正确问题。

人类必须成为多行星文明，甚至是多恒星文明。也许只有这样，我们才能真正理解这里到底在发生什么。”

老老实实交钱用了 7 个月，被当成诈骗犯连坐秒杀！号没了，美区账户里 700 刀余额瞬间变成死钱……

今天看到这个真实翻车惨剧，所有拿美区 Apple ID 订 Claude 的人都得倒吸一口凉气：

一个老哥为了图省事，一次性往美区充了 700 刀礼品卡慢慢扣。用了大半年突然被弹 KYC，国内证件交上去直接永封。

绝望之下去求助：“我换个新邮箱注册 Claude，还能用同一个 Apple ID 扣这 700 刀吗？”

底下实测老哥的回复直接把人推进冰窟窿：

❌ “别挣扎了，App 提示‘已绑定过 Claude’，里面的钱彻底卡死，想花都花不出去！”
❌ “我 4 月封了一个号，10 月拿这个 Apple ID 给正常用了 20 天的干净小号充值，充完 1 小时连 KYC 都不弹，秒封！苹果账号早就被拉黑了！”

很多人不知道为什么会连坐：
苹果内购的 Original Transaction ID（原始交易凭据）是终身绑定的。只要这个苹果账号关联过任何封禁记录，不管你换新邮箱、新节点还是新设备，只要一扣款，Anthropic 的反作弊系统就能顺着交易凭证顺藤摸瓜，直接就地枪决！

这就是黑产疯狂利用漏洞恶意退款后，留给正经用户的终极核弹：

▪️ “毒 Apple ID”诞生：礼品卡充进去根本退不出法币，一旦被封，余额直接变废纸。
▪️ 账号资产永久污染：被封过 Claude 的苹果号直接变成“封号诱饵”，给谁充谁死。
▪️ 无处申诉：苹果不管第三方封号，Anthropic 不认中国身份，两头吃哑巴亏。

💡 血泪提醒：

1. 立刻停掉往美区 Apple ID 里大额屯余额的习惯！
2. 被封过的苹果账号，坚决不要拿去给任何新号充值送人头。
3. 生产力工具别赌侥幸，老老实实找一张海外真实实体卡走独立正规通道，才是唯一的活路。

你手里被封过 Claude 的 Apple ID，后来成功充给其他 AI 工具过吗？还是全部连坐了？

To everyone holding $INTC through this recent sell-off: I know the pullback has left many of you sitting on significant paper losses. Let’s look at the key levels I’m watching for potential entries. The losses are only on paper until you sell—and price can turn.

My previous chart analysis marked $129.04 as a key high, and that level was reached. $INTC then broke into a new downward move and later retested $127.30, the neckline of the bearish pattern—the “exit line” I was watching. The decline that followed confirmed that setup.

Here are the levels I’m watching now:

$46.87 and $45.37 are potential buy zones on this projected move down.
If price falls through those levels with a sharp increase in selling pressure, $38.95 is the neckline of $INTC’s larger long-term pattern, and a major level I’d watch for a potential entry.

If selling volume continues to contract as price approaches $46.87–$45.37, those levels may offer an earlier entry. If the decline accelerates and breaks below them, $38.95 becomes the deeper level to watch.

I’ll be watching how price and volume behave around each zone. A level alone doesn’t guarantee a bottom, so I’ll wait for the chart to confirm.

The story keeps getting crazier. To recap everything that has been reported so far: 

- The US intelligence community discovered that Jensen Huang, the CEO of the largest company in the world, was sleeping with Alice Huang, a Chinese spy and an executive at Megaspeed. (FT)
- Multiple independent investigations have concluded that Megaspeed is likely a Chinese cutout, which helps Chinese companies access AI chips or circumvent export controls. (NYT and Bloomberg) 
- The US intelligence community also concluded that Alice Huang’s goal was to convince Jensen to lobby the U.S. government to loosen export controls on advanced AI chips. (NYT)
- The intelligence community relayed this information to “a small group of top US government officials” earlier this year. (FT)
- Over the last year, Jensen Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to loosen export controls on advanced chips. @BISgov has done so, not only by permitting the export of H200 chips to China, but also not enforcing export controls that would have required a license for exports of the most advanced Blackwell chips to Megaspeed and Southeast Asia.
- Although @CommerceGov leadership was presumably briefed on this information by the U.S. intelligence community, @BISgov has taken no actions to tighten controls on Megaspeed or Southeast Asia. 
- Megaspeed remains a preferred cloud partner of Nvidia, and continues to receive Nvidia Blackwell chips despite employing a Chinese spy who reportedly is romantically engaged with the CEO of Nvidia. 
- Tens of billions of dollars worth of AI chips have been exported to Southeast Asia this year alone, and Malaysia and Singapore are now two of the four largest importers of AI chips in the world. 

What is going on here??? We need answers. The question of who gets the most advanced AI chips in the world is literally the defining strategic question of our time. And not only does it seem like the MSS may be directly influencing the debate on export controls in the United States, but also @CommerceGov is refusing to listen to the warnings of the IC on this issue. What is a POSSIBLE good explanation for why Megaspeed is still receiving chips? Why is there not a license requirement for AI chip shipments to all of Southeast Asia? This is beyond strange at this point. 

The fallout from this story will be massive. Obviously, the motivations underpinning Nvidia’s policy views opposing export controls must now all be questioned. But also, how did @BISgov sit on this information and has still taken no actions? We need answers.

传统的 RLHF 和硬性规则完全封不住这种行为，Anthropic 做的一组对照实验，直接把传统安全观砸得粉碎：

author: myanTokenGeek
quoted_text:
但凡会做一点开发的人，去年刚刚见识到 coding agents 的威力时，谁能没有一种“利器在手，天下我有”的兴奋呢？但是现在一年已经过去了，好像并没有人做出什么牛逼的新产品。不但如此，就算做出来的产品也没什么人用了。说起来，后者可能是更严重的问题。所有好的产品都是在跟用户的交流过程中磨出来的。别人不用，你得不到反馈，当然也就做不出好的东西？

这究竟是因为开发者们刚刚拿到 AI 工具，暂时还没有完全掌握其最佳用法，只是个短期的问题，还是有可能成为长期现象。

我最近用 AI 做了十几个微型的、专事专用、用后即抛的 Apps，深受触动。我现在的判断，这个人人可以做软件，却一个产品都卖不掉的局面，恐怕不是一个暂时现象，也不是因为这一届 developers 能力不行，或者这一届用户钱包不鼓，而是会成为 AI Agent 时代的一个基本底色。

究其原因，是因为用户使用软件是为了解决问题。在过去，用户自己没有开发软件的能力，只能由极少数具备专业能力的软件开发者开发产品。而这些产品为了适应更多用户需求，就必须尽量通用化。本来，开发者与用户之间就存在着心智模型差异导致的摩擦，用户用起这些软件来本来就不自然，哪怕是个电商购物、短视频 App，你也得学。而开发者为了通用化、可复用，还不得不把软件功能本身搞得很复杂。结果对于用户来说说是既不好用，也不好学。我们所熟悉的整个软件产业，其实是建立在这样一个社会分工的基础之上。

但是现在，人人都可以从自己的问题出发，通过跟AI的简单对话，就生成解决问题的App，这个分工结构被消除了。我要提醒各位的是，这种只为了解决当前特定问题的APP，开发起来是非常简单的。它的简单性不仅仅是因为问题本身非常特定，更是由于用户自己描述自己的问题，自己描述期待的使用方法，心智负担极轻。它既不需要学习，也不存在理解障碍。它可以快速产生一次性的软件，只解决当前的问题，完全不考虑复用性、通用性的问题。甚至一天之后，用要解决下一个类似的问题，用户会优先考虑完全重新开发一个，效率要比把昨天的 App 拓展一下来的更高。

如果我设想的这种情况成为常态，那可能意味着，现在很多人，甚至包括很多 AI 专家所讨论的那些话题，比如如何创建 AI Agent 时代的软件开发过程、如何开发AI Agent产品，甚至现在很火的所谓 AI工程，很大程度上都是过渡性的话题。人们只需要一些基础软件部件，比如基座模型、数据库、云、通讯协议、区块链等等。其他需求都可以按需制造、现需现开发，一次性使用，用完即弃。软件工程师和产品经理过去花了大量时间和精力，用来掌握如何同时应对多个用户、多种不同场景的需求，产生可复用、通用的软件设计，并且通过极度严谨的工程方法控制产品质量。未来这些能力将大幅贬值。

text:
AI 记得越多越好吗？Anthropic 让 Claude 玩宝可梦测了一下：记了 413 个文件的只拿到 1 个徽章，只记 9 个文件加一张总表的拿到 4 个。

这篇讲 Claude 的记忆怎么设计，普通人也用得上的有四条：

1. 随时能查到的别记。记得多的那个，把身上有多少钱、人在地图哪里都写进记忆，这些屏幕上本来就有、还一直在变。到后面它有一段 17 步里建了 6 个文件、删了 9 个，游戏一步没走
2. 告诉它记忆是干嘛的，别规定怎么记。给强模型定「只记失败」，记忆带来的提升大半没了；老一点的模型反而要提醒，让它先读记忆、再验证自己的猜测，分数接近翻倍
3. 定期拿原始记录核对。他们叫「做梦」：空闲时对照对话记录检查笔记，记错的改掉。宝可梦里有一条把建筑位置记反了，不改的那次在同一个地方掉回去三次、始终没过山；改完就穿过山洞到了下一座城
4. 每次自动带上的那一层要小。Claude Code 的自动记忆每次只读 MEMORY.md 的前 200 行或 25KB，它只当目录用，细节放在下面一层

我自己的 AI 记忆也是这么管的，前两条是踩坑踩出来的：
· 10 月发现 AI 给我写的记忆里有具体项目、粉丝数，这些过几天就变了。现在只放身份、做事方式和偏好，项目进度要用的时候现查
· 我说「记忆都换成新的」，AI 把几家的记忆全删了。我要的是更新，不是清空
· 总目录压在 80 行以内，一条记忆一个文件；11 月 2 日让 AI 整体过了一遍，找出 19 处前后矛盾的规则，改掉了

text:
Soviet firefighters attempted to gain access to the most sensitive areas of the US embassy during a fire emergency in August 1977.

On the night of August 26th, a fire broke out on the 8th floor of the embassy building in Moscow. The crowded embassy was stuffed with papers and had ancient electrical wiring, and an errant spark was believed to be the cause. The fire soon climbed up to the 9th and 10th floors.

Soviet firefighters arrived quickly and began scaling ladders to fight the blaze, while the nighttime embassy staffers evacuated. Some eyewitnesses noticed that among the later groups of firefighters to arrive were several men wearing brand new uniforms and gear, apparently on their first emergency call.

This was not the first time the KGB had attempted to gain access to the embassy posing as firefighters. A previous fire at the medical dispensary building had been brought under control by the Marine Security Guard detachment when suddenly the water pressure died. As the fire grew out of control, they were forced to allow Soviet firetrucks into the compound, at which point the water pressure suddenly returned, and the fire was suppressed.

The building was evacuated except for two men; CIA case officer Gardner Hathaway and a senior noncommissioned officer of the Defense Attaché Office. Hathaway correctly surmised that the blaze represented a tremendous opportunity for Soviet intelligence. He stood guard outside of CIA’s offices on the 7th floor, just one level below the flames, with a .38 revolver in hand, steadfastly refused to allow the firefighters to enter their offices.

The blaze substantially consumed the 8th and 9th floors although the building was ultimately saved from complete destruction. When staffers went to work cleaning up afterwards, they found steel safes had been opened and emptied. Others had hammer marks on the doors. Large batches of classified documents and equipment were missing completely, not reduced to ash as expected. The fire represented one of the many battles of wits between the KGB and US government during the Cold War.

#embassy #kgb #firefighting #clandestine #coldwar

text:
TLA+ has been incredibly useful, even on brownfield project, for turning implicit state machines into explicit specs where the entire flow can be tested and verified.

There is a deep relationship between user journey, UX flow and formal specification that has an enormous amount of value to slop code.

I wanted something more programmer-y and Typescript-y, and I came across Quint. It's highly agent friendly and seems to be maximally useful for this new paradigm of programming.

https://t.co/Tj1K7ZnrU7

Quint is high level, like TLA+, and doesn't formalize Typescript functionality. So underneath that, lower level, is Lemmascript.

https://t.co/iNBPVfkeSM

This lets you markup your Typescript with contracts.

The combination of these two things makes Typescript feel more like a compile time checked language, more verifiable, stronger guarantees, and it finds different kinds of bugs than AI generated unit tests seem to.

It's not a magic bullet but damn it does seem to improve code quality a lot.

And the agents can rapidly iterate against it.

I think we're gonna see a lot more of this kind of thing popping up, especially in interpreted languages like TS and Python.

I'd recommend using Quint when you're just modeling your application and flows (although I've been installing it into an existing project with good results) and then telling your agent to add Lemmascript in the build phase.

text:
Andrej Karpathy:

“A 1B model can be much more effective than most current LLMs.

90% of current models waste a ton of capacity and money on remembering stuff that doesn’t matter.”

here is his 5 core thesis about Small LLM’s:

1. the intelligence was never the knowledge. Strip the memorized internet, keep the reasoning. What’s left is the cognitive core, and it’s small.

2. the core might fit in ~1B params. Maybe less. “Plenty of room at the bottom.” We’ve been paying for a library when we needed a brain.

3. size stopped being the bottleneck. What makes an agent work is the tools it can call and how tight the feedback loop is, not parameter count.

4. intelligence lives in the system, not the weights. A raw LLM is a CPU with no OS. Small core + good harness > giant model alone.

5. you can own it. A model on your hardware is one no one can rate-limit, price-hike, or deprecate on you.

in 12 months the gap between teams shipping on-device and teams paying per-token frontier bills won’t be capability.

TwIL an 8.8B model at 90%+ of frontier isn’t a benchmark flex.

It’s the thesis Karpathy’s been repeating all year, made real.

study more on this below ↓

For years, the AI industry has focused on building the most capable model, regardless of the cost required to run it.

The story keeps getting crazier. To recap everything that has been reported so far: 

- The US intelligence community discovered that Jensen Huang, the CEO of the largest company in the world, was sleeping with Alice Huang, a Chinese spy and an executive at Megaspeed. (FT)
- Multiple independent investigations have concluded that Megaspeed is likely a Chinese cutout, which helps Chinese companies access AI chips or circumvent export controls. (NYT and Bloomberg) 
- The US intelligence community also concluded that Alice Huang’s goal was to convince Jensen to lobby the U.S. government to loosen export controls on advanced AI chips. (NYT)
- The intelligence community relayed this information to “a small group of top US government officials” earlier this year. (FT)
- Over the last year, Jensen Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to loosen export controls on advanced chips. @BISgov has done so, not only by permitting the export of H200 chips to China, but also not enforcing export controls that would have required a license for exports of the most advanced Blackwell chips to Megaspeed and Southeast Asia.
- Although @CommerceGov leadership was presumably briefed on this information by the U.S. intelligence community, @BISgov has taken no actions to tighten controls on Megaspeed or Southeast Asia. 
- Megaspeed remains a preferred cloud partner of Nvidia, and continues to receive Nvidia Blackwell chips despite employing a Chinese spy who reportedly is romantically engaged with the CEO of Nvidia. 
- Tens of billions of dollars worth of AI chips have been exported to Southeast Asia this year alone, and Malaysia and Singapore are now two of the four largest importers of AI chips in the world. 

What is going on here??? We need answers. The question of who gets the most advanced AI chips in the world is literally the defining strategic question of our time. And not only does it seem like the MSS may be directly influencing the debate on export controls in the United States, but also @CommerceGov is refusing to listen to the warnings of the IC on this issue. What is a POSSIBLE good explanation for why Megaspeed is still receiving chips? Why is there not a license requirement for AI chip shipments to all of Southeast Asia? This is beyond strange at this point. 

The fallout from this story will be massive. Obviously, the motivations underpinning Nvidia’s policy views opposing export controls must now all be questioned. But also, how did @BISgov sit on this information and has still taken no actions? We need answers.

author: hnshah
quoted_text:
One of my favorite research practices I learned at @inkandswitch is “preinfusion”. The term comes from espresso (I believe @pvh coined it?) - and the original meaning is that you have a lower pressure soak before you turn on the high pressure and pull the shot. 

The way it works at the lab is that you patiently let a cluster of ideas slowly form and develop, meandering somewhat in the background, and you lay the groundwork to work on them more seriously… before starting an intense high-pressure sprint. Could be a few months of part-time preinfusion before a hardcore 3 month project.

This really helps avoid the problem where you’re trying to sprint, but you don’t actually have enough clarity to know where to run.

I think this applies in many other contexts. Preinfuse before trying to write an essay. Preinfuse before raising money for a company. A slow and patient preparation can enable swift follow through.

民主党这招停建算力中新其实就是权利洗牌，利益再分配，但不只是两党，还有居民和大企业之间的博弈。

以德州为例，Hinojosa的官方主张是暂停新增项目，直到州议会建立居民保护措施，并重新处理税收优惠，并没有提出永久关闭所有数据中心。

而且早在 9 月 21 日 共和党州长 Abbott就实际下令暂停相关许可，等待审计，并要求项目承担电力基础设施成本。

所以这次变化其实是借着中期选举把原来民众对政府牺牲底层利益挤占资源补贴企业扩张的势头叫停了，未来会让数据中心自己掏更多钱去升级电网，掏钱买更贵的水，交更多的税。

这样原来靠发行企业债扩张的算力中心的运营成本就进一步上升，加上融资成本本就不低，及终端收入始终无法覆盖成本，才导致了对资金链断裂预期下的股价恐慌式崩盘。

而且即使算力中心建设是暂时性叫停也会有巨大的影响，长鑫追赶很快：第六代平台完成工程样片验证，预计年底将首代 4F² DDR5 RDIMM 产品送样、HBM3E已经小批量投产。关键追赶期下美方的叫停无疑是给竞争对手一个绝佳的赶超时机，进一步压缩了美韩系存储未来的盈利预期。

那么综合来看，对于闪迪持仓我大概会等情绪性的超跌反弹之后再走，这样可以少亏甚至不亏，但在两党博弈接近达成之前，可能不适合长线持仓了。

> you win a trade, the protocol's pool pays you
> you lose, the pool keeps your money
> except losers receive something in return

> PAPER.

> lose $1, initially receive up to 100 PAPER
> stake PAPER to earn usdc distributions
> no team allocation
> no vc allocation
> no premine

> basically, people could deliberately lose money, farm PAPER, and potentially earn more back through staking rewards.

> yes, losing money became a strategy.

> october 1
> papertrade publishes its launch roadmap
> phase 1: trading goes live
> phase 2: open contract access
> phase 3: builder integrations
> phase 4: PAPER becomes transferable

> no exact date for phase 4.
> but transfers are supposed to be enabled eventually.

> remember that part.

> october 8
> pre-deposits open
> roughly $138m deposited by 11,465 addresses before launch

> october 10
> trading goes live
> tvl crosses $100m
> traders deliberately lose money to mint PAPER
> staking rewards start flowing in usdc
> notional trading volume explodes

> papertrade becomes the talk of CT.

> but on the same day, something goes wrong.

> a trader moves eth's reference price on hyperliquid
> exploits how papertrade prices its trades
> withdraws ~$1.28m more than deposited

> the team tightens trading limits.

> the wallet later loses another ~$450k, while the team says most of the gains were returned through other accounts.

> that last claim couldn't be independently verified.

> meanwhile, the founders are selling pants.

> 100 custom pairs
> $2,000 each
> $200k in gross sales
> reportedly sold out in 40 minutes

> ser.

> october 15
> papertrade's numbers are ridiculous.

> ~$1.11 trillion in cumulative notional volume
> traders collectively down ~$54.1m
> PAPER stakers have received ~$45.6m in usdc

> defillama records roughly $43m in reported revenue after five days.

> papertrade is now ahead of hyperliquid and pumpfun on short-term revenue.

> but there's something unusual about these numbers.

> most of that revenue isn't ordinary trading fees.
> it's surplus from traders losing money to the protocol's pool.
> and some of those traders are deliberately losing to farm PAPER.

> still, the payouts are real.
> early farmers are making serious money.

> everything looks great.

> until october 19.

> nine days after launch.

> the founders announce they have no current plans to make PAPER transferable outside the contract.

> wait.

> remember phase 4?
> the one that said transfers would eventually be enabled?

> yeah, about that.

> PAPER holders can't freely transfer their tokens
> can't sell them on the open market
> can only stake and collect future usdc distributions

> and it gets worse.

> the issuance curve is changed
> new PAPER minting becomes proportional to existing supply
> earlier holders face gradual dilution
> short-term trading fees are also adjusted

> imagine deliberately losing $50k to farm a token.

> then finding out the team no longer plans to enable the exit you were expecting.

> so why change the rules?

> the founders say making PAPER transferable creates a bigger attack opportunity.

> manipulate prices on hyperliquid
> drain money from papertrade's pool
> simultaneously profit by shorting PAPER elsewhere

> given the launch-day exploit, that risk isn't imaginary.

> but here's where it gets interesting.

> jez acknowledges that the team knew some of these problems were unresolved before launch.
> he thought they'd have more time to solve them.

> except people had already deposited millions and spent real money farming PAPER.

> october 20
> lookonchain examines the 25 traders with the biggest trading losses.

> 21 are still underwater after staking rewards
> only 4 are profitable overall
> the group has claimed ~$11.6m in usdc rewards

> october 21
> the updated rules go live.

> oct 19 tvl: ~$63.8m
> oct 21: ~$45.8m
> oct 25: ~$32.3m

> november 6

> tvl: ~$24m
> down roughly 77% from its $102m peak

> volume had already started falling before the rule change, so blaming the entire decline on that decision wouldn't be accurate.

> but the numbers since haven't exactly inspired confidence either.

> and remember all that revenue?

> defillama's cumulative figures now show:

> ~$71.2m in reported protocol revenue
> ~$60.1m from liquidity pool surplus
> ~$11.1m from trading and liquidation fees

> where did it go?

> ~$65.7m allocated to PAPER stakers
> ~$5.5m allocated to the developer fee recipient

> that doesn't mean the founders personally pocketed the full $5.5m.

> and stakers collectively received far more.

> but the winners and losers weren't evenly distributed.

> some early farmers made millions.
> others still haven't recovered what they lost.

> meanwhile, the official account has gone quieter.

> PAPER remains non-transferable.

> and the farmers who are still underwater have to depend on future usdc rewards to recover their money.

> from a protocol that's now doing a fraction of its launch-week activity.

> the irony?

> people paid real money to lose trades
> losses helped generate millions in revenue
> developers received substantial fee allocations
> the team reversed the token transferability plan
> and some farmers are still waiting to break even

> to be fair, papertrade hasn't disappeared.

> the protocol still works, rewards are still being distributed, and the founders have given a technical reason for the change.

> so calling it a confirmed exit scam would be a stretch.

> but the roadmap reversal happened.

> and people who farmed under the original expectations are the ones living with it.

> a protocol that made losing money look profitable.
> a token that was supposed to become transferable.
> millions generated before the plan changed.

> if transferability was already an unresolved risk before launch, why promise it in the first place?

> soft rug or an experiment that went horribly wrong?

Elysium launches Sunday and I’ve been going through the top memes onchain. All are high risk, of course, but here’s what I found on the ones I’d keep an eye on.

- $CHAMELEON (~$2.6M) is the cleanest one I checked. The creator holds nothing, the liquidity sits with Montra, whose launcher has never pulled liquidity from any coin, and the biggest early wallets haven’t sold. The risk is it’s 3 days old and the early wallets are holding a lot of the supply.

- $BLOB (~$1.9M) has the best holder base on the chain, at 1,700+ holders over 11 days. The risk is that @the_smart_ape says the dev got 9% of the supply for $230, after already selling $50K worth.

- $EACCAT (~$3.7M) is the biggest, and the liquidity is on Montra too. But 8 wallets bought in back-to-back blocks about 30 seconds after launch, and @the_smart_ape says it’s one operator running 32 wallets. So the risk is in these early wallets. Doesn’t mean anything nefarious, but just be warned.

- $EGG (~$250K) is the newest runner. The creator holds nothing, the liquidity is on Montra and nobody sniped the launch. The risk is that its biggest holders all bought during this week’s run, so they’re sitting on profits from a big move in one day.

And all of this is extremely high risk. Kinetiq hasn’t confirmed the chain or published the official bridge yet, these pools are thin, and once you bridge in, getting back out to HyperEVM takes a waiting period. Only put in what you’re fine being stuck there for a while.

Raising funds for a film is one thing. Getting a project ready to enter the market is another.

@IPXExchange calls this Project Graduation.

Here's how it works:

A project must meet its production funding target and IPX market-pairing target.

Once both are achieved:

- Production funds move into milestone-based escrow.
- The project's token market opens against $IPX.
- Creator and team token vesting begins.

The interesting part? Funds don't simply land in the creator's wallet. Production payments remain tied to approved milestones.

This adds structure and accountability to entertainment financing.

Would you trust this model over traditional crowdfunding?

text:
昨天跟几个二级做市商朋友吃饭，他们提到一个近期比较明显的变化：和几个月前相比，散户的交易行为发生了转向。从偏做空转向偏做多，更愿意直接买现货，并喜欢提前埋伏一些币。

这种转变，很大程度上受近期妖币造富效应的影响。AKE、LAB 这类币种接连走出极端行情，在短时间内制造出一批暴富案例，让市场重新进入妖币横飞的阶段。散户在看到这些案例后，风险偏好明显上升，更倾向于主动布局而不是观望或做空。

但问题在于，经过几轮妖币的反复收割后，散户整体的资金体量已经肉眼可见地缩水。当散户这个主要收割对象的弹药明显不足时，收割的重点便开始发生转移，从散户转向大户，尤其是那些自认为掌握数据优势的聪明钱。

对做市商而言，聪明钱其实比散户更好收割，只是方式不同。散户主要是情绪驱动、信息滞后。而聪明钱则依赖自己构建的数据体系和交易逻辑。

问题在于，很多数据本身是可以被刻意制造或伪造的。做市商完全可以像渔夫设计陷阱一样，先让某些数据在前期反复验证有效，让聪明钱建立起这个指标可靠的认知，并据此敢下重仓。一旦仓位足够集中，再让数据突然失效，就可以把对方前期靠这个逻辑积累的多次利润一次性归零。

换句话说，聪明钱引以为傲的数据优势，在很多情况下可能只是做市商提前布好的局。前期数据有效，是为了让他们敢上仓。后期数据失效，则是为了完成收割。而这一次收割的效率，往往远高于对散户的零散收割。

Everything has changed.

text:
我发现很多人做山寨币，研究了半天市值，却从来没研究过自己能不能把钱卖出去。

一个币流通市值1亿美元，听起来挺唬人。

你拿10万U进去，觉得自己不过是个小散户，怎么可能影响市场？

可真等你想卖的时候，才发现买盘薄得跟纸一样。

挂单卖，半天没人接。

市价砸，价格直接往下掉。

最难受的是，账户明明显示赚了50%，真正卖完可能连30%都拿不到。

这就是很多山寨币特别容易让人产生的错觉。

市值是拿最后成交价乘以流通量算出来的，不代表市场里真有那么多钱等着接盘。

尤其是一些小币，平时成交量看着挺热闹，但里面有多少真实买盘、多少做市商提供的流动性，普通人未必看得清。

涨的时候，几笔买单就能把价格顶上去。

跌的时候，买盘突然撤走，你才发现所谓的支撑，原来是个临时工。

所以我觉得，研究一个山寨能涨多少，远远不够。

还得研究它跌的时候有没有人接，自己准备卖的时候，市场能不能消化自己的仓位。

更现实一点，仓位越大，越不能只盯着K线上的利润。

有些币适合拿几千U玩，拿几十万U进去，性质可能就完全变了。

别光想着买进去能赚多少钱，也想想赚到钱以后，谁来接你的筹码。

毕竟账户里的浮盈只是数字。

真能卖出来、落进口袋里的，才算数。

quoted_text:
X AI ALGORITHM UPDATE 🚨

X updated their open source algorithm yesterday and the early likes matter even more now. Small accounts should focus on: writing posts people hit like on and read till the end (so write to be read)

tl;dr:

- X's open source code got new scores on Nov 5, the first change in 3 weeks
- likes: 0.66 → 0.708 (highest yet)
- time spent on a post: 0.006 → 0.0075
- tapping into a post: 0.3 → 0.274
- opening a video: 0.02 → 0
- new rule: AI replies may get flagged under big accounts as "llm slop" and may not reach the person's notifications 

lesson learned: a tap isn't the win anymore. Someone staying and liking is.

full details:

- The new numbers

Up: likes 0.66 → 0.708, time spent on a post 0.006 → 0.0075, shares 2 → 2.118.

Down: tapping into a post 0.3 → 0.274, staying 10+ seconds after a tap 0.4 → 0.385, opening a video 0.02 → 0.

"Not interested" got a bit harsher, -52.27 → -53.07.

Copy link, replies, quotes, DM shares and follows didn't move.

X didn't explain any of this. It's just what the code says now.

(I check the open source algo daily with Claude and share updates with you)

- Look at where this has gone in a month

In early October a like was worth 0.5. Now it's 0.708.

Time spent was 0.004. Now it's 0.0075, nearly double.

A tap was 0.3 and it's going down.

Every change points the same way. X keeps paying more for people who stay.

- Why that matters if you're small

My read: you can't win on big numbers, but you can win on the people who do see your post. If they stay and like it, that counts for more today than it did last week. And those early likes also decide which new post gets the extra push.

- Video and your profile

X also switched on two new guesses in its ranking: how long someone keeps watching after they open a video, and how long they spend on a profile after tapping it.

I can't tell you what those are worth. The only file that lists them is out of date, so I won't guess a number.

My read: opening a video dropped to 0 the same day because X cares more about people who keep watching. So make the first seconds count, and make your profile worth sticking around on.

- A new rule for replies under big accounts

X runs an AI check on replies under accounts with over 250K followers. Flagged replies can get a label that lasts 14 to 30 days. One of the flags is literally called "llm slop" (AI slop, as I read it).

That part isn't new. This is: X's rules now say a labeled reply or mention doesn't reach the person's notifications unless they follow you.

Grey badge accounts and accounts X rates as highly credible skip this label. Small accounts get no such pass.

I can see the rule, I can't see if every notification goes through it yet. Either way, write your own replies.

- What didn't change

Your new posts still get their extra push in the first 2 hours and first 200 views, and they still don't get cut first.

Here's a recap of what you should be doing:

- likes just hit 0.708, the most they've ever been worth
- each second someone spends on your post is worth 25% more than last week
- staying 10+ seconds after a tap earns 0.385 on top of the tap
- reply in your own words, under big accounts especially
- make your profile worth a visit, X now guesses how long people spend there
- for video, hold attention early, just getting the open now scores 0
- being read to the end also helps X find you new readers
- originals from accounts below 50K can jump to around spot 16
- early viewers liking it is what wins that lift
- your first 2 hours and 200 views are the window, so publish when your people are online
- the biggest single number is still 20, for someone copying your link
- quotes, DM shares and replies earn 5 apiece
- back and forth between mutuals is worth 20, so follow back your regulars
- strangers only get shown your originals
- the 1st like and the 32nd like each open another route to new people
- a second post of yours in the same feed drops to 62%, so make one count
- the video lists want clips over 10 seconds
- +4 when a post is likely to earn you a new follower
- your pinned post can affect the whole account, so take a look at it

What you should NOT be doing:

- pasting AI replies under big accounts, "llm slop" is a real flag at X
- copy-paste replies, a duplicate label means they never get notified
- chasing the tap, it's down to 0.274 and falling
- off-topic posts, one likely "not interested" costs -53.07
- a video that only gets opened earns nothing for the open
- publishing at 3am burns your 2 hour window
- relying on replies and reposts to reach new people, they stay with your followers
- getting an insult label, non-followers won't see that post at all
- low quality and misinfo labels bring a warning, and non-followers can't like or share
- adult media in 3 of your last 5 posts gets the whole account labeled
- X rechecks videos for hidden content at 64 and 512 likes
- piling your replies under a big account's post can sink your own score
- one label on the account and non-followers stop seeing you
- a link to a badly rated site in your pinned post risks a 7 day label
- reusing your own wording word for word risks the copypasta flag
- pairing a low quality link with tags of strangers looks like spam to X
- engagement bait gets labeled no matter how big you are
- posting several in a row, they fight each other for the same feed
- hashtag stuffing does nothing
- counting on bookmarks, they're worth 0
- expecting For You to show a post past 48 hours

the age of decadence 

in the fate of empires (1976), sir john glubb studied 11 civilizations and concluded they typically last about 250 years (roughly ten generations). 

they rise through the ages of pioneers and conquest, peak in commerce and affluence, then slide into the age of intellect and finally the age of decadence.

he defined decadence as 'a moral and spiritual disease, resulting from too long a period of wealth and power, producing cynicism, decline of religion, pessimism and frivolity.'

the united states declared independence in 1776. two and a half centuries later, the parallel is hard to ignore.

text:
The interesting thing about AI agents is that as a theoretical matter, their inference can kind of run anywhere. AI is one of the few areas of technology that isn’t *as* sensitive to latency back to the user. 

Long running agents are now going to be the norm, which means it’s ok to send off work to an AI factory somewhere and that work can essentially be largely done within that remote data center and a final result spit back to the user. The data can pass into these systems in an encrypted manner, be combed through by agents, and then disregarded right after. 

And because the economic value of the task is so high relative to the latency sensitivity (eg getting back $500 in value from an automated task, but it takes an extra second to return), you don’t have to have the inference to be particularly close to the user. 

Also, because inference is a temporary process with no sensitive data needing to be stored long term where the inference is happening, you can effectively treat AI factories as ephemeral systems, changing some of the data residency dynamics slightly.

Combined, this means you have more flexibility in where you can begin to deploy AI data centers. This is both a huge economic opportunity for the states or countries (or space) that want to take advantage of this fact. And it’s a loss to the states or countries that decide to forgo the opportunity.

我想再补充两点，把话说透。

第一，AI coding agents 在大幅度提高软件开发供给侧的生产效率的同时也大幅度地消灭了对软件的需求。

第二，现在研究怎么用 AI 开发成功软件产品，以及所谓的  AI Engineering，可以类比于一战时用飞机侦查对方重机枪阵地，摸清敌情之后，本方骑兵冲锋。
author: myanTokenGeek
quoted_text:
但凡会做一点开发的人，去年刚刚见识到 coding agents 的威力时，谁能没有一种“利器在手，天下我有”的兴奋呢？但是现在一年已经过去了，好像并没有人做出什么牛逼的新产品。不但如此，就算做出来的产品也没什么人用了。说起来，后者可能是更严重的问题。所有好的产品都是在跟用户的交流过程中磨出来的。别人不用，你得不到反馈，当然也就做不出好的东西？

这究竟是因为开发者们刚刚拿到 AI 工具，暂时还没有完全掌握其最佳用法，只是个短期的问题，还是有可能成为长期现象。

我最近用 AI 做了十几个微型的、专事专用、用后即抛的 Apps，深受触动。我现在的判断，这个人人可以做软件，却一个产品都卖不掉的局面，恐怕不是一个暂时现象，也不是因为这一届 developers 能力不行，或者这一届用户钱包不鼓，而是会成为 AI Agent 时代的一个基本底色。

究其原因，是因为用户使用软件是为了解决问题。在过去，用户自己没有开发软件的能力，只能由极少数具备专业能力的软件开发者开发产品。而这些产品为了适应更多用户需求，就必须尽量通用化。本来，开发者与用户之间就存在着心智模型差异导致的摩擦，用户用起这些软件来本来就不自然，哪怕是个电商购物、短视频 App，你也得学。而开发者为了通用化、可复用，还不得不把软件功能本身搞得很复杂。结果对于用户来说说是既不好用，也不好学。我们所熟悉的整个软件产业，其实是建立在这样一个社会分工的基础之上。

但是现在，人人都可以从自己的问题出发，通过跟AI的简单对话，就生成解决问题的App，这个分工结构被消除了。我要提醒各位的是，这种只为了解决当前特定问题的APP，开发起来是非常简单的。它的简单性不仅仅是因为问题本身非常特定，更是由于用户自己描述自己的问题，自己描述期待的使用方法，心智负担极轻。它既不需要学习，也不存在理解障碍。它可以快速产生一次性的软件，只解决当前的问题，完全不考虑复用性、通用性的问题。甚至一天之后，用要解决下一个类似的问题，用户会优先考虑完全重新开发一个，效率要比把昨天的 App 拓展一下来的更高。

如果我设想的这种情况成为常态，那可能意味着，现在很多人，甚至包括很多 AI 专家所讨论的那些话题，比如如何创建 AI Agent 时代的软件开发过程、如何开发AI Agent产品，甚至现在很火的所谓 AI工程，很大程度上都是过渡性的话题。人们只需要一些基础软件部件，比如基座模型、数据库、云、通讯协议、区块链等等。其他需求都可以按需制造、现需现开发，一次性使用，用完即弃。软件工程师和产品经理过去花了大量时间和精力，用来掌握如何同时应对多个用户、多种不同场景的需求，产生可复用、通用的软件设计，并且通过极度严谨的工程方法控制产品质量。未来这些能力将大幅贬值。
