昨天最火的新闻是，习近平在中南海选区怀仁堂投票站参加区人大代表的投票。要不是有这一出戏，我都忘了中国还有选票。说一些往事：

当初我一激灵，在微博宣布参选人大代表，一群认识的、不认识的人跟进，包括散人、夏商、曹天、吉四六，深圳有个还有十几天才满18岁精神小伙也宣布参选。看把国家给急的，我身边突然出现一帮热心肠的朋友和一些神秘的人，包括有个现在中国如日中天的投资人要给我打一笔钱。我拒绝了，理由就不解释了……

包括某著名国师也很热情地与我联络，给钱给资源。多好的资源多好的机会啊，那不飞天了吗。可是我说“家教不允许啊”，于是不识好歹一步步走上另一条路。

有一天跟散人聊起他为此丢了工作，他说的倒挺淡：反正也不想干了。那些天，吃个饭，旁边都跟着十几个国宝国安，还听说有位参选人私生活被录了像。这哥们，太不小心了吧。

那些事写出来，荒诞，苍茫，古怪，刺激，全是好文学作品。

其实当时我参选的理由一点不高大上，只是看不惯倪萍批评有人不爱国。WF？！你个拿着枫叶卡的人骂我们不爱国。

爱国，成了心照不宣的权贵游戏。所以刚刚看到习近平强调，选举人大代表是是国家政治生活中的一件大事，要践行全过程人民民主，坚持党的领导、充分发扬民主、确保选举风清气正，确保选出人民满意的代表。

我在午后阳光下，哈哈哈大笑三声。最珍贵的不是历史，而是合订本。

算了，看我的专治抑郁的脱口秀节目吧：https://t.co/QoU8Lbhbpb

我的油管第14期：《习近平能不能永久连任》

电影《黑社会》之龙城风云里，邓肥说：“黑社会也是有权力制约的，不能一人独大，要平衡。几十年的规矩改了，社团的叔父们一定会很不舒服。”

可中南海的叔父们，要么找马克思和毛主席报到去了，要么住进了秦城的豪华一居室，剩下的只能在特勤局监视下种种花、养养鸟、听听戏……

如果在一家公司，他必须是董事长、总裁、CEO一肩挑；在帮派，他必须是帮主、执法长老、执棒长老一肩挑。未来权力排序不是一号人物、二号人物、三号人物……而是一号人物之下，全是打工仔。中南海权力体系不再是金字塔形状，而是倒T字形。

习近平会永久连任吗？

党指挥枪VS枪杆子里面出政权，其实是孪生兄弟。谁当党老大，必须是枪老大，否则必然被拿下；谁是枪老大，就是党老大，你有枪别人就听话。

没有蓝玉没有年羹尧没有袁世凯，整个军队像玩乐高一样拆了拼、拼了拆。谁手里都凑不齐一支完整部队，没有中间管理层，瓜子二手车，没有中间商赚差价。

会上演《南山的部长们》吗？会有玄武门之变吗？张又侠老部下会拎着两把板斧劫法场吗？谁是“铁帽子王”？

世界上有个独裁者困境：如果指定接班人，接班人很快成为权力副中心，独裁者权力就被稀释；如果不指定接班人，死后又要被清算。

谜一般，习主席到底有没有指定接班人——指定早了，就成了刘少奇，晚了，就成了华国锋，能力强，就是林彪，能力差，就是王洪文。毛泽东临死前一年才让华国锋当副总理兼公安部长。汉武帝临死前，才立刘弗陵为太子。康熙临终病榻前，才传位给雍正，传位诏书放在“正大光明”牌匾后面，一点都不正大光明。

《威权统治的政治学》统计：从1946到2008年，303个非正常下台的独裁者，被民众起义推翻的只有32个，10个里面不到一个。而这303个非正常下台的独裁者里，205个是被统治集团内部的人赶下台的，占三分之二以上。独裁者真正防的不是街上的民众，而是会议室里的小弟。

最刺激的是突尼斯的布尔吉巴，他独裁三十一年，精心挑选最信任的本·阿里当接班人。可一个多月后的某天夜里，本·阿里把七个医生召到内政部，让他们签字证明——老领导精神失常了。

有医生不干，本·阿里一拍桌子“老子数到三”……医生马上服软。自从得了精神病，我的精神好多了。第二天老领导被软禁在一处大宅子里，一直到死去。

未来漫长岁月，总有天意，所谓天意，就是每个人的心意。

text:
有朋友问，为什么MEXC交易所被美国制裁了？

其实没那么糟糕，MEXC并没有被列入制裁名单。今天11月6日，FinCEN（金融犯罪执法局）发了一道命令，依据《打击俄罗斯洗钱法》第9714条，禁止美国的金融机构处理任何来自或流向MEXC Global的资金转移（包括加密货币）。命令在《联邦公报》刊登三十天后生效，没有截止日期。所以不算冻结资产，也不是宣布这家交易所破产，但确实在效果上把它从美国的金融体系里切了出去了，所以影响也是实实在在的。

按财政部的说法，MEXC 2018年成立，注册在塞舌尔，没有牌照，2021年5月到2026年5月，MEXC处理了至少一百六十亿美元跟规避制裁、网络犯罪等非法活动有关的资金。其中约十五亿美元与规避对俄制裁有关，两亿多美元是直接跟美国、欧盟、英国制裁的实体往来；俄罗斯交易所Garantex 2022年4月就被美国制裁了，四年多以后，到今年6月，MEXC还在跟它和它的后继平台Grinex做交易。伊朗那边，约十亿美元是跟四十多家伊朗加密交易机构直接往来，其中两千多万美元涉及伊朗央行和伊斯兰革命卫队。

最值得拿出来的，是一个落差。财政部说，MEXC有反洗钱和客户核验的制度，用户条款里也写明不许伊朗、朝鲜等地的人使用，可控制有严重缺陷，这些地方的人和机构照样用上了。写在条款里的禁止，但没有执行。一笔来路不明的转账没拦住，是一种情况；一个早已被公开点名的对象，四年多还在往来，是另一种情况。前者可以说难，后者就得问，是拦不住，还是没去拦。合规真正被检验的时候，往往就是它开始挡生意的时候，拒掉一笔交易，就少一笔收入。

美国关不掉一家塞舌尔的交易所，但它可以决定，自己管得着的银行、支付机构和加密公司，不再跟它往来。写Binance被盗那篇我说，区块链能保证的，是签过字的事一定会发生，它保证不了的，是签字的那一下是谁的意思。这一回是同一道题的另一头，链能保证钱一定到账，保证不了收钱的那一头是谁。这一段，链不替任何人问，只能平台自己问。平台如果自己不问，就会有别人来替它问，而且下手要重得多。

当然，这不是仅仅针对加密货币的。这道命令属于财政部8月启动的一项行动，名字叫Operation Economic Outcast，目标是切断伊朗政权和革命卫队的经济命脉，同一天，财政部还制裁了八家加拿大的货币兑换商。用的也是打击俄罗斯洗钱的法条，挂的是对付伊朗的行动，Bessent的话说得很直接，“要么支持伊朗政权，要么接入美国金融体系”。

按惯例，我还是要为普通用户问一句。MEXC的声明说，正在跟法律和合规团队研究这道命令，愿意跟FinCEN建设性地沟通，已经启动对反洗钱和制裁控制的独立审查，平台运营正常，用户资产安全。它没有否认，也没有反驳那些数字。“运营正常”说的是今天，三十天后，跟美国机构有关的入金、出金和稳定币通道会不会受影响，是用户最想知道的，声明里没有说。写Musk和赵长鹏那篇我说，用户保住本金，不是恩赐。这一次也一样，资产安全是本分，说清楚命令生效以后用户的钱怎么进、怎么出，也是本分。

钱从哪来，到谁手里，这道题，链无法替任何人答。所以平台得答，不能拿“去中心化”免掉。

text:
World Bank LEARN programme in Ukraine (P504171): school bomb shelters are a payment trigger.

Up to $65m is released only as more students and teachers gain access to built or rehabilitated shelters (target 32,000). Another $25m was tied to shelter-subsidy rules that put hub schools stuck in remote or hybrid mode in high-need regions first. An independent verification agency checks the results.

The baseline, from the World Bank programme paper: at end-2024 nearly half of Ukraine's schools still relied on online or blended learning, mainly because of safety concerns and missing shelters.

The envelope now stands at $737m (Education Ministry, 13 Oct). The Finance Ministry reports $60m for education arrived January–October.
Classrooms back in session are a daily public test of whether the state can protect normal life. Who should verify shelter access closest to the front line?
Sources: the World Bank LEARN programme paper for P504171 (30 Jun 2025), https://t.co/9HQwHUV9dQ on the Education Ministry's 13 Oct meeting with the Bank, and Ukrinform citing the Finance Ministry (3 Nov).

text:
Anthropic 的研究员，正在把研发 Claude 的工作交给 Claude 自己。

而且交出去的速度，比很多人想象得快得多。

《华尔街日报》最近刊登了一张图，标题非常夸张：「AI 领域最聪明的人认为，这是世界上最重要的一张图」。

图里是 Anthropic 内部的研发数据。

2026 年 3 月，Claude 只能主导约 1% 的模型研发工作。到了 8 月，这个数字已经涨到 26%。如果算上深度协作，Claude 已经参与了超过 90% 的研发工作。

这里的「主导」，不是帮研究员写几行代码。

比如一条数据管道坏了，工程师只需要把故障信息交给 Claude，它就能自己查日志、定位问题、修改代码、运行测试，最后把结果交给人类审核。整个过程，研究员不需要一直盯着。

更有意思的是，这张图本身也是 Claude 帮忙做出来的。Anthropic 用 Claude 分析了约 1.5 万项内部研发任务，再让 Claude 判断每项工作的自动化程度。

AI 在研发下一代 AI，也在参与评估自己研发 AI 的进度。

当然，这仍然是 Anthropic 的内部自评，目前还没有任何一类研发工作实现完全自主。

但我觉得，这张图真正重要的地方，不是 AI 已经能替研究员完成多少工作，而是它正在改变 AI 公司的研发组织方式。

过去，一家实验室的研发速度，很大程度上取决于它有多少顶尖研究员，以及这些人能同时推进多少实验。

但如果一个研究员可以同时指挥几十个甚至上百个 AI Agent，研发能力就不再简单地跟着人数线性增长。

模型越强，能承担的研发工作越多；研发推进得越快，又越有机会训练出更强的模型。

这才是递归自我改进真正值得关注的地方。

而且，这种变化未必需要等到 AI 完全自主研发才会发生。只要它能不断接管更多研发流程，整个实验室的迭代速度就可能被持续放大。

不过，这也意味着一个新的瓶颈：当 AI 可以同时推进成千上万个实验时，人类还有没有能力判断哪些实验真正有效，哪些只是把错误包装成了进步？

下一阶段 AI 实验室之间的竞争，可能不只是比谁拥有最聪明的模型，还要比谁能把模型组织成最高效、最可靠的研发系统。

过去，AI 研发的瓶颈是有多少人能做研究。未来，瓶颈可能是有多少研究结果能被可靠地验证。

text:
老板是假的，律师是假的，只有打出去的 1.29 亿美元是真的。

美国检方刚刚起诉了三名外国公民，指控他们利用 AI 冒充企业 CEO 和国际大所律师，在全球实施了一场规模惊人的商业诈骗。

这伙人的作案手法，几乎可以写成一部商业谍战剧。

首先，他们会盯上企业财务部门，冒充 CEO 发来邮件，说公司正在推进一笔高度机密的交易，需要你协助处理。

如果员工想进一步确认？没问题，老板可以亲自给你打电话，甚至视频连线。

只不过，电话里的声音、视频里的面孔，都是 AI 模仿的。

接下来，「老板」会把你介绍给一家大型国际律所的律师，说他正在负责这笔交易。律师会向你解释交易细节，强调保密的重要性，再一步步引导你把钱汇进指定账户。

而所谓的律师，依然是同一伙骗子。

检方披露了一个非常有意思的细节：其中一名嫌疑人甚至准备了一份手写的《Lawyer Call》话术脚本，专门研究怎样扮演律师，以及怎样让受害员工不要向同事透露消息。

就这样，一家英国金融科技公司据称损失了约 1158 万美元，两家美国医院系统分别损失了约 483 万和 297 万美元。整个团伙涉嫌骗走超过 1.29 亿美元。

我觉得这起案件最值得关注的地方，是 AI 正在改变商业诈骗的基本单位。

以前的骗子主要伪造一个人的身份，现在他们开始伪造一整套商业关系。

CEO 负责下指令，律师负责提供专业背书，机密交易负责解释为什么不能告诉别人。每一个角色都看起来合理，每一个环节都像是真实企业的工作流程。

但这些原本应该相互验证的角色，实际上可能完全受同一伙人控制。

AI 降低的不只是伪造一张脸、一段声音的成本，更是伪造一套组织权威的成本。

过去企业强调「遇到大额转账，一定要跟老板本人确认」。但当老板的声音和面孔都能被复制，这条规则本身就开始失效了。

未来企业真正需要防范的，可能不是一个冒牌 CEO，而是一整套看起来合规、专业、保密，却从头到尾都不存在的商业流程。

有时候，最危险的不是员工不遵守流程，而是骗子比员工更懂这套流程。

注：以上案件细节来自美国检方指控，目前三名被告尚未被定罪。

text:
Anthropic 开始让 Claude 参与设计未来运行 Claude 的芯片了。

据《The Information》报道，Anthropic 组建了一支约 15 人的芯片团队，正在用 Claude 辅助设计定制 AI 芯片。据称，Claude 已经能明显缩短部分设计工作的时间。

有意思的是，芯片还没量产，Anthropic 就已经把这件事讲给了潜在 IPO 投资者听。

我觉得这里有个很值得关注的变化。

过去，AI 公司要变强，主要靠买更多芯片、招更多工程师。现在它们开始尝试用自己的模型，反过来提高研发芯片的效率。

如果这条路走通，就可能形成一个很有意思的循环：更强的模型帮助设计更高效的芯片，更高效的芯片又降低下一代模型的训练和推理成本。

当然，设计提速不等于芯片能成功流片，更不等于能挑战英伟达。芯片验证、制造、量产，都是完全不同的难题。

但对投资人来说，Anthropic 想讲的故事已经变了。

以前是「给我更多钱，我就能买更多算力，训练更强的 AI」。

现在开始变成「给我更多钱，我的 AI 甚至能帮我研发下一代算力」。

AI 公司最有想象力的商业模式，可能不只是把智能卖给别人，而是先用智能改造自己。

今天又在加密书屋群里聊及美利坚全盘翻蓝以后的 Clarity Act。

1/我觉得之前 Clarity Act 在众议院以超多数票通过，绝对足以说明至少短期内 Clarity 中承诺的那些基础保障是两党共识。
参议院没过是党争问题，不是共识破灭。

这点最重要的表现是 Robinhood 的 Layer 2。
Robinhood 的政策法律团队一定认为，现在去发一个打着去中心化名号的 Layer 2，可以让他们做一些之前法律限制无法做的事情，可以让他们赚一些之前无法赚的钱，能享受一些他们之前如果做了就会被追责的法律豁免。
这个传统金融套个去中心化区块链的壳子做监管套利的趋势，绝对还没有力竭。

2/民主党手握两院，川普系最值得攻击的点必然包含 Trump memecoin 和 World Liberty Financial 这俩。
这俩不被咬两年不太可能，期间也必定波及其他的加密项目。

3/Vitalik 24 年大选前撰文说反对根据 pro-Crypto 与否来投票。川普牛是我们行业走的弯路，一定要还债的。
群友说得更好：川普实际上表现出了加密市场最烂的一部分，而且他表示这套我玩得比你们好——不就是喊单拉盘么，球长也可以亲自做。
https://t.co/37q9jgQhkZ

4/我们整个行业本质上都高度寄生于监管套利这个核心概念上。
但监管套利的基础是民族国家对金融或者对所有可监管世界都越来越家长化，而这个家长化的尺度一定是会矫枉过正的。
监管套利是否可持续这个问题背后其实是现在的监管有没有超越正常合理范围，有没有监管造成的磨损比诈骗造成的磨损更大等等。
我自己作为右派，当然觉得监管造成的后果已经事实上更鼓励所有人都做巨婴，但显然我这个观点不是共识。
群友追问：如果接下来监管不让你套利呢？

5/反过来说，Airbnb 和 Uber 本质上也是监管套利。
且无论是因为当时的环境整体宽松，还是传统旅店业、出租车业已经烂透到不改不行，后面确实都变成监管退，而 Airbnb、Uber 进。
回到我们一开始话题的由头，Clarity Act 在众议院通过，本质上也是美国明确有加密货币行业进、而监管退的苗头。

6/21 世纪是家长式政府的世纪。
纽约或伦敦或任何中心化的金融体系本质上一直都在用效率换安全、用公民主体性换安全。而这个几乎一直是单向的流动，一直在让渡更多的效率和主体性。
经过 30 年的让渡，有没有让渡到一个夸张、离谱、矫枉过正的程度？

如果有，则加密行业现在做的向监管要空间、搞主权个人的无许可金融就是拨乱反正；
如果没有，这 Clarity Act 当时表现出来的共识就会在短期内崩溃。

这段讨论的部分背景详见：https://t.co/iZAqHSw4Lq

7/还有一个东西在显著复杂化问题的情况：AI 时代大规模的 Cyber security 攻击。
目前听说某个韩国加密交易所已经准备改为 T+1 提现了，连加密行业本身都在主动尝试让渡更多自主性和效率去换安全。
所以这种共识应该就很脆弱，甚至完全可以消散倒流。
所以要挑战臃肿、低效、僵化、腐朽的传统金融，则至少我们要不断证明，我们的行业足以提供以一个值得信任的、总体上美好的 counter offer。

UPDATE: Citizen auditors report that Burnet County began its hand-count audit today.

 The later deadline is not a prohibition on starting early.

 Under §127.201(b-2), when a statewide risk-limiting audit is performed, the hand-count audit must begin no later than the first business day after SOS certifies the RLA’s completion. 

Contact your county elections office and ask:

 • When will the hand-count audit begin, and where is the public notice? 

• Which polling locations and mail-ballot precincts were selected?

 • Which ballot containers have been opened, and were seal numbers and resealing documented? 

• Were observers present, and how can candidates and their representatives observe?

 An important change: in-person ballots are now audited by polling location; mail ballots remain audited by precinct. 

The in-person audit should not require opening unrelated containers simply to retrieve selected resident precincts’ ballots. 

Watch the process. A matching hand count checks the tabulation of the paper presented; it does not, by itself, establish that the paper is original and lawfully cast.

text:
昨天跟几个二级做市商朋友吃饭，他们提到一个近期比较明显的变化：和几个月前相比，散户的交易行为发生了转向。从偏做空转向偏做多，更愿意直接买现货，并喜欢提前埋伏一些币。

这种转变，很大程度上受近期妖币造富效应的影响。AKE、LAB 这类币种接连走出极端行情，在短时间内制造出一批暴富案例，让市场重新进入妖币横飞的阶段。散户在看到这些案例后，风险偏好明显上升，更倾向于主动布局而不是观望或做空。

但问题在于，经过几轮妖币的反复收割后，散户整体的资金体量已经肉眼可见地缩水。当散户这个主要收割对象的弹药明显不足时，收割的重点便开始发生转移，从散户转向大户，尤其是那些自认为掌握数据优势的聪明钱。

对做市商而言，聪明钱其实比散户更好收割，只是方式不同。散户主要是情绪驱动、信息滞后。而聪明钱则依赖自己构建的数据体系和交易逻辑。

问题在于，很多数据本身是可以被刻意制造或伪造的。做市商完全可以像渔夫设计陷阱一样，先让某些数据在前期反复验证有效，让聪明钱建立起这个指标可靠的认知，并据此敢下重仓。一旦仓位足够集中，再让数据突然失效，就可以把对方前期靠这个逻辑积累的多次利润一次性归零。

换句话说，聪明钱引以为傲的数据优势，在很多情况下可能只是做市商提前布好的局。前期数据有效，是为了让他们敢上仓。后期数据失效，则是为了完成收割。而这一次收割的效率，往往远高于对散户的零散收割。

text:
I would *love* to sit down with everyone who came up with this report.

I was the independent person responsible to do patch analysis for very large companies and facilities for many years. By that I mean I was at one point the single person responsible for pulling the $12+ million dollar switch for several Forbes 100 companies. Matter of fact that's how most of my old school followers know me, I used to dump the work in real time here on Twitter to get more customers (it worked).

So what does that mean?

Patch Tuesday is a great example, it used to drop 10AM PST Tuesday.

I would have an approx 50 page report Friday EoB to customers covering EVERY patch, ease of exploitation, profile the discovery team or person behind it, use in the wild, IoCs, weaponization likelihood in the next 24h, 72h, 7 days, 14 days, 30 days. No AI. Just IDA, DarunGrim, BinDiff, some tools I wrote and a dream. I would be in the office, Tuesday leave Friday, yes, that's correct, no home, straight working. I performed this service from 3 different companies to various customers. Sometimes it was with a select team, most of my career it was solo.

So what was the $12m switch? Well that was the cost it would be for just one of my customers to push out an emergency patch that wasn't in their already accepted patching procedures. That cost was electricity costs, server down time, service availability impact, employee costs, testing etc.

I was the person that said: this patch needs to be pushed and that break glass needs to happen due to impact being greater than X million in a 72h period.

I made that specific call maybe 11 times, in the 14 years that I did this service and I got that call twice. 

The last time I got the call wrong was one of the TCP.sys icmp vulns, ping of death style. I failed to account that another vendors vulnerability would come out to put it to shame and be far more easier to exploit with a PoC.

The other time I got it wrong was exploitation happened about 96h instead of 72h.

The science to get this precision is hard, I got lucky a few times. What I will say is the goal of the attackers, what is at risk, and level of sophistication that attackers will use completely vary from target to target. Also there's a ton of this exploitation data is simply not visible, a lot of this data isn't public and requires lots of embedded resources, sources, and detailed tracking.

In almost all cases and scenarios during those 14 years: 0days are not kings, it's your trash exploits (auth bypass, file upload, hash leaks etc) that are 2 to 6 years old that got forgotten, unpatched, suddenly exposed to the Internet, or bridged over by a contractor that lead to massive incidents over and over.
author: thegrugq
quoted_text:
For two decades, writing the exploit was the bottleneck in a cyberattack. AI made that step cheap, and patching hasn't gotten faster:

- On average, attacks went from landing 63 days after disclosure in 2018-19 to 7 days before it in 2025

- A working exploit went from a skilled person's month to a few hours of machine time

- The median time to fully fix a known-exploited bug rose to 43 days

a16z's @asaf_ez and @steph_zhang expect a long, expensive worm era, hitting hardest where systems can't update fast: hospitals, schools, small water systems.

"When attacking is nearly free, attackers no longer need to want a target."

Full piece from Asaf Ezra and Steph Zhang: https://t.co/8L3D9mnL44

text:
Ordering food from a Google ad? Read this first.

Researchers just found 820 fake ordering sites copying 35 US chains: Jimmy John's (404 clones), Firehouse Subs, Jersey Mike's, Chipotle, Dave's Hot Chicken, Waffle House.

They look real because they almost are. Each one loads the real restaurant's site live, with the real menu, real prices, real cart, and the padlock saying "secure". Only the payment box is swapped.

What happens next:
- You enter your card
- You see "card declined, try another" or "enter the code your bank just texted you"
- A person on the other end uses that code to push a charge through on your card
- You get sent to a different chain's real site. No food ever comes

They spread through at least 47 Google Search ads run from 46 different advertiser accounts. Google pulled those, but 367 of the sites were still live on Nov 4.

Stay safe:
- Skip the ads at the top of search. Use the app or type the address yourself
- Check the domain before paying. 808 of the 820 end in .delivery
- Got "declined" right after entering a bank code? Stop, and check your bank app for charges you didn't make

text:
One Ample NFT could earn boosted staking rewards again and again, across different users.

During Ample Protocol's staking audit, Zealynx found that NFT ownership was checked only when a position opened. The boosted reward was then stored permanently.

A holder could lend the NFT for one staking transaction, take it back, and repeat. `closePosition()` never checked ownership again, so every position kept the boost.

Ample fixed the Medium finding by making the final reward depend on NFT ownership when the position opens and when it closes. Zealynx verified the remediation.

text:
Airbnb 的 CEO，给自己开了一家 AI 公司，然后从 Airbnb 买走了一部分技术。

据 The Information 报道，Brian Chesky 正在个人出资运营一家由自己控股的 AI 实验室。Airbnb 最新披露，这家实验室向 Airbnb 支付了约 710 万美元，用于收购部分知识产权和补偿相关费用。

更有意思的是，Airbnb 的 CTO Ahmad Al-Dahle 也持有这家实验室的股份，并为它提供服务。

作为交易的一部分，Airbnb 获得了未来投资这家实验室的权利，以及内部使用其部分技术的许可。

这笔关联交易已经获得独立董事特别委员会批准，程序上有相应的治理安排。

但我觉得，真正值得关注的不是 710 万美元，而是一个更微妙的问题：

当一家上市公司的 CEO 认为 AI 是未来，他为什么选择在上市公司之外，另起一家自己控股的公司？

这背后其实涉及 AI 时代一个越来越重要的利益分配问题：技术在谁的公司里开发，知识产权归谁，未来的股权增值又由谁享有？

过去，创始人创办公司，投资人购买股份，大家分享同一家公司的增长。

现在，创始人可能一边经营上市公司，一边用私人资本押注下一代技术。

一旦后者成为真正的增长引擎，上市公司的股东和创始人，未必还坐在同一张利益分配表上。

AI 不仅在重塑商业模式，也可能在重塑创始人与股东之间的利益边界。

每个人在币安都只会有一个UID，且是独立的，并不存在撞号。我理解你的感受，从联系我开始到现在，全程我和4个员工跟踪了前因后果。
我简单描述一下背景：您把币安的钱转到币安（泰国），正常这属于跨站转账，需要用地址或者二维码，但你在转账过程中在币安直接输入UID转账，虽然我们有二次确认环节，但你没有仔细看。你发现转错后，直接找了我。我本人和4个人的团队一直在协助，第一时间帮忙冻结了这笔钱，但因为这个收到钱的持仓用户并不活跃，我们也在反复联系对方，但对方没有响应。我们做了应该做的，甚至设身处地考虑你打错了钱会着急，所以尽可能帮忙。
对方并不是犯罪，是您打错币，如果对方坚持不退只能我们客服介入谈判。你着急，我们建议让你通过报警执法介入，我们再协助沟通。但你在泰国报警，您在您希望收款的泰国报警要求币安主站把另外一个国家的币安用户的资产直接划拨给你，这不符合执法流程，报警应该在你希望找的用户国家所在地而不是泰国。
之前处理过很多打错币的情况，大额打错几千万美金，也是我们及时拦住帮忙追的，而且当时用户坚持不退，也是我们协助谈判，最后到双方能接受的范围和解。
我理解你的难处，团队也一直在跟踪进展，得到的就是这篇长文，我们会继续联系另外一个用户协商，但你打错币这事儿，在泰国报警确实帮不上忙，那是你的钱想去没去成的目的地。
最后提醒大家，币安土耳其，币安泰国，币安美国等本地法币交易平台是独立平台，并不共享账号系统，日常转账提币时请仔细检查地址和UID。

作为一位meme玩家，如何用20u六天之内赚到6500u呢？对于像我一样的没有跟单的普通人来说，这听起来似乎很难，简直是个奇迹，但并非不可能，我的确做到了，而且你只需要一部手机加一个冷静的大脑。
如果现在你的账户只有20u，兄弟，首先放弃一切十倍百倍幻想，你当下要做的只是让它翻倍，你的第一个目标是50刀。
这是你到达6500u中最难的阶段，但请你战胜恐惧，说实话在我回撤到只剩20刀的时候，对市场的恐惧几乎占据了我的大脑，那是我最后的入场资格了，如果亏完，我应该要滚回去打工了，我非常的沮丧，但好在我不是第一次归零了，所以我很快调整了我的心态，将20u分成了3u 5u，5u，7u这样的四份，抛弃一切杂念，静静等待那个属于自己的底部机会，因为你的资金有限出手机会有限，所以你一定不能追高，你的击球区，几乎只有内盘，我认为只有三种
第一个：8-20k的叙事流盘子，而且这里的8k和20k一定要是支撑位，买红不买绿，这里我讲一下我的观点，我认为bsc是分流派的，不同流派的kol们小角度互不接盘，所以你选的叙事角度如果不够大，那就注定不会有人来合力来帮你搞射它、他们更大概率是开一个新的，然后捆绑拉到20k，所以这种角度我们直接忽略，而这种角度大多出现在抖音叙事，很多人觉得抖音叙事简单易懂，但其实是最难的那一类，充斥着捆绑，组局，浇给，喊单割韭菜，在这里我要提醒的另一点是，如果一个盘子刚出来，3s拉到20-25，谨慎，兄弟，这个时候不能上，仔细去看它的叙事，是否值得这个价格，很可能下一秒一根红色柱子就会砸到10甚至8k，这是最容易亏钱的一种内盘
你要找的是那种一眼看上去不仅能发射，还能200k的盘子，然后在最多20k时买入，如果超过20，请你多思考一遍再做决定，然后发射出本，静静等待市场看懂它，如果并没有像你的预期那样发展，果断走弱离场，不要去当一个倔强的小孩，你只有20u，你没有资格。
第二种：阴谋盘，是的你没听错，阴谋盘一定要玩，也可以叫庄盘，特点是kol底部几乎全体卖飞或者没上车，你的位置一定要低，注意那些一出来拉到30k左右然后回调到10k，并没有死掉的盘子，时刻注意它异动，特别是应用类，或者某个税率或者底池不同与普通meme的猫猫狗狗，我建议多去扫描即将发射的盘子，隔一两分钟就扫一眼目前全部的，你几乎能一眼看出来哪些突然动了，然后思考要不要上一点，这种盘子由于底部筹码都在庄手里，如果它想做会拉到很高，但也伴随着剧烈的洗盘，拿不住是正常的，不要追求吃满，吃一段就足够了。
OK第三种：7k以下的蝴蝶社区盘，这种很难判断，似乎只有赌它是不是真的社区，我暂时没想到总结经验的方法，我大多凭借直觉或者盘感去判断，但我能确定的一点是，你如果要买一定要趁早，便宜的筹码会给你带来更大的容错率，我在他们那里赚到钱很多次，等我有空仔细思考一下再写出来，相信任何事情都有规律。
其实写到这里，我自己也觉得这是一件几乎无法复刻的事情，我自己重来一遍也大概率失败，20-6500，我为我自己感到骄傲的同时，更多多是感谢市场给了我机会，赋予了我运气，我能做的只是写一点我的经验，今天开了蓝v，目的是和更多志同道合的高手交流经验，往后我应该还会发表很多自己的看法，也欢迎每一位朋友和我交流，希望每一位看到这个帖子的meme玩家，在离开这个市场时，都是因为你赚够了不想玩了，而不是因为亏完了，感谢大家，感谢市场

text:
Your Claude memory file is probably making it dumber.

Anthropic just published how Claude's memory actually works, and they tested it on Pokémon Red:

- Sonnet 3.7 saved everything: 413 files in 225 folders. It earned 1 badge
- Fable 5 saved only what it couldn't see on screen: 9 files plus one global.md. It earned 4 badges
- Opus 5.5 kept a few short notes and beat the game

What they found:
- Tell Claude what memory is for, not strict rules. Forcing "only record failures" wiped out much of the gain
- Claude Code only loads the first 200 lines or 25 KB of MEMORY.md. Anything below that never makes it into the session
- Longer instruction files make Claude follow them less
- "Dreaming": letting Claude reread its old sessions to fix wrong notes. On a 350,000-file company archive, accuracy went from 13% to 48%

The fix takes 2 minutes: open your CLAUDE.md or MEMORY.md, cut it under 200 lines, and delete anything Claude can already read from your code.

https://t.co/P78CmdFTnG

"메모리가 잘되길 바란다. 그런데 이번 상하이 출장 이후로는 확신이 없다."

(하필 같은 주에 미·중·한 메모리주가 같이 무너지면서 논란은 더 커졌고요.)

자...이 상황을 쉽게 정리하면 이렇습니다.

1. 상하이에서 메모리 가격이 내년 3분기부터 꺾일 수 있다는 전망을 구체적으로 들었다

2. 강세론자인 그가 반박해 봤지만, 끝내 납득하고 말았다

3. 그 이유는 "앤트로픽·OpenAI의 다음 매출 엔진(ARR)은 뭐냐"는 질문에 답할 다음 서사가 없었기 때문이다

1번은 사실 시장도 어느 정도 인정하는 분위기입니다.

10월 낸드 계약가가 21개월 만에 처음으로 상승을 멈췄거든요.

DRAM은 아직 사상 최고지만, 오르는 속도는 확실히 느려졌고요.

그래서 저는 진짜 문제는 3번이라고 봐요.

가격이 언젠가 꺾이는 건 다들 압니다.

문제는 꺾인 뒤를 받쳐줄 다음 수요 이야기가 구체적으로 없다는 것.

그런데 여기서 좀 의아한 지점이 있습니다.

Jukan은 Citrini에서 앤트로픽의 다음 엔진을 고민할 기회가 누구보다 많았던 사람입니다.

심지어 본인 후기에서도 대안으로 AI4S(과학용 AI)를 직접 언급했어요.

결론은 "당장 돈이 되긴 어렵다"는 회의론이었지만...

앤트로픽과 바이오 쪽 흐름을 누구보다 가까이서 볼 수 있었던 사람이 회의적이다?

저는 이 지점이 이번 논란의 핵심이라고 봅니다.

자, 여기서부터는 저의 관점입니다.

지난 분기, 거의 모든 AI 기업이 학습에서 추론·에이전트로 선명하게 방향을 틀었습니다.

앤트로픽은 Claude Code와 Claude Science

메타는 Muse

SpaceX는 Grok Bot.

모델을 "얼마나 똑똑하게 만드냐"에서 "얼마나 일을 시키냐"로 넘어간 거죠.

그럼 그들의 다음 질문은 하나로 좁혀질 겁니다.

"어디에 일을 시켜야 가장 큰 돈이 되느냐"

앤트로픽은 그게 코딩이 아니라 의료·바이오라고 좁히고 있는 것 같습니다.

이유는 세 가지입니다.

① 누가 이 AI를 막을 수 있을까

지금 AI 규제 압력은 크게 두 갈래입니다.

1. 일자리를 뺏는다.

2. 위험하다(생물무기 같은).

코딩 에이전트는 사실 첫 번째에 정면으로 걸립니다.

"개발자 일자리 뺏는 AI".

유권자에게 불편할 수 있는 서사죠.

그런데 의료로 오면 같은 모델이 "병 고치고 병원비 줄이는 AI"가 됩니다.

이건 압도적으로 표를 얻는 서사입니다.

(미국은 의료비가 굉장히 비싸니까요)

규제하는 쪽이 오히려 막기 어려워집니다.

신약 개발을 막는 정치인이 되고 싶은 사람은 없으니까요.

두 번째 갈래도 흥미롭습니다.

생물무기 공포는 언뜻 바이오 AI의 최대 리스크처럼 보이죠...??

그런데 저는 이게 거꾸로 쓰일 수 있다고 봐요.

"최상위 모델은 밖에 풀지 않고, 검증된 우리 워크플로와 실험실 안에서만 쓴다."

공포가 닫힌 생태계의 명분이 되는 겁니다.

규제가 효능과 안전에 집중될수록, 그 규제 자체가 진입장벽이 되고요.

그럼 그 닫힌 생태계에 한 번 들어온 고객은 나갈 수 있을까요..??

② 한 번 들어오면, 나갈 수 있을까

코딩은 오늘 Claude Code를 쓰다가 내일 다른 도구로 넘어가도 코드는 그대로 남습니다.

갈아타기가 굉장히 쉽죠.

(SpaceX가 @cursor_ai 를 인수한 것도 같은 과점에서 고민할 수 있습니다)

어째든 토큰은 결국 원자재 가격 싸움으로 갑니다.

(어쩌면 이미 원자재 그 자체인지도 모르겠어요)

제약은 다릅니다.

FDA에 제출하는 데이터를 다루는 시스템은 '검증'을 받아야 합니다.

한 번 검증받은 시스템을 바꾸면 처음부터 다시 검증해야 하고,

진행 중인 임상 신청까지 흔들릴 수 있어요.

이게 얼마나 강한지는 이미 증명된 사례가 있습니다.

제약 소프트웨어 회사 Veeva.

대형 제약사가 Veeva에 쌓인 임상 문서를 다른 곳으로 옮기려면 진행 중인 신약 신청과 FDA 데이터 무결성 지적을 각오해야 합니다.

전환 비용이 '몇 년치 규제 리스크'로 계산되는 구조.

AI가 이 검증된 워크플로 안으로 들어가는 순간, 강력한 락인이 생깁니다.

사실...앤트로픽이 조용히 깔고 있는 순서도 정확히 이겁니다.

(이건 Jukan이 저보다 훨씬 더 잘 이해하고 있을 거라고 생각해요)

Claude Science 출시(모델이 아니라 '워크벤치'라고 스스로 못 박음)

→ 생명과학 해커톤으로 빌더 확보
→ 연구 프로젝트 50개에 크레딧 지원, 논문으로 검증
→ 생명과학 인수·투자 담당자 채용

Claude Code가 개발자의 터미널을 가져갔다면, Claude Science는 과학자의 연구실을 가져가려는 거죠.

다들 Claude Science에 큰 관심이 없지만, 저는 이게 코딩보다 훨씬 깊게 박히는 도구가 될 거라고 봐요.

그리고 이게 가장 중요합니다.

③ 못 나간다면, 그들은 얼마를 받을 수 있을까

코딩 매출은 "좌석 수 × 월 구독료" 혹은 "토큰 × 단가"입니다.

천장은 결국 기업의 개발 예산에 막힙니다.

(심지어 앤트로픽 코딩 매출의 상당 부분은 Cursor·Copilot 같은 중간 유통사를 거칩니다. 내 고객이 아니라 남의 고객이라는 뜻.)

제약은 가격을 매기는 방식 자체가 다릅니다.

상위 16개 빅파마가 2025년 R&D에만 쓴 돈이 약 1,590억 달러.

신약 하나 개발에 20억 달러 이상.

블록버스터 약 하나가 1년에 10억 달러 넘게 팔립니다.

AI가 개발 기간을 1년만 당겨도, 그 1년치 매출이 통째로 가치가 됩니다.

그래서 AI-제약 계약은 좌석이 아니라 마일스톤과 로열티로 묶입니다.

구글 계열 아이소모픽 랩스가 노바티스·릴리와 맺은 계약만 로열티를 빼고도 30억 달러 가까이죠.

물론 앤트로픽이 지금 파는 건 아직 워크벤치, 그러니까 좌석입니다.

하지만 연구실 안에 먼저 들어가 있는 회사만 다음 단계, 약의 몫으로 넘어갈 수 있죠.

최근 생명과학 인수 담당자를 따로 뽑는 이유도 거기에 있다고 봐요.

좌석으로 들어가서, 약의 몫으로 넘어가는 구조.

(아, 약값 인하는 어떻게 하냐구요? 괜찮아요. 결국 돈은 돈이 넘치는 상류층에게서 벌면 되니까요)

이게 코딩과 비교가 안 되는 이유라고 봐요.

그런데 여기까지 오면 이런 질문이 남습니다.

"그래서 이게 메모리랑 무슨 상관인데?"

④ 그래서, 메모리는 이 서사에서 어디서 돈을 벌까

메모리 입장에서 중요한 건 토큰이 몇 개냐가 아닙니다.

모델 회사가 2028년에도 컴퓨트 청구서를 낼 수 있는 돈줄이 있느냐죠.

그게 보이냐, 안보이냐가 전부입니다.

바이오는 그 돈줄을 "토큰 단가 싸움" 밖에서 만들어 줄 수 있는 거의 유일한 곳이라고 봐요.

둘째, 기억입니다.

2023년 GPT가 만든 쇼티지는 반도체였습니다.

병목이 연산이었으니까요.

바이오는 조금 다릅니다.

연구 에이전트는 한 가지 연구를 몇 주, 몇 달씩 끝까지 붙잡고 갑니다.

읽은 논문, 세운 가설, 실패한 실험을 전부 기억한 채로요.

그 기억이 올라가는 곳이 바로 메모리입니다.

(실험 결과를 기다리는 며칠 동안은 DRAM, 낸드로 내려가서 대기시키면 되죠.)

코딩 에이전트가 짧고 많은 작업이라면, 바이오 에이전트는 상당히 길고 무거운 작업.

셋째, 결정권 경쟁입니다.

그럼 누가 이 손님을 가장 많이 받게 될까요.

전임상 실험실 자리는 비싸고, 한정돼 있습니다.

이미 병목 중 병목.

그래서 가치는 "그 자리에 무엇을 넣을지 고르는 권한"으로 모입니다.

잘 고르려면, 그 전에 컴퓨터 안에서 가장 많은 설계를 가장 길게 밀어봐야 하죠.

결국 결정권자는 가장 많은 에이전트를 돌리는 쪽입니다.

아이러니하죠?

실험실이 모자랄수록 에이전트가 줄어드는 게 아니라, 오히려 더 많이 돌아가는 구조.

이미 일라이 릴리는 엔비디아 GPU 1,000개가 넘는 슈퍼컴퓨터를 직접 깔고, 이걸 자기 실험실과 연결했습니다.

제약사가 컴퓨트를 직접 사기 시작했다는 것.

바이오에도 하이퍼스케일러가 생기고 있다는 뜻.

2023년의 경쟁이 "누가 더 큰 모델을 학습하느냐"였다면,

다음 경쟁은 "누가 더 많은 설계를 끝까지 밀어보느냐".

저는 이게 2027년 이후를 받쳐줄 서사라고 봐요.

시장이 충분히 이해하면 말이죠.

물론 한계도 분명합니다.

설계를 많이 돌린다고 무조건 잘 고르는 건 아닙니다.

점수를 매기는 모델이 틀리면 10만 개를 돌려도 틀린 걸 고르죠.

그리고 시계도 두 개입니다.

워크벤치 매출, 계약 마일스톤, 제약사의 컴퓨트 투자는 가까운 시계.

로열티와 임상 성공률은 먼 시계.

임상은 연산의 시간이 아니라 생물학의 시간이라, AI로도 압축이 안 되는 구간이 있으니까요.

그래서 이게 2027~28년 메모리 이익을 받쳐준다고 단정할 순 없습니다.

다만 "다음 서사가 없다"와 "다음 서사가 아직 숫자로 안 보인다"는 다른 얘기라고 봐요.

그래서 Jukan에게 직접 묻고 싶습니다.

추론·에이전트로의 전환이 지난 분기 이렇게 선명했는데,바이오에서 "누가 더 많은 설계를 끝까지 밀어보느냐"는 결정권 경쟁이 

2027년 이후 메모리 수요를 받칠 수 있다고 보는지.

상하이에서 들은 회의론이 이 부분까지 포함한 건지.

@jukan05 의견이 정말 궁금합니다.

혹은 다른 누군가의 의견도 좋아요.

Today I met with a veteran investor who argued that memory stocks are not cheap even at a P/E of 3. Below is an edited version of our conversation.

Memory LTAs are basically meaningless. The best the LTAs being signed today can do is get customers to shoulder part of the memory makers' capex. Once prices fall, customers will gladly forfeit their deposits (prepayments) and walk away from the LTAs.

Historically, whenever prices fell more than 60% from the peak, customers broke their LTAs even after signing them.
So even if a 2027 shortage is certain and the stocks trade at a P/E of 3 on 2027 operating profit, 2028 operating profit is uncertain, which makes it hard to justify a higher valuation.

He went on to argue that even if 2028 operating profit were certain, we would still have to account for 2029 operating profit.

I pushed back and asked why the market doesn't discount TSMC the same way. Why does TSMC get such a high valuation? Wouldn't TSMC also take a big hit if the AI boom fades?

His answer: the problem was how violently memory prices rose in the first place.
If memory makers had raised prices in a healthy way like TSMC, it might be a different story. But because they hiked prices like a commodity, the market has no choice but to treat memory stocks like commodity stocks.

Even if memory makers stay in shortage through 2030, he said, the market will price in the risk of oversupply in 2031.

He closed his argument this way: even at 3x 2027 earnings, if memory prices fall in 2028 by enough to break LTAs, that 3x multiple on 2027 works out to 7.8 to 10x on 2028. So current valuations are not cheap.

So the Anthropic one can actually be a (somewhat) pure arbitrage, but there are also other things that are apparently delta neutral, but hide semi-directional trades:

1. MSTR mNAV, shorting the mNAV premium is not as simple as saying BTC is going down, although BTC going down certainly correlates with mNAV premium reduction. One could say if you believe BTC is going down, then why even bother longing the BTC leg, but in reality the mNAV premium can contract even on the way up, if MSTR doesn't collect hype/craze anymore at the same level and Saylor has to keep tapping ATM (although now he could emit more STRC too if he wanted)

2. BOT is still trading at almost 2x NAV premium, however in this case we're talking about private market valuations and you could be squeezed out by just the companies raising another round higher, before maybe IPOing and going to zero (some of them).

3. Equilibria wind down is a proper trade with just a bit of execution risk, but it's almost a 60% PT with 2 years timespan.

4. SK Hynix premium is also tricky, generally you would have imagined SKHY premium goes down when stock goes down but this hasn't been the case as korean bid has been destroyed faster than us demand. On the long horizon, there's no hard mechanism for which this premium has to go to zero unless things change, but more likely than not if memory stocks keep cooling down it won't stay at 45% ish.

So there's a lot of talking about "Anthropic arbitrages"

To the best of my understanding though it's pretty straightforward. There are platform trading valuations (a) and there are platform trading shares (b).

A are: Variational, Binance, Polymarket, Lighter, Hyperliquid(io)
B are: Hyperliquid(XYZ)

Trading Hyperliquid/Variational is NOT an arbitrage.
However, there ARE real arbitrages:

1. Polymarket is currently trading almost 15% off Vari/Binance/Lighter, yes the OI is very small ($300k on Polymarket), but it's a real difference.
2. Every now and then Lighter trades off vs Variational.

To go more in-depth on these type of arbitrages.

A. You can hedge same $ quantity, in this case essentially you're longing MORE shares than you're shorting (because on the short leg, shares cost more than on the long leg). This means that your premium that you're capturing is denominated in shares (so you're neutral + long ANT).

B. You can hedge same ANT quantity, in this case you're fixing the dollar payoff.

“人走了，芯片卖了，公司还在。”

彭博 11 月 6 日的消息：Groq 正在谈新一轮融资，估值 80 亿美元，8 月那轮才 31.5 亿美元，三个月翻了两倍半。

背景够惨：去年 12 月，英伟达 200 亿美元把 Groq 的推理芯片技术连创始人 Jonathan Ross 一起打包带走，Groq 转头估值腰斩到 35 亿美元。

9 月司法部对这单开了反垄断调查，嫌它披着授权的外衣绕开审查；10 月，两名前工程师还告上法庭，说这就是一场没经过股东投票的变相出售。

现在的 Groq 不卖芯片了，改做推理算力云，专啃网络安全客户的单，还放话明年收入翻 8 倍、2028 年赚 20 亿美元。

更狠的是卖点：不借钱、不举债，跟那些靠债堆机房的同行反着来。

说白了，投资人赌的不是芯片，是这家被打劫过的公司还能不能活：活下来了，估值就先涨回去。

去年 12 月 200 亿卖身，今年 11 月 80 亿再出发，你敢赌它三年后比被买走那会儿更值钱吗？

每个交易所之间或多或少都会有系统性的资金费率差别，比如过去一个月，BTC在Gate的资金费率年化是5.76%，而在Hyperliquid是8.64%。

这3%不到的潜在收益如果想要通过在交易所两边开仓套利是不容易捕捉的，因为有资金利用率、合约仓位开仓磨损等原因，即使加上杠杆，也无法线形提高收益。

而boros新推出的spread刚好可以做类似的交易。

无需开合约的仓位，通过boros的资金费率市场交易直接获得类似的资金费率敞口。

需要注意的是，这和之前分享过的boros四腿固定收益策略刚好相反：
 - spread 像YT，并不是固定收益的，且有可能亏损，但是对于本金来说，收益率可以非常高。如果想要参与，一定要研究清楚了。

text:
Anthropic 的研究员，正在把研发 Claude 的工作交给 Claude 自己。

而且交出去的速度，比很多人想象得快得多。

《华尔街日报》最近刊登了一张图，标题非常夸张：「AI 领域最聪明的人认为，这是世界上最重要的一张图」。

图里是 Anthropic 内部的研发数据。

2026 年 3 月，Claude 只能主导约 1% 的模型研发工作。到了 8 月，这个数字已经涨到 26%。如果算上深度协作，Claude 已经参与了超过 90% 的研发工作。

这里的「主导」，不是帮研究员写几行代码。

比如一条数据管道坏了，工程师只需要把故障信息交给 Claude，它就能自己查日志、定位问题、修改代码、运行测试，最后把结果交给人类审核。整个过程，研究员不需要一直盯着。

更有意思的是，这张图本身也是 Claude 帮忙做出来的。Anthropic 用 Claude 分析了约 1.5 万项内部研发任务，再让 Claude 判断每项工作的自动化程度。

AI 在研发下一代 AI，也在参与评估自己研发 AI 的进度。

当然，这仍然是 Anthropic 的内部自评，目前还没有任何一类研发工作实现完全自主。

但我觉得，这张图真正重要的地方，不是 AI 已经能替研究员完成多少工作，而是它正在改变 AI 公司的研发组织方式。

过去，一家实验室的研发速度，很大程度上取决于它有多少顶尖研究员，以及这些人能同时推进多少实验。

但如果一个研究员可以同时指挥几十个甚至上百个 AI Agent，研发能力就不再简单地跟着人数线性增长。

模型越强，能承担的研发工作越多；研发推进得越快，又越有机会训练出更强的模型。

这才是递归自我改进真正值得关注的地方。

而且，这种变化未必需要等到 AI 完全自主研发才会发生。只要它能不断接管更多研发流程，整个实验室的迭代速度就可能被持续放大。

不过，这也意味着一个新的瓶颈：当 AI 可以同时推进成千上万个实验时，人类还有没有能力判断哪些实验真正有效，哪些只是把错误包装成了进步？

下一阶段 AI 实验室之间的竞争，可能不只是比谁拥有最聪明的模型，还要比谁能把模型组织成最高效、最可靠的研发系统。

过去，AI 研发的瓶颈是有多少人能做研究。未来，瓶颈可能是有多少研究结果能被可靠地验证。

- The US intelligence community discovered that Jensen Huang, the CEO of the largest company in the world, was sleeping with Alice Huang, a Chinese spy and an executive at Megaspeed. (FT)
- Multiple independent investigations have concluded that Megaspeed is likely a Chinese cutout, which helps Chinese companies access AI chips or circumvent export controls. (NYT and Bloomberg) 
- The US intelligence community also concluded that Alice Huang’s goal was to convince Jensen to lobby the U.S. government to loosen export controls on advanced AI chips. (NYT)
- The intelligence community relayed this information to “a small group of top US government officials” earlier this year. (FT)
- Over the last year, Jensen Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to loosen export controls on advanced chips. @BISgov has done so, not only by permitting the export of H200 chips to China, but also not enforcing export controls that would have required a license for exports of the most advanced Blackwell chips to Megaspeed and Southeast Asia.
- Although @CommerceGov leadership was presumably briefed on this information by the U.S. intelligence community, @BISgov has taken no actions to tighten controls on Megaspeed or Southeast Asia. 
- Megaspeed remains a preferred cloud partner of Nvidia, and continues to receive Nvidia Blackwell chips despite employing a Chinese spy who reportedly is romantically engaged with the CEO of Nvidia. 
- Tens of billions of dollars worth of AI chips have been exported to Southeast Asia this year alone, and Malaysia and Singapore are now two of the four largest importers of AI chips in the world. 

What is going on here??? We need answers. The question of who gets the most advanced AI chips in the world is literally the defining strategic question of our time. And not only does it seem like the MSS may be directly influencing the debate on export controls in the United States, but also @CommerceGov is refusing to listen to the warnings of the IC on this issue. This is beyond strange at this point. 

The fallout from this story will be massive. Obviously, the motivations underpinning Nvidia’s policy views opposing export controls must now all be questioned. But also, how did @BISgov sit on this information and has still taken no actions? We need answers.

text:
Citrini's "State of the Themes" article kinda strengthens the Onchain/Decentralized AI thesis
 
The article argued that the AI infra/semis trades are ending because Neoclouds/Hyperscalers CAPEX is hitting ~$1T while AI eco ARR is only $200B and the huge gap won't be filled any time soon. Plus, financing constraints, construction delays and model price competition add pressure to the trade
 
That creates an interesting setup for projects helping operators monetize existing capacity and buyers access cheaper compute.
 
This is where Onchain/Decentralized AI gets interesting
 
1. Turning idle/crowdsourced GPUs into revenue
 
GPU marketplaces like @lium_io help operators rent out unused capacity, connecting existing hardware with paying customers.
 
For data centers and smaller operators, better utilization means more revenue from assets they’ve already paid for. Buyers get more options and competitive pricing (e.g. rent idle B200s on @lium_io for $4.25/hr).
 
As financing gets tighter, making existing hardware earn more becomes increasingly valuable.
 
2. Building markets for surplus/excess inference
 
Inference Providers and AI gateways have inference capacity they can sell. Some are expirables because they run subsidy campaigns but they couldn't get users to fully use them.
 
@AskSurplus connects these participants through an inference marketplace, routing requests across discounted supply. Selected offers carry discounts of 50–99% relative to listed API prices.
 
This creates a way for sellers to monetize unused allocations and buyers to reduce their inference bills.
 
Onchain settlement and tokenized credits add building blocks for developers to create new markets, routing tools and products around that supply.
 
3. Bootstrapping inference networks with existing GPUs
 
Decentralized AI crowdsources idle GPUs across the world.
 
Token emissions are used to pay for compute & inference instead of debt & equity financing huge CAPEX for data center buildouts.
 
Teams like @engyai and @dphnAI are already proving that it's possible to host top open-weight models on a hybrid/fully decentralized network that's fast, reliable, and cheap for users.
 
The opportunity is to turn fragmented hardware into useful, competitively priced inference.
 
The economics become stronger as paying customer demand grows enough to support suppliers with progressively smaller subsidies.
 
4. Expanding access to GPU financing
 
@USDai_Official connects onchain capital with operators financing GPU infrastructure.
 
That gives smaller operators another route to funding hardware purchases and deployments, with loans secured by GPUs and supported by their cash flows.
 
As traditional financing becomes more selective, access to additional capital sources could become increasingly valuable.
 
5. Making inference access a tradable asset
 
Pilots of inference tokenization are happening onchain first
 
@AskVenice tokenized its platform credits into "DIEM", people are buying & selling inference like a commodity and builders are building on top of it, creating venues where users can speculate & earn from their credits.
 
This creates the market for future inference access. Users can acquire capacity, trade the token representing that access, and earn revenue from it (if they don't use it).
 
Other teams are experimenting with similar models, creating more ways to price, distribute and monetize inference.
 
For tokens, this creates a link with extraneous demand outside of crypto. The more people use the platform, the more valuable the credits, the more valuable the token.
 
The investment case gets stronger when usage translates into value for token holders
 
The best part is that this sector is growing fast and teams are starting to align interest with token holders through buybacks & burn, revenue distribution, and more utilities.
 
Onchain/Decentralized AI provides the opportunities for better GPU utilization, cheaper inference, new financing channels and tradable access to compute/inference.
 
All real economic problems that crypto teams are building products around them.
 
2025-26 is the year of AI infra/semiconductors
 
2027 will be the year of Onchain/Decentralized AI

18 of the 20 best open models today are Mixture-of-Experts. Dense is basically over.

And yet the know-how to train a good MoE still lives mostly in the heads of a handful of teams.

So we spent 800k GPU hours running the experiments ourselves and wrote everything down. Super happy to finally release "The Ultimate MoE Training Handbook", free and open, organized around the questions training teams hit:
- how many experts, how big, shared or not?
- why is half my step spent in all-to-all, and how do I hide it?
- why is my run 25x slower with no error in the logs?
- softmax, sigmoid or sqrt(softplus) router, and why keep it in fp32?
- aux loss or DeepSeek's loss-free bias?
- upcycle a dense checkpoint or train from scratch?
- can I serve with fewer experts per token than I trained with?

⚠️ Warning: it's long (~70k words, budget a few days, sorry) but with 55 interactive figures, code you can run and numbers from our own runs.

text:
加密行业的安全边界，正在从代码延伸到人和组织。

币安遭遇约 63.4 亿美元的安全事件后，调查显示，攻击者通过虚假招聘、恶意软件和被攻陷的员工设备，逐步获取了核心系统的访问权限。类似的入口也出现在其他事件中：硬件钱包经销渠道、第三方服务商和员工电脑，都可能成为攻击者的突破口。

据 CertiK 上半年报告，钱包入侵和钓鱼分别造成 4.44 亿美元、3.66 亿美元的损失。相比之下，代码漏洞虽然发生了 204 起，只占总损失的 11.5%。

AI 的普及又给攻防带来了新的变化。黑客可以用它批量伪造招聘信息、定制面试话术、辅助寻找漏洞；拥有钱包权限的 AI Agent，也可能受到恶意输入诱导。

从智能合约审计到员工设备、密钥管理和第三方服务，项目方面对的问题越来越复杂：即使某个环节失守，能否阻止攻击者继续深入，把损失控制在局部？

text:
Over a decade ago, the 1st working prototype of Aina was developed at IISc by Apoorv as part of his CAD coursework.

This version of Aina was a ring designed for women's safety. It gradually evolved into a ring which could predict what users wanted and control the smartphone.

He spent months working through the engineering challenges. A year later, he co-founded LazyCo with Yogansh Namdeo.

In 2019, they'd raised nearly $40k from 166 backers on Kickstarter for the original Aina ring (similar form factor but very different functionality).

LazyCo was too early for its time, COVID disrupted the business momentum and the team had a shoestring budget of ~₹70 lakhs of grant funding

Ultrahuman acquired LazyCo. Apoorv joined as VP of Hardware

> Developed UH’s 1st ring in 2022 - the iconic R1 ring which won the Red Dot Design Award in 2023

> Developed Ring AIR in 2023 - their flagship unit (selling 50k units per month at peak)

> Established UH’s in-house manufacturing capabilities

UH’s hardware pedigree & design aesthetic has spawned multiple companies e.g. Abhishek Sahu who started Dreamspan, Anant Sharma who started Moware etc.

When I spoke to Apoorv last year, he shared one key lesson from his UH experience: “If you're serious about software, you have to build your own hardware.”

He is a man with deep conviction. In 2025, he stepped out of UH to pursue a question that had occupied him for nearly a decade: what is the most natural interface between humans and computers?

He didn't go back and rebuild his old ring. Instead, he took a 1st principles customer discovery led approach which led to 3 launches at CES 2026: 

(a) Radiance, a dedicated controller for video meetings.

(b) Shift, a physical button to trigger AI-agent workflows.

(c) Dune, a context-aware three-key keyboard that changed its functions depending on what you were doing.

Dune resonated most. The team shipped 500 units and gathered feedback from early adopters. They explored multiple form factors and ended up identifying the ring with a screen as the only practical solution. 

Apoorv's original insight has survived all these years: the fastest, most effortless actions are often tiny movements of the human body. But, a LOT has changed since.

AI now understands far more context. Software agents can increasingly act on our behalf. Apoorv now has years of experience building and manufacturing consumer hardware at scale.

This time around, the timing might just be right. Apoorv is also much better capitalized: Aina has raised $5.5m from Info Edge, 360 ONE & a roster of fantastic Angel investors.

Apoorv’s bet is that as AI makes software intelligent and proactive, we'll spend less time telling computers what to do and more time making quick decisions about what they propose.

It is always delightful to see a founder overcome adversity, find success in his next act & now pursue his life’s work.

Aina’s 148 second feature video is 148 months of Apoorv’s life, soul & hardwork:

text:
Even though I disagree with some of the assumptions made, this is a good write-up of the discussion, and I appreciate the perspective on the benefits and the conclusion that Glamsterdam should proceed.

There really are two classes of “invariants”
- *Parameters*, eg, gas cost of an operation or block time
- Pricing *mechanisms* for operations

Contracts should not rely on the first class not changing. However mechanisms should be updated ideally in a non-breaking manner.

Glamsterdam has a mix of both changes. Unfortunately, a planned mechanism update (EIP-8037) produces breaking changes where we should not expect some to be, hence the additional delay

In any case, if either of the two categories sees some change, every effort should be made to identify and support apps that are directly or indirectly affected. It could be that the gas cost update makes a specific use case relatively more expensive, or cheaper, changing app economics.

A repository was released for app devs to identify the changes https://t.co/H3XuZZZZVL Internal and external audits have already led to active outreach, this step is designed for last mile coverage

text:
Subagents are the biggest cause of AI failures

In most harnesses:
1. Main agent writes a summary of what it knows
2. Subagent starts from that summary only, and makes assumptions
3. Subagent works and sends back a new summary of what it did

Same flaw as compaction: all summaries are lossy. This is how your assistant makes emails you never wanted, or purchases what you told it just to get the price of

So I tried something new: checkpoint agents

The initial agent has complete context of what needs to be done. And that input is already cached

Fork the session where it is. Send the fork ahead to do the task and it will do exactly what the main agent would have done; their context is identical

What is even better is when the fork finishes, the cache of the main agent is kept warm by the subagent (they share the same prefix)

I measured it on a 137k-token session with Opus 5.5:
→ Main agent does it on its own: 67 s, $0.38, context +8-17k
→ Checkpoint: 117 s, $0.68, context +2k
→ Classic subagent: 123 s, $0.57, context +4-5k

But here is what I found: avoiding large input is even more important than keeping cache. And most subagent tasks were done better either in series with retrieval, or split up to be parallel over fresh sessions from the start

I do not think there is a place for subagent delegation at all. There should either be a super-agent that orchestrates and does no work, or a long running agent that can retrieve from previous sessions, not a worker that completes tasks partially and delegates the rest to other workers

Don't design harnesses based on our assumptions of human behavior

quoted_text:
This time, $FLOAT presents an interesting situation.

Bv1a7cEj5aRnJQhMw4kRQqAFesMSd5LwcDnUzq52BMmr 

Platform metrics are still growing rapidly, while the token price has fallen from its $5 million peak to around $2.2m.

The two are no longer moving in sync.

I remain positive about its fundamentals. Over the past few days, Float has expanded its tokenized gold pairs, while continuing to improve its trader airdrop, buyback mechanism, launch infrastructure, and security. The platform is clearly becoming more mature.

However, I don't want to ignore what the price is telling us: trading turnover remains high, but liquidity is declining. FLOAT's fundamentals are stronger than before, while its short-term market structure has become weaker.

But this raises a question: If FLOAT's fundamentals are still growing, why is its price falling?

Previously, I was more focused on whether Float could make the stock-paired memecoin model work. Now, I'm more interested in whether it can turn its trading activity into sustainable user demand, especially after generating hundreds of thousands of dollars in platform fees and continuously buying back and burning FLOAT.

Let's start with the data. The numbers have improved considerably.

In the previous official website snapshot, cumulative fees were approximately $260.65K, with $36.94K paid to holders, $13.03K earned by creators, approximately $91.23K used for FLOAT buybacks, and $94.73K accumulated in the trader airdrop vault.

The latest Analytics page now shows cumulative fees of $343.34K, holder distributions of $48.43K, creator earnings of $17.16K, buybacks of $120.18K, and an airdrop vault balance of $123.44K.

Several major metrics have increased by roughly 30% during this period. The buyback and burn figures are particularly worth watching: the total number of FLOAT burned has reached 59,724,253, representing approximately 5.97% of the total supply, compared with 5.09% previously.

This shows that Float's fee mechanism is actually operating. Every trade on the platform generates fees, which are distributed among traders and project participants, while a portion is continuously used to buy and burn FLOAT.

One thing I particularly like is that the buyback records have become more transparent. The team has established a dedicated Burn page, where every buyback has a corresponding Solscan transaction. Users can check the actual amount spent, tokens burned, and historical records.

Recently, the team also changed its buyback execution method. Instead of making small purchases every 10 minutes, funds accumulate until reaching 5 SOL before a buyback is executed. If the amount still hasn't reached 5 SOL after four hours, the accumulated funds are used to execute the buyback rather than waiting indefinitely.

Product-wise, there are two recent developments worth watching.

The first is the official launch of GOLD. Users can now launch memecoins paired not only with stock tokens, SOL, and other tokens, but also with tokenized gold.

I think this is a reasonable expansion. Stock assets offer exposure to companies and the technology sector, while gold represents an entirely different market narrative. Float is no longer focused exclusively on U.S. equities. It is beginning to bring more real-world assets into the memecoin launch market.

For creators, a wider selection of paired assets means more narratives to build around. For the platform, expanding the range of assets creates more potential trading scenarios.

Of course, the underlying backing, liquidity, and redemption conditions of tokenized gold still need to be verified. Trading a token paired with tokenized gold should not be confused with owning physical gold.

Another update is the branding of its launch contracts. Tokens launched directly through Float's website now receive contract addresses ending in "Float". This applies to stock, SOL, and other token pairs, and developers' initial purchases can be included in the same transaction as the launch.

Previously launched tokens will not be affected, and tokens created through third-party tools that directly call the program may not have this suffix.

This might seem like a minor detail, but standardizing the launch experience and adding a recognizable identity can help improve the platform's brand recognition.

More importantly, the team has also migrated to a larger dedicated server and strengthened security across its launch process and infrastructure. It has consolidated launch transactions across different pairs into a single transaction, added additional safety checks for holder reward payouts, and introduced price protection for FLOAT purchases made by the buyback wallet.

These improvements may not immediately generate more trading volume, but they show that the team is beginning to address the practical challenges that come with scaling a platform.

Especially after several Solana websites experienced frontend attacks, I think Float taking the initiative to review and strengthen its own infrastructure is a positive development.

The next clear catalyst is the first USDC trader airdrop.

The vault has now accumulated approximately $123.44K in USDC. According to the official rules, the platform will select the top 100 wallets based on cumulative trading volume and distribute rewards proportionally according to each wallet's share of the total volume. USDC will be sent directly to users' wallets, with no manual claiming required.

The leaderboard will be locked at the designated snapshot time, and trading activity after that point will count toward the next round.

The anti-bot rules have also become more specific. Wallets executing more than 300 trades in a single hour, or more than 100 trades per hour across five different hours, will be disqualified. Wash trading and bot activity will also be excluded, and the final leaderboard will undergo an on-chain history review.

This mechanism can encourage short-term trading activity on the platform. Traders have an incentive to keep trading on Float to compete for USDC rewards, while greater trading activity could theoretically generate more platform fees and FLOAT buybacks.

But there is one question I particularly care about: What happens after the airdrop ends?

If users are only increasing their trading volume to compete for a place in the top 100, some of that activity could disappear rapidly once the snapshot is completed. What really matters is whether those traders continue using the platform after receiving their rewards.

Another easily overlooked detail is that rewards are distributed proportionally to trading volume, rather than equally among the 100 wallets. This means the final rewards could be heavily concentrated among a small number of high-volume accounts.

This is a trader incentive program, not a universal airdrop for all token holders.

Now let's return to FLOAT's chart.

At the time I am preparing this post, the market cap is approximately $2.2 million, liquidity is around $319.3K, and 24-hour trading volume is approximately $3.4 million.

Compared with the previous market cap of around $3.29 million, it has declined by roughly one-third. Measured against the historical high of approximately $5 million shown on the latest chart, the drawdown exceeds 50%.

Interestingly, trading volume has not declined alongside the price. It has actually increased from approximately $3 million to $3.4 million, while pool liquidity has fallen from around $408.6K to $319.3K.

In other words, trading activity remains high, but it has not translated into sufficiently stable price support. High turnover can produce impressive trading statistics, but it can also mean that large amounts of capital are constantly moving in and out rather than accumulating as long-term holdings.

Based on these developments, I see three main areas worth watching for future upside.

First, whether the initial USDC airdrop can bring in users who stay. The distribution itself is only one milestone. Trading activity after the airdrop will determine whether the incentive program has actually succeeded.

Second, whether stock and gold pairs can generate new launch and trading demand. Float now offers a wider range of asset options. If it continues adding pairs with genuine liquidity and more projects successfully graduate, the platform still has room to expand its market.

Third, whether buybacks can continue accelerating alongside business growth. Approximately $120K in cumulative buybacks and nearly 6% of the total supply burned already represent a measurable value-capture mechanism. If platform fees continue growing and buybacks expand accordingly, FLOAT's supply-demand dynamics could improve further.

The previously mentioned application for a dedicated FLOAT/SOL liquidity pool is also worth monitoring. If Raydium approves it, this could become another catalyst. However, it should not be treated as an implemented feature yet.

Of course, the biggest risk remains the gap between the number of tokens launched and the number of projects with genuine staying power.

An earlier official website snapshot showed approximately 972 tokens launched, with 9 graduating. The project's latest update has reported 1,172 launched tokens, while the latest graduation page now shows 11 projects.

At least we can see that more projects are successfully graduating. However, compared with the total number of launches, the proportion that actually reaches graduation remains relatively small.

If the number of launches continues increasing but graduations and post-graduation trading activity fail to keep pace, platform revenue may become increasingly dependent on new launches rather than sustained trading activity from existing projects.

Therefore, my current view of FLOAT is that its fundamentals are continuing to strengthen, but market sentiment and price momentum have clearly cooled down.

The recent updates are not simply about adding a few more features. They are gradually improving trader incentives, asset availability, launch infrastructure, server capacity, and buyback transparency. Float is becoming much more like a trading platform with actual fee revenue and a functioning token buyback mechanism than it was when it first launched.

However, I wouldn't conclude that FLOAT should return to a $5 million market cap simply because cumulative fees have increased from $260K to $343K. Ultimately, the market prices future expectations, not historical cumulative fees.

What I want to see is that users don't disappear after the first airdrop, gold and other newly added pairs begin generating sustained trading activity, more projects graduate, and buybacks continue growing alongside platform activity.

If these developments materialize, the current price correction could give the market a reason to reassess FLOAT's growth potential.

But if trading volume drops sharply after the airdrop, launches continue increasing while graduations remain stagnant, then the impressive revenue figures we see today may simply reflect the temporary prosperity created by early-stage incentives.

Float has already demonstrated that it can generate trading activity and platform fees at scale. What it needs to prove next is that users are still willing to come back when there are no airdrop incentives driving them.

In other words, user retention is the next metric that really matters.

text:
I think all of this stuff is actually very simple tbh. 

You act as a billboard for these coins by retweeting, interacting or hosting spaces etc with the celebrity. Then the coins rug and the celeb or Sahil or whoever makes money. 

Their plan is obvious: make the coin go up by getting attention to it via you (as you have written and acknowledged, attention is very valuable). Your followers will gamble on stuff that you have mentioned in a hope you’ll mention it again, or that they’ll hit an Iggy-style multiple. And that injection of $ makes it possible for celeb to make 100k or whatever and leave. 

And, you have been a proponent of select celebrity coins, which endorses a “meta” even without direct endorsement of some coins — since there is no explainable framework where Iggy’s coin is good but Soulja Boy’s is bad. The only difference is how long they are waiting to sell. 

The answer for you is simple: completely stop interacting with these people in public until you have evidence of good faith — which is likely them taking significant financial risk (eg buying a lot of something) rather than taking zero financial risk (eg only selling something). 

If you have a large account and a bunch of followers that ape a lot of stuff, unfortunately extractive actors will try to groom you or use you for their own personal gain. 

It sucks actually, and it’s almost impossible to entirely defend against without becoming a jaded recluse. But celebrities are at least very easy to avoid.

If they want to “get into crypto” then they should put $ where their mouth is and buy coins like the rest of us do. That’s what being in crypto is. If they don’t want to do that, ask yourself, why would these celebrities want to suddenly be your friend?

Ruby-OPD is a breakthrough for Japanese text-to-speech: it finally delivers both raw-text naturalness and fine-grained pronunciation control.

How? By mixing inline Ruby annotations (for explicit user overrides) with a clever on-policy distillation scheme—no extra paired audio needed. On the Joyo-Kanji-Yomi benchmark, it hits 97.13% Kanji accuracy (up from 94.1%), halves phoneme errors, and achieves near-perfect control when users annotate tricky words.

Speech quality (UTMOS 3.19) and voice cloning stay strong. No more trade-off between accuracy and author flexibility; just add Ruby for override, or let the model handle it.

This is a major advance for audiobooks, voicebots, dubbing, and language apps—anywhere Kanji readings matter.

quoted_text:
I burned a shitload of compute so you don't have to. Releasing the Harness Leaderboard.

Which harness should you run your open model in? I ran 28,849 trials to find out.

The leaderboard compares nine coding-agent harnesses on open models. In each comparison only the harness changes: the model, provider and reasoning effort stay fixed, and every task gets three attempts.

The trials ran GLM-5.3-Flash, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Flint on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE, for $4,746 of inference.

Averaged over the three models, mini-swe-agent (@KLieret), a bash-only agent, solves 51.4% of tasks and @openclaw 27.3%. Four others are statistically tied with mini-swe-agent.

One of them is Pi (@pidotdev), at 49.4% for $0.29 per solved task, about 45% less than mini-swe-agent's $0.53.

The best harness depends on the model: mini-swe-agent on GLM-5.3-Flash, Hermes Agent (@NousResearch) on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Kimi Code (@Kimi_Moonshot) on Flint.

@opencode costs $3.35 per solved task, 11.7 times as much as Pi.

See Harness Hub's Harness Lens for what the nine harnesses do differently. It documents the prompts, tools and compaction of 34 coding-agent harnesses and links every claim to its source.

text:
Introducing Factory Intelligence.

I've walked through 70+ American factories. 

From a distance they look incredible. 

Up close, most run on buildings from last century, machines older than your dad, and overworked people holding it all together. 

Electrical prefab for data centers is the clearest example: 95%+ of it is still done by hand with power tools, and there aren't enough people to hire. 

So we're not bolting robots onto old factories. 

We're building new ones from the ground up for autonomy: the cells, the robots, and the software that runs them. 

Our first cell is live at an electrical contractor in Indiana. 

It learned to bend wire, break tabs and drive screws to build wall outlets, and the pilot became a 3 year production contract expanding to 12 cells. 

Next is our own factory: 20 cells with mobile robots moving material between them, building power components for data centers by the end of Q1 2027.

- 220,000 high voltage outlets

-440,000 coils of conduit wire

-36,000 junction boxes 

Switch gears next.

text:
I actually agree with a lot of what @poteto is saying except for the central point. IMO most people don't have actual software factory systems. They've just made it much easier for people to ship with AI, so they assume the category doesn't exist. That's more a lack of vision than anything else.

Our conceptualization of a software factory is a system where every piece of work goes through the same stages to standardize the process not the work output.

For us, this standardized process begins with what we call a signal. This is anything that tells you how your software should evolve, including the first signal that your software should exist at all. A Slack thread, a Linear ticket, a Sentry alert, a failing CI job, a tweet, someone's idea. 

There's two ways in for a signal. A person picks it up and builds it with Droid, or a workstream picks it up on its own, triages it against a goal someone set, and has droids write the spec and open the PR. Most work still starts with a person, but a growing share comes from workstreams.

Then every change goes through the same checks no matter who or what wrote it. Droid review, security review, a risk judge that can't see who wrote it, CI, and an agent that QAs it on a live preview. Your validation has to be really high quality whether a human or AI built it. The goal of validation is to hillclimb your "regret-free merge rate" until you can automatically merge most changes (or fix them until they can be automerged).

Then it ships, and when something breaks in production we trace it back to the PR that caused it. That becomes another signal. It's also how we know if the checks actually work. If the risk judge approved something that later broke, we find out.

It's the same way we let self-driving cars on the road. Nobody just flipped a switch. We agreed that once they crashed less than human drivers, they could drive. Do the same thing with code. Once AI-written changes break things less often than human ones, and you can actually measure that, you let them merge.

That doesn't mean you turn on automerge tomorrow. Most of our changes still get a human stamp. But once you have automerge, workstreams and a risk score together, you basically have software that improves itself from the signals you choose to track.

The human element becomes obvious if you have a system like this. People remove themselves from the actual process line and begin to define the rules by which the process operates. What to watch, goals and owners, skills, review guidelines, and how much autonomy each workstream gets. They're the regulators.

I think the 1920s factory that a lot of people picture is the wrong idea. That was people doing the same motion on a line all day. This is closer to a Star Trek replicator. You say what you want and it gets made, because the patterns are already stored and how things get made is the same every time, and checked every time.

author: ishmeow_hl
quoted_text:
While crypto bros are pumping Starknet and Quantus, Morgan Stanley just published a quantum computing report yesterday and upgraded Quantinuum $QNT to Overweight with a $62 price target, about 88% upside. 

It also started covering Infleqtion $INFQ and Xanadu $XNDU at Equal-weight, and kept IonQ $IONQ at Equal-weight.

2027 is a key test year. Every one of these companies has a major milestone due next year, and their roadmaps all point to early fault-tolerant machines around 2029-30. MS estimates the quantum market at about $10bn in 2030, growing to more than $100bn a year by 2040.

MS uses an 8-stage scale, starting with basic encoding, then breakeven (where protected qubits perform better than unprotected ones), then fault-tolerant logical operations, and finally scaled fault-tolerant computation. 

On this scale, Quantinuum is ahead. It is at Stage 7, IonQ is at Stage 4, Infleqtion at Stage 3 and Xanadu at Stage 1. 

For crypto, no company has reached Stage 8 yet, so no quantum computer today can break $BTC or $ETH. But IonQ estimates that about 20,000 physical qubits could break 256-bit elliptic curve signatures and says that fits its 2028 roadmap. 

Next comes a contest between US quantum stocks and post-quantum crypto and security names. Each logical-qubit milestone from these companies also shows us how close that threat really is.

这波感觉Binance没啥问题，但是这个回复感觉越抹越黑了，我大概看懂了，冒昧中译中一下。

Binance Global用户有一套UID.A，Binance TH用户有一套UID.B，两个站完全就是独立站（不能通过UID转账），两边就是存在用户UID一样的情况，就像你的QQ号和Binance UID也有可能一样。

这个用户从Binance Global想转账到Binance TH的账户，因为不知道两个站点是独立站，所以用了UID转账（但其实不互通的），输入了Binance TH的UID，但是这个UID在Binance Global是对应另一个用户的账户。转账的时候其实会弹出二次确认，要用户检验收款账户的用户名是否一致，这一步其实是能发现问题的。

Binance作为金融机构在没有授权的情况下不能直接转走已经收到资金的用户资产，只能冻结后帮转错的用户联系Global这边的用户确认退回，或者等待执法机构介入配合。

$FLOAT fees have surpassed $680K. The real growth is entering its next stage.

Bv1a7cEj5aRnJQhMw4kRQqAFesMSd5LwcDnUzq52BMmr 

The challenges FLOAT faces today are very different from those it faced when it first launched.

In the early days, it needed to prove that people were interested in stock-paired memecoins and that the platform could attract traders. Now, cumulative fees have reached $684.37K, cumulative buybacks have reached $239.54K, and approximately 8.72% of the total supply has been burned. The platform is also shifting its focus from simply increasing token launches toward developer incentives and project quality management.

I believe FLOAT's fundamentals have strengthened considerably compared with before. More importantly, it is beginning to build a sustainable business model rather than relying on short-term traffic generated by new token launches.

Let's start with the most important data.

In the previous analysis, the official website showed cumulative fees of approximately $505.79K. That figure has now reached $684.37K, an increase of approximately $178.58K, or more than 35%.

During the same period, holders have received a cumulative $94.35K, creators have earned $34.21K, FLOAT buybacks have reached $239.54K, and the second trader airdrop vault has accumulated $117.70K.

The buyback and burn figures are particularly worth watching. A total of 87,240,904 FLOAT has now been burned, representing approximately 8.72% of the total supply, compared with 7.69% previously. This means another 10 million-plus FLOAT have been burned in a relatively short period.

However, what I care about is not the burn percentage itself, but the revenue behind it.

Float allocates 35% of platform trading fees to buying back and burning FLOAT. As long as the platform continues generating trading activity, this mechanism has the potential to provide consistent buying pressure for the token.

The team has also introduced a dedicated Burn page, where every buyback can be verified through its corresponding Solscan transaction. Buybacks are now executed based on accumulated funds: once the amount reaches 5 SOL, a buyback is executed. If the threshold is not reached within four hours, the accumulated funds are still used to execute the buyback.

This is much more meaningful than simply announcing a quarterly burn plan.

User incentives are evolving as well.

The first trader airdrop has already distributed approximately $127.57K in USDC, while the second airdrop vault has accumulated $117.70K so far. The project has expanded the number of eligible wallets from the previous top 100 to the top 250, with rewards distributed proportionally according to eligible trading volume.

The second round's measurement period started from the first airdrop snapshot on November 4, with the leaderboard scheduled to lock at 11:00 AM CST on November 11. Bots and wash trading remain ineligible, and the final list will undergo an on-chain history review.

On the product side, Float has also been noticeably expanding its range of assets. It is now bringing gold, privacy-related assets, and other market themes into its launch ecosystem. However, what really matters is whether these new pairs can generate sustained trading activity and maintain sufficient liquidity.

This actually makes me more interested in another feature that is still under discussion: Builder Launch.

Float is gathering community feedback on a dedicated launch mode for developers. The preliminary proposal includes allowing launches only through the official website, offering developers a larger share of trading fees, and locking developer fees for 24–48h before releasing them, provided the project is confirmed not to be a rug and the developer remains actively involved in building.

If a developer rugs, their allocated fees will instead go toward the trader airdrop and FLOAT buybacks and burns.

Developers would also have to lock their token supply at launch, with the lock duration chosen by the developer. The platform plans to introduce dedicated Builder tags and filters, allowing users to distinguish developer-led launches from ordinary community launches.

I believe this is a very important direction for Float's next stage.

The platform is no longer short of token launches. The real challenge is getting developers to take their projects seriously, helping more tokens graduate, and keeping trading activity alive after graduation.

For a launchpad, solving this problem could create more long-term value than simply adding hundreds of new trading pairs.

Looking ahead, I see three main potential catalysts: trading retention after the second airdrop, the adoption of Builder Launch once it officially goes live, and whether platform fees and FLOAT buybacks can continue growing together.

Of these, Builder Launch is what interests me most. Float already has trading activity and actual revenue. If it can now align developers' incentives with the long-term performance of their projects, it has a chance to evolve from a simple launchpad into a platform with a higher-quality supply of projects.

The risks are still worth keeping in mind. Airdrops can create temporary trading activity, growing launch numbers can mask weak graduation performance, and Builder Launch is still a proposal rather than a finalized product. Its actual implementation rules have yet to be confirmed.

Furthermore, buybacks depend on platform trading fees. If incentives lose their appeal and trading activity declines, the rate of token burns will also slow down.

My current view on FLOAT is that its fundamentals continue to strengthen, and this improvement is supported by clear data. Float is also entering a new stage of development.

Previously, the market needed to answer one question: Were people actually willing to launch and trade tokens on Float?

It now has an answer.

The platform has generated more than $680K in cumulative fees, completed more than $230K in buybacks, and continued expanding its range of paired assets.

The next metrics worth watching are no longer the number of launches, but trading retention after the second airdrop and whether Builder Launch can actually go live.

These two factors will determine whether Float can move from traffic-driven growth to quality-driven growth.

I don't believe a launchpad can sustain growth forever simply by increasing the number of new tokens it launches.

A genuinely resilient platform needs developers who are willing to keep building, traders who are willing to come back, and an economic model capable of generating recurring revenue as the ecosystem grows.

Float has already demonstrated that it can generate trading activity and platform fees. What it needs to prove next is that users will stay even when incentives become less attractive, and that developers are willing to commit real effort to building for the long term.

That is the next development I believe is most worth betting on with FLOAT.

text:
Tl;dr of my views on AI safety: 

1. My main threat models involves (a) non-state actors asymetrically exploiting cheaper technologies over time (see Bobbitt's 'Terror and Consent'); and (b) the road to state overreach and creeping authoritarianism being paved with good intentions. Misuse, bad engineering, and institutional failure more than alien 'scheming'.

2. Safety and capabilities are intertwined, just like a caduceus. You actively need powerful systems for better monitoring, system reliability, societal defenses etc. Unsafe systems are generally commercially useless and/or a liability risk, though there are reasonable disagreements incentive structures.

3. Focusing solely on a model's 'inner alignment' in isolation is insufficient. The difficulty of specifying 'alignment' in the abstract + principal-agent problems suggests that engineering system-level boundaries is the way to go. Also ASI is not a joker card, this applies to powerful systems too. 

4. Automating AI R&D is harder than people make it out to be, and does not mean you suddenly lose control. Model gains also remain tethered to bottlenecks, deployment feedback, costs/limited compute, and human normative direction. Humans delegating more does not mean they're out of the loop.

5. AI futurism is too often fatalistic. I disagree that competitive pressures will *necessarily* reduce humans to pets or a sideshow. Automating 'execution' actually pushes humans up the ladder of abstraction toward normative direction and governance; but for the good world we should actively protect and improve liberal democracy.

I'm a MEXC VVIP user, and I keep funds on the exchange, so I took the time to read through the actual FinCEN order myself.

Here's what I found:

- The order does not require user assets to be frozen. Restrictions on financial institutions should not be confused with a blanket freeze on individual users' funds.
- It does not order MEXC to shut down.
- It prohibits U.S. financial institutions from processing funds transfers to or from MEXC Global.
- It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register.

MEXC says it's operating normally and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

I'm still keeping a close eye on how things develop, but the actual order is quite different from some of the claims circulating online.

quoted_text:
币安办学习营，其实就是希望能和社区有更多面对面交流的机会。

最初的想法也非常简单。一方面，面对面交流，能听到很多平时在线上可能不太好表达的观点和信息。另一方面，我们也确实希望通过这样的交流，让社区能更完整地了解我们。

我相信，对于用户和从业者来说，无论是关注还是来参加这样的活动，大多都是带着善意的。

但就是这样一个活动，这两天还是出现了一些明显不符合事实的讨论。对于这些声音，我们不想去揣测动机，但确实让人感受到了一些恶意。这对于所有参加活动的朋友，特别是对那些认真交流的人来说，其实是很不公平的。

当然，我们也相信活动本身肯定也有不够完善的地方，对于理性的批评和建议，我们一直愿意听，也希望能够不断改进。

其实说到底，币安也是一家商业机构，同样要遵循市场的规律。我始终相信，一家企业能够长期走下去，归根结底还是因为它能够持续为用户和行业创造价值。

币安能够发展到今天的规模，离不开过去为用户创造的实际价值，也离不开大家长期以来的信任和选择。规模本身没什么值得炫耀的，它更多是价值创造之后的结果。如果有一天，我们不能继续为用户创造价值，那么今天的规模也就失去了意义。

我想表达的是，我们希望我们能够始终带着善意做事，坚持对用户有益的方向，把更多精力放在真正有价值的事情上。而不是其他。

相信时间会检验很多事情，行动也比言语更有说服力。

月底 BBW，期待曼谷再见！💛

text:
I'd like to believe LTAs are durable too. But take one example.

Analog chipmaker onsemi said this in 2023.
On January 5, 2023, at JPMorgan's CES forum, CEO Hassane El-Khoury was asked how much LTSAs would still hold once the shortage eased. His answer: “They are a legally binding agreement ’cause they’re a liability for the customer because they’re take or pay.” He also said he would not accept a customer reopening price talks just because it could get the same parts 10% cheaper elsewhere.

On October 30, 2023, on the Q3 earnings call, onsemi cut its SiC shipment forecast for the year from $1 billion to more than $800 million after one automotive OEM reduced demand. An analyst asked how this could happen when the company had been saying its LTSAs were legally binding. The same CEO reaffirmed that they were binding, but said he did not want to enforce the contracts just to push inventory onto a customer whose demand had dropped. If it worked for both sides, terms could be adjusted customer by customer, whether by a quarter, a year, or longer.

In its 10-K filings, onsemi also states that it amended LTSAs with some strategic customers by mutual agreement in 2024, and changed delivery schedules and committed volumes on some LTSAs in 2025 as demand shifted.

Microchip is another case. Customers in its Preferred Supply Program (PSP) originally had to place 12 months of orders and could not cancel or reschedule them unless Microchip raised prices. On its November 2025 earnings call, however, the CEO said the company had accepted some cancellations and pushouts so customers could adjust their backlog. On the same call, the CFO separately addressed the multiyear LTSAs the company had signed. Some of those contracts were still in effect, he said, but customers had been allowed to defer taking delivery of committed volumes by one to two years if they needed to.

Every time I see cases like these, I doubt how much memory makers' LTAs will protect earnings in a downcycle. Right now the most reliable thing is the prepayments and deposits themselves. That cash can go into capacity expansion today.

I can picture hyperscalers with no DRAM inventory continuing to buy at current prices. But once inventory has piled up, will they keep taking every committed unit at the same price? I have a hard time picturing memory makers holding customers to the high contract price all the way through.

The LTA itself may never be broken and may stay in place. But if both sides agree to push this year's volumes into next year or two years out, this year's earnings estimates come down. If price gets renegotiated too, margin estimates have to come down as well.

Again, I agree LTAs are sturdier than they used to be. What I question is whether, after demand turns, memory makers can still earn 80% margins on contracts signed during the upturn and keep collecting hundreds of billions of dollars in profit because of those LTAs.

My Unofficial @variational_io week 47 points update:

-Weekly distribution count is stable around 32k accounts.

-The top 100 is consolidating. The 3k–5k band is where rank is most fluid. The bottom half of the board is largely dormant. 

-The tail is long. Most of the ~80k wallets sit below 100 points.

-The 200–300 band is tight. Cutoffs here move week to week depending on who stays active.

TLDR: quite similar observations as last week. It’s nearing the end of the points program and with API still not live, consistent point earners are holding steady, mostly in the 3K band.

Distribution shape is power-law with a sticky head, a competitive mid-board, and a long inactive tail.

Top 100 holds 28% of all points distributed. The remaining drips down across the board.

Is it still worth to farm? In my view, points are actually easier to earn compared to last 2 months. Metrics have softened a little as the markets is in “cool off”, but remains steady near ATH.

Will continue to observe if public mainnet + API starts to change the equation, which will likely happen soon.

If you’re interested in trying Variational, check it out here: https://t.co/nCSN02I4fX

My unofficial @variational_io Week 46 points distribution update:

- About 9.95M points issued so far, up to 10.4M if all the trader onboarding rewards get claimed.

-Out of 79.99K wallets that crossed the 100K volume threshold, 32,293 wallets earned points last week, representing 40% of the cohort.

-Weekly distribution count has been stable around 32K wallets for several weeks.

-Volume cooled off this week, so competition for points was softer vs the prior month.

-Top 100 holds about 28% of issued points, while combining with the top 500, they collectively hold 46% of points supply.

Distribution remains power-law shaped with a sticky head, a competitive mid band and a long inactive tail. 

Top 100 is consolidating and the 3000-5000 ranks are most fluid. The bottom cohort is largely dormant.

Overall pretty comparable to typical pre-TGE setups. Relatively speaking, it is better distributed than Hyperliquid and Lighter at the same stage of growth.

Bitget CEO (Gracy) 最近上《When Shift Happens》播客，用这个比方形容交易所安全问题：攻守天生不对称。

text:
AI 投资正在反噬云巨头的现金流？

美股 AI 七姐妹开始面临一个新问题：钱投进去了，什么时候才能赚回来？

微软、谷歌、亚马逊和 Meta 第三季度经营现金流，已经无法覆盖固定资产支出，合计出现约 264 亿美元资金缺口。而一年前，四家公司还有约 617 亿美元现金流盈余。

几个值得关注的变化：

- 亚马逊：过去 12 个月自由现金流从净流入 148 亿美元，转为净流出 424 亿美元。
- Meta：自由现金流十多年来首次转负。
- 谷歌：长期债务从约 200 亿美元增至 1250 亿美元。
- 微软：英伟达芯片订单交付高度依赖数据中心持续扩建，建设放缓可能影响收入兑现。

更大的变量来自美国政治。

中期选举后，数据中心建设监管趋严。美国 10 个州涉及数据中心的 41 项地方提案中，40 项投票倾向限制开发，27 项限制性或反对性提案获得通过。

但 AI 需求本身还没有明显降温：谷歌云三季度营业利润达到去年同期的 3 倍，AWS 营业利润从 114 亿美元增至 178 亿美元，微软 Azure 收入增长 48%。

所以，市场真正担心的可能不是 AI 没有需求，而是：数千亿美元的 AI 基建投资，究竟需要多久才能转化为足够的现金流？

AI 泡沫论的下一场争论，可能不在模型能力，而在资本回报率。
