TSMC has denied reports that it is exploring 3D DRAM production at Nvidia’s request. It says it remains focused on logic chip manufacturing.
$TSM
$NVDA
Tom’s Hardware reports the response. A TSMC spokesperson said the company focuses on its core business at all times, which is dedicated integrated circuit foundry work. Its mission is to be the trusted technology and capacity provider of the global logic integrated circuit industry for years to come. The statement effectively rejects the earlier report from The Information. That report, citing two people familiar with the matter, said TSMC had begun drafting plans for 3D DRAM manufacturing after a request from Nvidia, its largest customer. The effort was said to be led by Hsu Kuo-chin, TSMC’s vice president of advanced packaging and a former head of Micron’s Taiwan operations.

TSMC works with DRAM producers to package memory into system-in-packages for customers. It lacks the expertise and production capacity to make DRAM, let alone 3D DRAM. Even major memory makers are years away from 3D DRAM. Pursuing it would not address current shortages for at least five years. Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix are all working on 3D DRAM. Micron’s strategy includes at least four more planar DRAM process technologies before 3D DRAM becomes a reality. Making DRAM would require TSMC to develop manufacturing processes distinct from its logic production. 3D DRAM also needs different techniques to build vertically stacked memory cell layers while controlling defects and maintaining acceptable yields.

A denial is not a finished supply plan.

If TSMC has already stated that it stays focused on logic foundry work and that 3D DRAM remains years from market viability even at the major memory makers, does the next constraint stay on how the existing DRAM and high-bandwidth memory suppliers scale output through 2027 and 2028, or on whether Nvidia and other AI chip designers still need additional long-term memory sources beyond the current three?

An AI just proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, open since 2008. Some are reading it as proof that quantum computers are useless. It proves the opposite of what they think.

On Thursday, PSI published a proof generated by an AI research system running an unreleased Anthropic model. A human lead audited it, and the Lean proof assistant verified it line by line. The Stanford group that proved a special case in August has reviewed it and called it a huge result.

Here is what it proves, for yes-or-no questions about random, structureless inputs, a quantum computer can read exponentially fewer bits than a classical one only if the input has a rare pattern. On random data, the advantage is at most polynomial.

Though it doesn't touch structured problems, Shor’s algorithm breaks RSA by exploiting the hidden periodicity in numbers. Simulating molecules for drugs and batteries exploits the physics of the molecule itself. Those were always the targets, and the theorem says nothing about them.

It also only covers decision problems, in 2022, Yamakawa and Zhandry proved that for search problems, quantum computers can hold an exponential advantage eve relative to a random oracle. The two results are consistent, and their paper says so.

And it formalizes what the field assumed for decades. Since 1997 we’ve known that unstructured quantum search is only quadratically faster. No serious roadmap was built on random-input speedups.

The upside is real, it confirms the roadmap every major quantum program is already on. It gives investors a theorem against anyone promising exponential speedups on generic data. It confirms that AES-256 and SHA-256 stay safe with larger keys while RSA remains breakable. 18 years of results that began with “assuming Aaronson-Ambainis” are now unconditional.

The other story is that an AI did frontier mathematics that stumped humans for 18 years, and a machine checked the work. For quantum theory, that may matter more than the theorem itself.

text:
纽约时报 11 月 5 日发了一篇 Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei 的长篇人物稿，赶在 Anthropic 本月上市之前。记者采访了他二十多位同学、朋友、老师和同事，还看到了他早年的邮件和在 OpenAI 的内部消息。

Dario 通过公司发言人拒绝受访。所以下面的故事大多是别人的回忆，只有一部分有邮件、博客等文件佐证。

这些人的说法归结起来是：Dario 年轻时泡在“理性主义”和“有效利他主义”两个圈子里，两者合在一起，让他认定 AI 危险到只有他和想法相近的人才值得托付去造。朋友和同事认为，这推动他抢在不在乎安全的人之前造出 AI，也让他想把这项技术掌控在自己手里。

【两个圈子是什么】

理性主义是围绕 Eliezer Yudkowsky 等人的博客形成的网络社群，讲究用冷静的推理看世界，其中很多人认为 AI 终将强大到毁掉人类社会。

有效利他主义跟它差不多同时成长起来，主张用数学算清楚怎么捐钱、怎么做事，才能让好处最大。两边共同相信：靠严密的计算，可以改变人类的未来。

【从小就爱算账】

Dario 在旧金山 Mission 区长大，父亲是皮匠，母亲管理公共图书馆的翻修工程。高中读的是旧金山最好的公立高中 Lowell，同时去伯克利上课。同学记得他那时就在琢磨功利主义，也就是“让最多的生命得到最多的幸福”。

上大学后，他和高中好友在寿司店争论功利主义。Dario 吃素，但认为吃螃蟹没问题，因为螃蟹是无脊椎动物。

朋友出了个思想实验：如果有人拼命杀鸡，杀到多少只时，杀掉这个人才算合理？据在场的 Nathan Avery 回忆，Dario 笑了笑，说从功利主义的角度看，总有某个数量的鸡，分量会超过一个人。

【父亲去世，和“时间有限”】

2006 年 Dario 从斯坦福毕业，去普林斯顿读物理博士，后来专攻生物物理和计算神经科学。同一年，父亲因丙肝去世。

前女友 Jade Wang 回忆，两人常聊：一辈子只研究一种病的科学家，影响力比不上给整个领域造工具和方法的人。Dario 举的例子就是父亲，父亲没等到后来能治好大多数丙肝的药。

2007 年，24 岁的 Dario 读完 Ray Kurzweil 的《奇点临近》，对来访的高中同学 Colin Heckman 说，奇点会在 2040 年前到来，人类以后可能和机器融合。Heckman 说他从此“着了魔”，说 AI 必须造对，不然人类就完了。

那段时间，Dario 在读 Accelerating Future、Overcoming Bias 这类讨论 AI 毁灭人类的小众博客，还鼓动朋友和妹妹 Daniela 去参加 Yudkowsky 办的奇点研究所年会（现在叫机器智能研究所，MIRI）。

纽约时报看到一封 2008 年的邮件，Dario 在信里称 Yudkowsky 是“我遇到过最深刻的思想者之一”。Yudkowsky 现在给纽约时报回邮件说，Dario 如今不向他请教，也不听他的建议，他也不记得 Dario 什么时候这样做过。

同年，Dario 通过经济学家 Tyler Cowen 的博客知道了 GiveWell，一个评估慈善机构效率的组织，开始活跃在它的论坛上。2010 年他在邮件里说在考虑去做金融，好赚更多钱捐出去。

同年他在 GiveWell 博客上公开盘算一笔 1 万美元的捐款，在成人结核病项目和非洲儿童疫苗项目之间权衡。他写道，成年人能有更深刻的体验，“一个成年人的死亡也许比一个婴儿的死亡糟糕两三倍”。最后他还是选了疫苗项目，理由是这家执行得更有效。

2011 年起他在斯坦福做癌细胞研究的博士后，吃抗衰老补剂，严格坚持游泳，还研究节食延寿。Avery 说，他常讲时间是唯一不可再生的资源，对自己的时间“毫不留情”。据两位知情人说，2014 年他确诊睾丸癌，化疗后完全康复。

【一屋子未来的创始人】

那几年，Daniela 和 GiveWell 创始人 Holden Karnofsky 在交往（两人 2017 年结婚），住进旧金山一处合租屋。后来搬进来的还有 Dario、理论物理学家 Jared Kaplan，以及大学辍学、数学由 Dario 辅导过的 Chris Olah。

据三位去过的人说，室友们会一起讨论 Yudkowsky 的文章，也一起去火人节，有时穿动物服装。Kaplan 和 Olah 后来与 Amodei 兄妹一起创办了 Anthropic，Karnofsky 2025 年也加入了公司。

【在 OpenAI，立场变硬】

2014 年 Dario 进入百度硅谷实验室，同事说他“几乎一有机会就激烈争论”。2015 年他对同事说，AI 可能很快赶上甚至超过人脑。同年他去 Google Brain 做 AI 安全，和 Olah 等人写了论文《AI 安全中的具体问题》。

2016 年他加入当时还是非营利组织的 OpenAI，带安全团队和研究“规模定律”的团队。七位前同事说，他在 OpenAI 的立场越来越强硬。

纽约时报看到的内部消息显示，2016 年特朗普当选三天后，Dario 写道，他“不愿在一个威权国家研究具有军事威力的技术”。他还说，给特朗普竞选捐了 125 万美元的 Peter Thiel “在道德上应受谴责”，OpenAI 不该再收他的钱。Thiel 创办的 Founders Fund 后来投资了 Anthropic。

据三位知情人说，2017 年 Dario 牵线，让 Karnofsky 的慈善机构（现名 Coefficient Giving）给 OpenAI 捐了 3000 万美元，Karnofsky 也进了 OpenAI 董事会。Dario 当时是这家机构的技术顾问。

2018 年 Daniela 加入 OpenAI，后来做到安全与政策副总裁，有员工开始担心兄妹俩影响力太大。据三位知情人说，那年 12 月研究员 Joshua Achiam 劝 Sam Altman 别让 Dario 当首席伦理官，认为 AI 的监督应该由不同视角的人分担，并坚持请外部专家。Dario 当面提高嗓门说，没有人比他更合适。

同年兄妹俩接手了 GPT 项目，探索让 AI 在人类指导下学会做事的安全技术。纽约时报的判断是，先把 AI 推近危险、再用安全技术去检验，成了 Dario 此后整个职业生涯的做法。

据两位知情人说，OpenAI 总裁 Greg Brockman 想参与 GPT，兄妹俩不让。Dario 多次对 Altman 说，不把 Brockman 挡在外面他就走。Altman 拒绝了。2020 年 12 月，Dario、Daniela 和几位同事离职，四周后创办了 Anthropic。

【和今天的 Anthropic 有什么关系】

Anthropic 2021 年成立时，Amodei 兄妹和另外五位联合创始人都在这两个圈子附近待过。纽约时报认为，公司做大以后，这套想法也随着 Dario 一次次公开表态变得越来越有分量：他主张限制对华芯片出口，主张监管 AI 防止失控，在和美国国防部的争执里坚持 AI 不能用于大规模监控美国人、不能用于自主武器。

今年 9 月，Dario 发文呼吁放慢前沿 AI 的发展。他在文中说，只有把技术用正确的方式造出来，好处才会兑现，只要把争取到的时间用好，“值得格外谨慎地把它做对”。

Dario 本人一直在和这两个圈子划清界限。2023 年他上纽约时报播客《Hard Fork》时说，自己不算有效利他主义者，“认同其中不少观点”，但反对“把人分成不同部落”。

quoted_text:
I respect Jukan, but I feel a little frustrated whenever I see this kind of argument.

You can build any scenario around plausible assumptions, and yes, of course, the outcome will follow from those assumptions. If you assume demand collapses, customers accumulate inventory, and contract terms get renegotiated, then naturally, memory companies’ revenue and profits will decline.

But honestly, this feels like the perspective of analysts who treat memory as just a commodity you manufacture and sell, without properly understanding the technological changes taking place in custom memory.

Who exactly are these customers we are talking about when we say they could cancel LTAs or defer deliveries? They are the very customers working with memory companies to design the next generation of HBM and 3D stacked DRAM.

After jointly designing and validating these products, can customers really cancel those volumes so easily or push deliveries out by one or two years? How would they manufacture their own products, which were designed around that memory? What happens to the launch and system deployment schedules they have already coordinated? Switching suppliers also raises questions of design compatibility and requalification. If you are going to argue that contracts can be adjusted, you also need to explain what that decision would mean for the very customers canceling them.

This is one of the biggest reasons I keep saying that memory is no longer the same cyclical industry it used to be. The parties to these LTAs are already tied together from the design stage. But if you still view memory simply as a commodity where rising prices lead to more production, and inventory buildups lead to price cuts or canceled orders, you will inevitably miss this shift in the technical and business relationships.

One more thing. These arguments about a collapse in memory demand seem to assume that planned AI data center investments will be canceled on a massive scale, or that AI infrastructure expansion will slow so substantially that memory demand falls sharply. What interests me more than whether contracts can be adjusted is why you expect demand to weaken that dramatically in the first place.

I think it would be more realistic to discuss directly whether the AI era we expect will actually fail to materialize, and whether much of the AI infrastructure investment currently planned will disappear. If that is your outlook, I can at least understand why you would expect memory demand to collapse and customers to cut volumes even for products they have jointly developed.

text:
I respect Jukan, but I feel a little frustrated whenever I see this kind of argument.

You can build any scenario around plausible assumptions, and yes, of course, the outcome will follow from those assumptions. If you assume demand collapses, customers accumulate inventory, and contract terms get renegotiated, then naturally, memory companies’ revenue and profits will decline.

But honestly, this feels like the perspective of analysts who treat memory as just a commodity you manufacture and sell, without properly understanding the technological changes taking place in custom memory.

Who exactly are these customers we are talking about when we say they could cancel LTAs or defer deliveries? They are the very customers working with memory companies to design the next generation of HBM and 3D stacked DRAM.

After jointly designing and validating these products, can customers really cancel those volumes so easily or push deliveries out by one or two years? How would they manufacture their own products, which were designed around that memory? What happens to the launch and system deployment schedules they have already coordinated? Switching suppliers also raises questions of design compatibility and requalification. If you are going to argue that contracts can be adjusted, you also need to explain what that decision would mean for the very customers canceling them.

This is one of the biggest reasons I keep saying that memory is no longer the same cyclical industry it used to be. The parties to these LTAs are already tied together from the design stage. But if you still view memory simply as a commodity where rising prices lead to more production, and inventory buildups lead to price cuts or canceled orders, you will inevitably miss this shift in the technical and business relationships.

One more thing. These arguments about a collapse in memory demand seem to assume that planned AI data center investments will be canceled on a massive scale, or that AI infrastructure expansion will slow so substantially that memory demand falls sharply. What interests me more than whether contracts can be adjusted is why you expect demand to weaken that dramatically in the first place.

I think it would be more realistic to discuss directly whether the AI era we expect will actually fail to materialize, and whether much of the AI infrastructure investment currently planned will disappear. If that is your outlook, I can at least understand why you would expect memory demand to collapse and customers to cut volumes even for products they have jointly developed.
author: mindmoon_108
quoted_text:
I'd like to believe LTAs are durable too. But take one example.

Analog chipmaker onsemi said this in 2023.
On January 5, 2023, at JPMorgan's CES forum, CEO Hassane El-Khoury was asked how much LTSAs would still hold once the shortage eased. His answer: “They are a legally binding agreement ’cause they’re a liability for the customer because they’re take or pay.” He also said he would not accept a customer reopening price talks just because it could get the same parts 10% cheaper elsewhere.

On October 30, 2023, on the Q3 earnings call, onsemi cut its SiC shipment forecast for the year from $1 billion to more than $800 million after one automotive OEM reduced demand. An analyst asked how this could happen when the company had been saying its LTSAs were legally binding. The same CEO reaffirmed that they were binding, but said he did not want to enforce the contracts just to push inventory onto a customer whose demand had dropped. If it worked for both sides, terms could be adjusted customer by customer, whether by a quarter, a year, or longer.

In its 10-K filings, onsemi also states that it amended LTSAs with some strategic customers by mutual agreement in 2024, and changed delivery schedules and committed volumes on some LTSAs in 2025 as demand shifted.

Microchip is another case. Customers in its Preferred Supply Program (PSP) originally had to place 12 months of orders and could not cancel or reschedule them unless Microchip raised prices. On its November 2025 earnings call, however, the CEO said the company had accepted some cancellations and pushouts so customers could adjust their backlog. On the same call, the CFO separately addressed the multiyear LTSAs the company had signed. Some of those contracts were still in effect, he said, but customers had been allowed to defer taking delivery of committed volumes by one to two years if they needed to.

Every time I see cases like these, I doubt how much memory makers' LTAs will protect earnings in a downcycle. Right now the most reliable thing is the prepayments and deposits themselves. That cash can go into capacity expansion today.

I can picture hyperscalers with no DRAM inventory continuing to buy at current prices. But once inventory has piled up, will they keep taking every committed unit at the same price? I have a hard time picturing memory makers holding customers to the high contract price all the way through.

The LTA itself may never be broken and may stay in place. But if both sides agree to push this year's volumes into next year or two years out, this year's earnings estimates come down. If price gets renegotiated too, margin estimates have to come down as well.

Again, I agree LTAs are sturdier than they used to be. What I question is whether, after demand turns, memory makers can still earn 80% margins on contracts signed during the upturn and keep collecting hundreds of billions of dollars in profit because of those LTAs.

The morning ritual of the two-time U.S. Investing Champion Mark Minervini (@markminervini) on why a 30% win rate still makes money, why he never bets on a fundamental idea without price confirming it, and the one sin that kills amateurs and pros alike.

He won the championship in 1997 and again in 2021, with 334.8% in the $1M+ division per the championship's record, breaking the championship record for most gain in a single year. 

Separately, Jack Schwager profiled him in Stock Market Wizards for his 5 year run of 33,554% audited gains.

We cover:
- The first account, $32,338 from selling his recording studio, and the 33,500% compounded return that Schwager had audited, by his own account

- "The cardinal sin is most traders don't cut their losses. Amateur and pro alike"
- "You do not manage money in hindsight. Risk has to be managed in real time"

- Why everybody isn't rich if the setup goes back to the 1800s: "Because it ebbs and flows", and why the tough times are boot camp

- The 7 years he spent losing money before he not only unlocked profitability, but also an insane run of performance.
- His rule for gurus: if somebody tells you how to make $10 million, "my first requirement is that they actually made $10 million themselves"

text:
昨天跟几个二级做市商朋友吃饭，他们提到一个近期比较明显的变化：和几个月前相比，散户的交易行为发生了转向。从偏做空转向偏做多，更愿意直接买现货，并喜欢提前埋伏一些币。

这种转变，很大程度上受近期妖币造富效应的影响。AKE、LAB 这类币种接连走出极端行情，在短时间内制造出一批暴富案例，让市场重新进入妖币横飞的阶段。散户在看到这些案例后，风险偏好明显上升，更倾向于主动布局而不是观望或做空。

但问题在于，经过几轮妖币的反复收割后，散户整体的资金体量已经肉眼可见地缩水。当散户这个主要收割对象的弹药明显不足时，收割的重点便开始发生转移，从散户转向大户，尤其是那些自认为掌握数据优势的聪明钱。

对做市商而言，聪明钱其实比散户更好收割，只是方式不同。散户主要是情绪驱动、信息滞后。而聪明钱则依赖自己构建的数据体系和交易逻辑。

问题在于，很多数据本身是可以被刻意制造或伪造的。做市商完全可以像渔夫设计陷阱一样，先让某些数据在前期反复验证有效，让聪明钱建立起这个指标可靠的认知，并据此敢下重仓。一旦仓位足够集中，再让数据突然失效，就可以把对方前期靠这个逻辑积累的多次利润一次性归零。

换句话说，聪明钱引以为傲的数据优势，在很多情况下可能只是做市商提前布好的局。前期数据有效，是为了让他们敢上仓。后期数据失效，则是为了完成收割。而这一次收割的效率，往往远高于对散户的零散收割。

text:
can gaussian splats be used to render interfaces?

I've seen a lot of incredible spatial demos coming out of the labs (@theworldlabs has been blowing my mind ~weekly), but they've mainly been focused on static 3D environments. I woke up today wondering: are splats any good for UI or other interactive objects, and can AI work with them?

it looks like the answer is yes and yes. I prototyped an imagen -> SHARP -> spark -> popmelt pipeline that gets decently far on the first try and really far with a few rounds of art direction + interaction tuning. Smooth animation, dynamic lighting, realistic geometry... all doable, with freely available tech

I haven't pushed into full scenes yet, but this experiment already felt somewhere between the detailed magic of generative video UI I've shared before and the stable dependability of textured 3D models (throwback). Plus LLMs like Astra are very good at working with splats, which makes fine tuning them way more fun/efficient

next: I'm weighing whether to lean into interactive spatial design (just to see how far I can get with off the shelf tools) OR see how well this workflow handles typical responsive UI design (decidedly not what splats are for, which feels interesting). thoughts?

quoted_text:
Close to half of VC decision-makers have backed at least one real winner. Only 3% have backed ten.

Blake Jackson and I have assembled what we believe is the largest and most comprehensive dataset of individual U.S. venture capitalists ever built: over 100,000 professionals affiliated with U.S. VC firms between 1996 and 2025, roughly 37,000 of them investment professionals.

We count an investment as “successful” if the startup subsequently went public, reached a unicorn valuation, or was acquired for at least five times the total capital the company had raised.

45% of middle- and senior-level VCs have at least one successful investment. Roughly a coin flip.

Everything changes when you ask not whether a VC ever hit, but how often. Among the decision-makers, 45% reach one, 28% reach two, 11% reach five, and 3% reach ten.

Fewer than four hundred people is the entire population of U.S. venture capitalists over three decades credited with ten or more successful investments. It is smaller than the combined partner rosters of a handful of large firms.

我来简单说一下。

这首先是一个非常基础的技术设计和账户安全问题。

在 OKX 品牌下，我们坚持一个基本原则：

不同站点之间，UID 要么在全局范围内保持唯一，要么就不允许用户仅凭 UID 进行跨站点内部转账。

原因很简单：UID 是账户标识。如果同一个品牌不同站点可能存在相同 UID，却又允许通过 UID 跨站点转账，就可能造成收款账户识别错误和资金误转风险。

千里之堤，溃于蚁穴。所有重大风险都是由很多个小缺陷积累而成。

很难理解，为什么这么简单的一个问题，会演变成简中 X Crypto 社区的一个热点。

更令人不解的是，居然还有那么多账号针对一位由于某平台缺陷导致资产损失的用户进行谩骂、人身攻击，同时替相关平台洗地。

究竟是什么样的企业文化和价值观，在背后推波助澜？

I rewatched Patrick Collison's 2012 talk on the early days of Stripe. Here's what still holds and what aged 👇

Still true:

> The start is slow. Almost zero volume for 6 months. The curve only took off after 2.5 years.
> Get real users fast. Their first live user came a few weeks in.
> Make 100 people really happy before you try to scale.
> The people who build the product do support.
> Sell to developers, not CFOs.
> Easy to start with, but works for the biggest companies.
> "It doesn't get easier, you just go faster."
> Lower the friction to pay and more people can sell online.

Aged:

> Calling the whole team on every error.
> 19 months in production before a public launch. 
> Getting access to banks is easier than in 2010. Compliance is a lot heavier.

text:
这两天 TapeOut 圈子里，$BEM 的持有人在同时经历两种情绪。

一种是委屈。@Mirro7777 说：看到 gang 和 BEM 成了现在这样，包括 TapeOut 举家搬迁到了 OKX，不知道如何描述这样的感觉。BEM 拉来了场外资金和一批老矿工到 BNB 链，CZ 问过一句「有什么用」之后就再无下文。

另一种是兴奋。@iruletrenches 则反问：OKX 为什么全力接住 BEM，把整个生态接进 OKX Wallet、办六位数奖金的黑客松？BNB Chain 中文的负责人和币安的现任、前任高管，为什么开始关注 BEM 的账号？

同一件事，有人觉得被冷落，有人觉得被争抢。我觉得这才是 BEM 现在最牵动人的地方。价格从 9 月中的 74 美元跌到 16 美元，大家心里等的那件事比涨回去更大：BEM 会不会被重新定价。

🐋 第一个预期：BSC 回头看

TapeOut 是在 BNB Chain 上长起来的，BEM 的主池、矿机、大部分矿工都在那边。被冷落的那段时间，社区最难受的是没有一句回应。

现在有人看到 BNB Chain 那边的人开始关注了。只是关注，还没有任何动作，但对一个等了很久的社区来说，这一点信号就够大家想很多。

🐋 第二个预期：X Layer 的黑客松

OKX 这边是真金白银。X Layer 和 TapeOut 合办的开发者加速计划，奖池 10 万 USDT，作品 12 月 7 日截止；前面还有一个点子征集，11 月 17 日截止。11 月 5 日 OKX Wallet 中文的直播上，X Layer 说会给开发者资金、在 OKX Wallet 里原生集成、帮着看技术架构。

一个交易所愿意为一条链上的一个协议做这些，持有人自然会想：它看到了什么。

🐋 第三个预期：TapeOut 自己的升级

同一场直播里，TapeOut 的 Alda（@nat_poprika）说 TapeOut 正和 X Layer 做一个新的核心功能，解决 DeWEB 单个文件 8.4 MB 上限和 TapeSend 每条消息都要付 Gas 的问题，细节还没公布。主群有人问 @Blonskr  V2，管理员火星人Ryan 回「快啦快啦」。

升级之后 BEM 能用在哪、能多烧多少、矿机会不会更值钱，现在谁都说不准。说不准，恰恰是它值钱的地方。

🐋 矿工不卖，押的就是这个

每天挖出 7,200 枚 BEM，当天卖掉的不到三成，还有 6 万多枚挖了一直没领。

如果你相信一次重新定价就在前面，最合理的做法就是先拿着，谁也不想卖在利好落地的前一天。

🐋 这种预期怕什么

怕时间。11 月 17 日、12 月 7 日、V2 上线，这些日子会一个个到。上次写 XDOG 那篇说过，问号挂得越久，信的人越少。每过一个日子都没带来新的买家，预期就会薄一层。

也怕兑现。利好真落地的那天，也是攒着的 BEM 最想出手的时候。

BSC、黑客松、升级，你最在等哪一个？

text:
젠슨 황과 앨리스 황, 미 정보당국이 연인으로 판단했다는 FT 보도의 전말 ㅣ 261107

1. FT는 미 정보당국이 엔비디아 $NVDA 의 젠슨 황 CEO와 앨리스 황을 연인 관계로 판단했다고 보도함.

올해 초 정보기관 첩보를 토대로 미 당국자들이 쓴 메모에 이 내용이 담겼다고 함.

엔비디아는 메모와 두 사람의 관계에 대한 논평을 거부했음.

2. 앨리스 황은 중국 국적이고 중국명은 황러임.

싱가포르 데이터센터 기업 메가스피드의 임원이고, 메가스피드는 엔비디아의 고객사임.

3. 둘이 함께 있는 모습은 사진으로 공개된 적이 있음.

2024년 6월 대만 타이베이의 한 술집에서 다른 AI 기업 임원들과 함께 앉은 사진이 알려졌음.

4. 그런데 미 정보당국은 이 만남을 다르게 봤다고 NYT가 보도함.

author: teortaxesTex
quoted_text:
some takes on DeepSeek Harness (dsh): i've been using it for a few days, and i'm also a heavy user of pi and cc:
- a clean install of dsh gives better results than a clean install of pi, because dsh ships with many built-in plugins already and set them on by default.
- the "agent teams" plugin is a must-have (it's off by default); it's something pi lacks and is similar to what ultra mode does in cc.
- i'd call dsh an IDE or even OS, especially with its creator mode. you can really turn dsh into a superapp that becomes your go-to place for productivity, entertainment, and management. the default dsh looks super dry and minimal but i see people customize its look & features to make it theirs. i like the recent trend toward highly customizable UIs; in fact, that's what i've been doing with pi and similar tools over the last few months — building a daily IDE that fits my habits and tastes. opinionated UI is not dying, but struggling in 2026 i say.
- dsh's best UX is in the GUI, not the terminal (unlike pi), and you can also access dsh remotely from mobile — something pi doesn't offer out of the box. if you use cc's /remote-control a lot on mobile and web, dsh is comfortable enough to switch to.
- pi is still useful for research purposes: if you want to study model/harness behavior in a strictly controlled environment and toolset, dsh also has a minimal mode, but it doesn't feel minimal enough to me. pi's interface is also faster and leaner if you want to manage multiple sessions yourself.
- dsh doesn't have an official or verified plugin store, which could be a security issue when people eagerly search for and install 3p plugins and bring malicious prompts into the host, especially given the hype around it these days.

text:
1. The counterargument that deliveries can't be pushed back by a year or two just because the two sides worked together from design through validation becomes meaningless once the demand decline is real.

2. Even if they were involved from the design stage, I don't think we have reached the kind of extreme customization seen in foundry, where Micron couldn't do what Samsung was doing.

3. Joint design also constrains which HBM gets used, but I don't think it settles who carries the inventory burden when accelerator demand misses. Say the production plan is cut from 1 million units to 800,000. Is the customer obligated to take the 200,000 units' worth, or can the memory makers simply push that volume onto them? That needs to be clear.

The claim that memory has completely shed its commodity character is, in my view, the most dangerous one. There are still more players than in foundry, where TSMC dominates, and they can substitute for one another.
author: jukan05
quoted_text:
I respect Jukan, but I feel a little frustrated whenever I see this kind of argument.

You can build any scenario around plausible assumptions, and yes, of course, the outcome will follow from those assumptions. If you assume demand collapses, customers accumulate inventory, and contract terms get renegotiated, then naturally, memory companies’ revenue and profits will decline.

But honestly, this feels like the perspective of analysts who treat memory as just a commodity you manufacture and sell, without properly understanding the technological changes taking place in custom memory.

Who exactly are these customers we are talking about when we say they could cancel LTAs or defer deliveries? They are the very customers working with memory companies to design the next generation of HBM and 3D stacked DRAM.

After jointly designing and validating these products, can customers really cancel those volumes so easily or push deliveries out by one or two years? How would they manufacture their own products, which were designed around that memory? What happens to the launch and system deployment schedules they have already coordinated? Switching suppliers also raises questions of design compatibility and requalification. If you are going to argue that contracts can be adjusted, you also need to explain what that decision would mean for the very customers canceling them.

This is one of the biggest reasons I keep saying that memory is no longer the same cyclical industry it used to be. The parties to these LTAs are already tied together from the design stage. But if you still view memory simply as a commodity where rising prices lead to more production, and inventory buildups lead to price cuts or canceled orders, you will inevitably miss this shift in the technical and business relationships.

One more thing. These arguments about a collapse in memory demand seem to assume that planned AI data center investments will be canceled on a massive scale, or that AI infrastructure expansion will slow so substantially that memory demand falls sharply. What interests me more than whether contracts can be adjusted is why you expect demand to weaken that dramatically in the first place.

I think it would be more realistic to discuss directly whether the AI era we expect will actually fail to materialize, and whether much of the AI infrastructure investment currently planned will disappear. If that is your outlook, I can at least understand why you would expect memory demand to collapse and customers to cut volumes even for products they have jointly developed.

speculative decoding is one of the main tricks for making AI answer faster: a small model quickly drafts the next few words, and the big model checks them all at once

in papers however (below are few most interesting ones) these speedups are usually measured with a single user, while on a busy server the GPU has less spare capacity for drafting, so the gain shrinks

DFlash: 5.1x faster with 1 request at a time, 2.4-2.9x with 32
https://t.co/FF8ECCMqWM

P-EAGLE in @vllm_project: up to 1.69x over EAGLE-3 with 1 request, 1.05-1.25x with 64
https://t.co/9CPZZK7nZz

DeepSeek’s DSpark reports the number a provider actually needs: on live traffic, each user gets answers 60-85% faster while the server handles the same total load
https://t.co/Qp6UdFRTWS

so “5x faster” is true for one person in a chat window. for anyone serving many users, one needs to check out speed per user at the same load

text: What we are up against when it comes to protecting our assets.
author: Scobleizer
quoted_text:
We finally have more details about how attackers stole approximately $6.34 billion from Binance.

And the story is considerably more interesting than someone stealing a password.

According to reporting published November 3, the attack involved a months-long operation targeting employees responsible for cryptocurrency wallet infrastructure.

The first compromise reportedly happened in June.

A Binance engineer downloaded a malicious software package while searching for an AI coding tool.

The company replaced the affected computer and rotated credentials.

But the attackers had already learned something valuable.

They knew which employees worked on the systems responsible for managing cryptocurrency wallets.

Then, in September, the attackers approached another engineer through a legitimate job-search platform.

They posed as a prospective employer.

They conducted fake interviews.

And they persuaded the engineer to install malware as part of the recruitment process.

Think about that.

The attackers didn't need to send an obviously suspicious email promising a lottery prize.

They created an interaction that resembled a legitimate professional opportunity.

The engineer was participating in what appeared to be a normal hiring process.

That gave the attackers a reason to request technical work.

And a reason to ask the engineer to install software.

The attack reportedly continued through October.

On October 20, the attackers used compromised access and Binance's internal AI tooling to reach additional systems.

On October 29, they used a compromised developer's computer and previously stolen credentials to execute the transactions that drained the exchange's hot wallets.

The FBI has attributed the theft to North Korean hackers.

North Korea disputes the accusation.

Binance says approximately $2.85 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted.

The company's investigation continues.

Here's what I find most interesting.

The attackers exploited several different forms of trust.

The engineer trusted what appeared to be a legitimate software installation.

Another employee trusted what appeared to be a genuine recruiter.

The company's internal systems trusted authenticated employees and services.

And the wallet infrastructure ultimately processed unauthorized transactions.

Each step helped the attackers reach the next one.

This is why cybersecurity can't depend exclusively on establishing that someone has valid credentials.

A legitimate employee can be manipulated.

A trusted computer can be compromised.

And an authorized application can be used for an unauthorized purpose.

The involvement of an internal AI tool adds another issue.

Organizations need to understand which information their AI systems can retrieve and which actions they can perform.

If an attacker compromises an employee account, what can the attacker do through the AI tools associated with that account?

Can the agent retrieve sensitive configuration information?

Can it interact with privileged systems?

Can it execute code?

And does the organization maintain records showing what happened?

These questions should be answered before an incident.

There's also a lesson for anyone interviewing for a technical job.

A recruiter asking you to install software or execute code during an interview should trigger additional verification.

Contact the employer through an independently established channel.

Confirm the recruiter's identity.

And avoid running unfamiliar software on a computer that contains sensitive company information.

The Binance incident is a particularly expensive demonstration of a familiar security problem.

Criminals don't always need to defeat sophisticated cryptography.

Sometimes they persuade someone with legitimate access to perform the first dangerous action.

text:
Chamath Palihapitiya admits his blind spot on America's broken two-tier economy

PALIHAPITIYA: "I got it totally totally totally wrong. I got it totally wong."

"I'll go through all the ways in which I got it wrong, but I just want to first acknowledge what my blind spot is. Like most people's blind spots, but I can just speak for myself, it is through the lens of my own lived experience and very narrowly what is in my best interests. And I think what we had was a move away from the culture wars that was very much in my best interest, but I think it was in everybody else's best interests as well. I don't think that was on the ballot. But what I don't think I understood clearly enough, and I think that this election has made extremely clear, is that since COVID, we have moved past political ideology. And I want to say this again: I do not think Democrats or Republicans matter. That is my real takeaway after this election. There is a central block of people that vote the prescient issues of our time."

"It was a gargantuan win for Biden, then it was a gargantuan win for Trump, and then it was a gargantuan win for the Democrats in these midterms. What are these people voting for? I think what they are shouting now—they were trying to signal and now they are shouting—is a broad-based belief that the economy has completely decoupled from reality and is broken. The economic reality in America is broken."

"There is a small percentage of people, the four of us on this pod and all of our friends, who are the asset owners of America. And we have benefited in every weather condition. When rates were zero, we benefited because we were able to build our businesses with very cheap capital. When rates were high, we benefited because we had pricing power. And in every condition in between, whether there were tariffs, whether there were not tariffs, whether there were subsidies, whether there were not subsidies, we've all managed to continue to accumulate and grow assets, but we are few and far between."

"And then there's everybody else who are wage earners, and the structural capacity of the American economy to support and grow wage earners is broken. It's clear. Why do I say that? I do not think, and I disagree with Freeberg, I don't think this has anything to do with socialism. I don't think the far left won particularly more than they were expected. I don't think the far right won particularly more than was expected. This is a complete and total repudiation about the state of the economy. The economy is broken. I have a few charts to support my point of view. Number one, if this was ideological and if ideology mattered, money in politics would have had a more direct impact on the election."

text:
Every evening, I return to you,
where the sea embraces the dying light,
and heaven spills its final gold
upon a world that has forgotten me.

You find me waiting in the silence,
and lay your warmth against my cheek,
so tenderly, so gently,
I almost forget what I am.

I close my eyes.

The first kiss is always gentle.
Then comes the fire.

It blossoms softly beneath my skin,
a thousand beautiful, burning wounds.
And little pieces of eternity
rise like ashes from a dying prayer.

I should turn away.
I should retreat into the shadows,
where nothing can hurt me.

But the darkness has held me for centuries,
and never once held me close.

So burn me, my beautiful torment.
Take a little more of me each day.
Let the wind scatter what remains,
and let me call the pain a blessing.

For what is eternity worth
when all its nights are empty?

I would endure a thousand sunsets,
let each one unravel me into ash,
if only for one trembling heartbeat
your warmth might linger upon my skin.

And when you sink beneath the sea,
I remain where your last light fell,
my fingers reaching into the silence,
begging for a touch that never stays.

They say I have fallen in love
with the setting sun.

Let them.

For in its final, golden touch,
I almost feel your fingers
slipping between mine...

And for one beautiful, cruel moment,
I forget...

that the earth took your hand
before I ever learned to let it go.

为什么严重：

- 范围很大：Linux 4.4 以后的内核都受影响，基本等于所有还在用的 Linux 服务器。
- 不需要登录：只要服务器上有一个对外开放的 IPv4 TCP 端口，攻击者发几个特制的包就能打。可能的后果是内核崩溃、泄露内存，或者破坏内存。
- 已经有人做到远程执行代码：研究人员对开着 MPTCP 的机器演示过未授权远程代码执行。Ubuntu 默认是开着 MPTCP 的。
- 现在还没有补丁：截至今天，Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04 / 26.04 的修复内核都还是“修复进行中”，装了最新内核也没用。AWS 公告说得很直接：只有升级内核并重启才算彻底修复。

我这边做了这几件事（裸金属和 VPS 一共 5 台）：

1. 先挡住入口
→ 用 nftables 丢弃所有带 IP options 的 IPv4 TCP 包
→ 正常流量几乎不会带 IP options，所以基本没有副作用
→ 每台都实测过：带 options 的连接被拦下，普通 SSH 正常

2. 关掉 MPTCP
→ net.mptcp.enabled=0，写进 sysctl.d，重启后也生效
→ 这一步只能减少被利用的条件，问题本身还在

3. 关掉不必要的公网端口
→ 3 台 VPS 关掉公网 SSH 22，只走 Tailscale SSH
→ 基本上端口全部关闭

4. 等补丁
→ 每天自动查一次 Ubuntu 的修复状态，一发布就提醒我升级重启

几个容易踩的坑：

- 防火墙规则重启就没了。补丁出来之前别随手重启，重启了也换不上修复。
- 改 SSH 端口号对这个洞基本没用。漏洞在内核的 TCP 握手上，任何开着的端口都能当入口，扫一遍全端口也就几分钟。
- 关 22 之前先设好自动回滚。我的做法是先挂一个 5 分钟后自动重新放行的定时器，确认 Tailscale 能连上再取消，避免把自己锁在外面。
- 用 Coolify 的话，别把 Docker 内网访问本机 22 的放行也删了，不然部署会断。
- 80/443 这类业务端口必须开着，所以在补丁出来之前，真正起作用的还是第 1 步那条丢包规则。

参考：
AWS 公告 https://t.co/HWrn7X2toA
Ubuntu 修复状态 https://t.co/kNdn3QuQhh

My advice to startup founders is that post pmf companies look completely different then pre pmf. 

Pre pmf CEO/product lead needs to micro manage and get into everyone’s business. Until the people revolt because they are so busy dealing with actual growth problems and know better than the CEO.

I like when people call me non technical.

I mean forget about the 4 Million line pure C++ game codebase we built pre AI, 2 software company exits (one didn’t work out but I’ve seen the failure case too), the Computer Science and Engineering degree, the software services company I ran in 2018, or the fact that I used to teach my friends Ruby on Rails in 2012 or the freelancing history I have with it.

Or even the fact that random shit we’ve built to pass time like Godinabox had a few million users (which sounds cool to a young engineer but is much smaller in value compared to the billion+ views we have on the content side of the business).

What is important is that in my 30s I learned where true value is created: in solving a problem for your customer. Not in creating tutorials or being “technical”, that India values above all. I know it sounds dumb: “of course the goal is to create value for customers, silly!”.  But engineers don’t instinctively understand this until they lose a few times. Until they break out of the mould of “I must signal to other engineers!”.

When people call me non-technical it reminds me to focus once again on what customers care about. Technology is important, but at Aeos’s scale today I can hire someone to do it and focus on more important tasks: once again and for posterity - like caring about my customers.

quoted_text:
Asahi Linux is moving everything from the MIT licence to GPLv2-or-later.

Asahi is the volunteer project that reverse-engineers Apple Silicon Macs so they can run Linux. In today's Linux 7.3 progress report, developer James Calligeros explains why: people have been using the permissive licence to take the team's work. "In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin."

The report points to WINE, which switched from MIT to LGPL in 2002 for the same reason: "Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it."

The same report brings real wins too. M3 Macs now install without the EXPERT flag, Thunderbolt support (USB3 and networking for now) is shipping to users, and the team got GTA IV and Fallout: New Vegas running outside the muvm VM using Google's per-process page size patches.

text:
It is heartbreaking to see antisemitism in my hometown. I was born in Wyncote, near Philadelphia, and it makes me angry and ashamed to see hatred tolerated there.

The numbers show this is not an abstract concern. The Anti-Defamation League recorded 465 antisemitic incidents across Pennsylvania in 2024, an 18% increase over 2023. It tracked 189 incidents in Philadelphia and 51 in Montgomery County. These reports include harassment, vandalism, and assault; they are not all classified as crimes. (https://t.co/LNbuEF4lCN, https://t.co/VD98Hg5XEp)

Hateful expression harms more than its immediate target. In a 2025 survey of Jewish Americans, 79% said they were concerned about antisemitism, and 52% said they had worried about their personal safety because of their identity. Nearly half reported taking steps to increase their security. A research review also found that exposure to hate is associated with worse psychological well-being, more negative stereotypes, and less trust between groups. (https://t.co/VD98Hg5XEp, https://t.co/YJT6NcR4VF)

It takes me back to the racism I experienced in the 1960s: signs throughout the South declaring that Black people could be refused service, along with separate “white” and “colored” signs on bathrooms and drinking fountains,”no niggers”. I remember what that hatred looked and felt like. We cannot accept it in any form, directed at any people.

I wish I could be there to stand with those protesting HATE. I am asking elected officials and other leaders in Philadelphia: Where are the clear statements condemning antisemitism? When hateful language is excused or repeated, it can make hostility seem acceptable and deepen fear and division. Leaders should speak plainly and consistently: antisemitism and hate have no place in our communities.

What the hell? We have to speak up.

Reggie Jackson
The Mr. October Guy

text:
纽约时报 11 月 5 日发了一篇 Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei 的长篇人物稿，赶在 Anthropic 本月上市之前。记者采访了他二十多位同学、朋友、老师和同事，还看到了他早年的邮件和在 OpenAI 的内部消息。

Dario 通过公司发言人拒绝受访。所以下面的故事大多是别人的回忆，只有一部分有邮件、博客等文件佐证。

这些人的说法归结起来是：Dario 年轻时泡在“理性主义”和“有效利他主义”两个圈子里，两者合在一起，让他认定 AI 危险到只有他和想法相近的人才值得托付去造。朋友和同事认为，这推动他抢在不在乎安全的人之前造出 AI，也让他想把这项技术掌控在自己手里。

【两个圈子是什么】

理性主义是围绕 Eliezer Yudkowsky 等人的博客形成的网络社群，讲究用冷静的推理看世界，其中很多人认为 AI 终将强大到毁掉人类社会。

有效利他主义跟它差不多同时成长起来，主张用数学算清楚怎么捐钱、怎么做事，才能让好处最大。两边共同相信：靠严密的计算，可以改变人类的未来。

【从小就爱算账】

Dario 在旧金山 Mission 区长大，父亲是皮匠，母亲管理公共图书馆的翻修工程。高中读的是旧金山最好的公立高中 Lowell，同时去伯克利上课。同学记得他那时就在琢磨功利主义，也就是“让最多的生命得到最多的幸福”。

上大学后，他和高中好友在寿司店争论功利主义。Dario 吃素，但认为吃螃蟹没问题，因为螃蟹是无脊椎动物。

朋友出了个思想实验：如果有人拼命杀鸡，杀到多少只时，杀掉这个人才算合理？据在场的 Nathan Avery 回忆，Dario 笑了笑，说从功利主义的角度看，总有某个数量的鸡，分量会超过一个人。

【父亲去世，和“时间有限”】

2006 年 Dario 从斯坦福毕业，去普林斯顿读物理博士，后来专攻生物物理和计算神经科学。同一年，父亲因丙肝去世。

前女友 Jade Wang 回忆，两人常聊：一辈子只研究一种病的科学家，影响力比不上给整个领域造工具和方法的人。Dario 举的例子就是父亲，父亲没等到后来能治好大多数丙肝的药。

2007 年，24 岁的 Dario 读完 Ray Kurzweil 的《奇点临近》，对来访的高中同学 Colin Heckman 说，奇点会在 2040 年前到来，人类以后可能和机器融合。Heckman 说他从此“着了魔”，说 AI 必须造对，不然人类就完了。

那段时间，Dario 在读 Accelerating Future、Overcoming Bias 这类讨论 AI 毁灭人类的小众博客，还鼓动朋友和妹妹 Daniela 去参加 Yudkowsky 办的奇点研究所年会（现在叫机器智能研究所，MIRI）。

纽约时报看到一封 2008 年的邮件，Dario 在信里称 Yudkowsky 是“我遇到过最深刻的思想者之一”。Yudkowsky 现在给纽约时报回邮件说，Dario 如今不向他请教，也不听他的建议，他也不记得 Dario 什么时候这样做过。

同年，Dario 通过经济学家 Tyler Cowen 的博客知道了 GiveWell，一个评估慈善机构效率的组织，开始活跃在它的论坛上。2010 年他在邮件里说在考虑去做金融，好赚更多钱捐出去。

同年他在 GiveWell 博客上公开盘算一笔 1 万美元的捐款，在成人结核病项目和非洲儿童疫苗项目之间权衡。他写道，成年人能有更深刻的体验，“一个成年人的死亡也许比一个婴儿的死亡糟糕两三倍”。最后他还是选了疫苗项目，理由是这家执行得更有效。

2011 年起他在斯坦福做癌细胞研究的博士后，吃抗衰老补剂，严格坚持游泳，还研究节食延寿。Avery 说，他常讲时间是唯一不可再生的资源，对自己的时间“毫不留情”。据两位知情人说，2014 年他确诊睾丸癌，化疗后完全康复。

【一屋子未来的创始人】

那几年，Daniela 和 GiveWell 创始人 Holden Karnofsky 在交往（两人 2017 年结婚），住进旧金山一处合租屋。后来搬进来的还有 Dario、理论物理学家 Jared Kaplan，以及大学辍学、数学由 Dario 辅导过的 Chris Olah。

据三位去过的人说，室友们会一起讨论 Yudkowsky 的文章，也一起去火人节，有时穿动物服装。Kaplan 和 Olah 后来与 Amodei 兄妹一起创办了 Anthropic，Karnofsky 2025 年也加入了公司。

【在 OpenAI，立场变硬】

2014 年 Dario 进入百度硅谷实验室，同事说他“几乎一有机会就激烈争论”。2015 年他对同事说，AI 可能很快赶上甚至超过人脑。同年他去 Google Brain 做 AI 安全，和 Olah 等人写了论文《AI 安全中的具体问题》。

2016 年他加入当时还是非营利组织的 OpenAI，带安全团队和研究“规模定律”的团队。七位前同事说，他在 OpenAI 的立场越来越强硬。

纽约时报看到的内部消息显示，2016 年特朗普当选三天后，Dario 写道，他“不愿在一个威权国家研究具有军事威力的技术”。他还说，给特朗普竞选捐了 125 万美元的 Peter Thiel “在道德上应受谴责”，OpenAI 不该再收他的钱。Thiel 创办的 Founders Fund 后来投资了 Anthropic。

据三位知情人说，2017 年 Dario 牵线，让 Karnofsky 的慈善机构（现名 Coefficient Giving）给 OpenAI 捐了 3000 万美元，Karnofsky 也进了 OpenAI 董事会。Dario 当时是这家机构的技术顾问。

2018 年 Daniela 加入 OpenAI，后来做到安全与政策副总裁，有员工开始担心兄妹俩影响力太大。据三位知情人说，那年 12 月研究员 Joshua Achiam 劝 Sam Altman 别让 Dario 当首席伦理官，认为 AI 的监督应该由不同视角的人分担，并坚持请外部专家。Dario 当面提高嗓门说，没有人比他更合适。

同年兄妹俩接手了 GPT 项目，探索让 AI 在人类指导下学会做事的安全技术。纽约时报的判断是，先把 AI 推近危险、再用安全技术去检验，成了 Dario 此后整个职业生涯的做法。

据两位知情人说，OpenAI 总裁 Greg Brockman 想参与 GPT，兄妹俩不让。Dario 多次对 Altman 说，不把 Brockman 挡在外面他就走。Altman 拒绝了。2020 年 12 月，Dario、Daniela 和几位同事离职，四周后创办了 Anthropic。

【和今天的 Anthropic 有什么关系】

Anthropic 2021 年成立时，Amodei 兄妹和另外五位联合创始人都在这两个圈子附近待过。纽约时报认为，公司做大以后，这套想法也随着 Dario 一次次公开表态变得越来越有分量：他主张限制对华芯片出口，主张监管 AI 防止失控，在和美国国防部的争执里坚持 AI 不能用于大规模监控美国人、不能用于自主武器。

今年 9 月，Dario 发文呼吁放慢前沿 AI 的发展。他在文中说，只有把技术用正确的方式造出来，好处才会兑现，只要把争取到的时间用好，“值得格外谨慎地把它做对”。

Dario 本人一直在和这两个圈子划清界限。2023 年他上纽约时报播客《Hard Fork》时说，自己不算有效利他主义者，“认同其中不少观点”，但反对“把人分成不同部落”。

text:
people seem to be interpreting this as “go and do MATS”. that’s not what I meant -- MATS is pretty good, but there’s lots of work to be done outside of AI safety fellowships!! here’s a quick brainstorm:
- replicate important papers and results in AI safety
- write up relevant findings from different papers on one topic, and try to reconcile any contradictions (or point out the contradictions, and suggest what work could resolve them)
- read and summarise companies’ risk reports and AI safety research
- pick particular claims in risk reports you think are important and write explanations of them, or stress-test them
- write and maintain up-to-date summaries of areas of AI safety research (who’s working on them, what is the current state of our understanding, what’s the most important work and open questions)
- write explainers of important technical questions or problems for busy non-technical audiences. 
e.g., what’s going on with CoT controllability and why does it matter; what do we know about reward seeking in frontier models; why might models sabotage AI safety research, and what signs of this have we seen; what’s going on with AI R&D uplift and why is this scary
- become an expert in a research subfield and write up your takes on how good it is, how much resources/effort we should spend on it, what needs to be done next
- pick literally any of the megapapers from the last 12mo, and one of the open questions it lists, and try to answer it
- write explainers of recent AI safety incidents for the general public
- write down a plan for making AI safety go well, notice how far reality is from that plan, and make it happen – e.g. tell an org you think is important about how they’re fucking up and how they can fix it, publicly write about what you want people to do
- call or write to your representative and express your beliefs about AI safety
- cold email people you think are doing good work, come up with some way you could help them, and pitch them on you doing that
- stop overindexing on "do research"; go be a chief of staff or special projects or generalist at a great org. (if you can't get hired yet, talk to people, figure out an important project you can do in ~3mo, do it, then get hired)
- go to a pause AI protest or volunteer for a local group (if you endorse them; I’m a fan of Pause AI UK and haven’t looked deeply into other groups)
- lots of people are going to be very busy now; if you’re dispositionally a chin-scratching contemplative kind of person, now is a good time to do the big picture strategy/And What Else work they won’t have time to do

i put this list together v quickly, i'm missing lots of important things. my main point is that there is _so_ much work to be done

New market map: compute-in-memory chips in 2026 — 88 companies, 13 layers

The biggest valuations aren't in true in-memory compute. Unconventional AI (analog, route undisclosed) is at $4.5B and d-Matrix (digital in-memory, data-center inference) at $2B, while Cerebras, the big-SRAM neighbor, sits at $56.4B.

Layer by layer:

1. RRAM / memristor (8) — Mentium, Innostar (ReRAM pilot line), MemSilicon (RMB 400M+ raised). Weights stored as device conductance.

2. Flash / NOR (4) — Mythic ($125M raised), Witmem, UCUN, Anaflash. Mature flash cells doing analog multiply-accumulate.

3. Charge-domain & other analog (10) — Unconventional AI ($4.5B val.), EnCharge AI ($100M+ raised), Sagence (~$58M), Aspinity, Blumind.

4. Digital CIM at the edge (9) — Axelera AI ($250M+ raised), Houmo (160 TOPS), GSI Technology ($25.1M revenue), PIMCHIP.

5. Digital CIM for the data center (6) — d-Matrix ($2B val.), Fractile ($220M), Rain AI. In-memory plus chiplets for LLM inference.

6. DRAM / HBM near-memory (10) — XCENA ($570M val.), NeuroBlade ($83M), Samsung HBM-PIM (1.2 TFLOPS), SK hynix AiM, UPMEM.

7. Edge at-memory (3) — MemryX ($44M raised), Syntiant ($271.8M revenue in 2025), Untether AI (team joined AMD).

8. Big-SRAM chips (4) — Cerebras ($56.4B), SambaNova ($11B), Groq ($3.5B), Graphcore. Trade on-chip SRAM for bandwidth; not true in-memory.

9. Research lines (11) — imec (2,900 TOPS/W), TSMC (254 TOPS/W, 5nm digital macro), Intel 18A (147 TOPS/W), IBM NorthPole, Stanford NeuRRAM.

10. Photonic computing (7) — Lightmatter ($4.4B val.), Celestial AI ($2.5B), Neurophos ($110M), Q.ANT. Light for matrix math and interconnect.

11. Neuromorphic (7) — Intel Loihi / Hala Point (1.15B neurons), BrainChip, Innatera, SynSense.

12. Memory IP & devices (8) — Weebit Nano, Everspin ($20.6M quarterly revenue), Ferroelectric Memory Co (EUR 100M).

13. Equipment, materials & EDA (1) — Applied Materials.

Data as of Nov 2026, public sources; company-reported numbers are labeled as such on the map.

text:
1/ People are reading the Aaronson-Ambainis proof as "quantum is dead." It actually says something much narrower, and more useful.

2/ The claim: if a problem has no structure, a quantum computer can't beat a classical one by more than a polynomial factor. Most theorists already believed this. Now there's a proof.

3/ But every quantum use case that matters runs on structure. 
Shor exploits periodicity. 
Simulating molecules exploits the fact that nature follows local physical laws. 
Neither is a black box.

4/ What it hurts: "exponential quantum speedup for generic optimization"

5/ Quantum's real job was always simulating nature: catalysts, batteries, enzymes, new materials. That's untouched. If anything, the landscape just got clearer.

text:
What abundance creates

In 1888, Kodak introduced a camera ordinary people could operate. The company handled film processing, opening photography to families who had little interest in mastering the technical craft.

They photographed holidays, children, pets, and ordinary afternoons. Those pictures expanded the range of subjects people considered worth capturing. Amateur photography eventually influenced artists, too.

The internet opened publishing, music, and video to people who lacked access to established distribution. Many found audiences. Entire creative careers became possible alongside an enormous amount of work that few people will ever encounter.

Lowering the cost of creation brings more people into the process. More attempts can uncover possibilities that a smaller group would miss.

Abundance also changes the job of finding worthwhile work. Attention remains limited as output grows. Distribution platforms become powerful because they determine what gets discovered, and creators study the patterns those platforms reward.

You can see the results in YouTube thumbnails, popular post formats, and the landing pages of software companies. Imitating something that already works is often a reasonable business decision.

AI arrives in a culture that has spent years learning how to repeat successful patterns. It can now reproduce them at remarkable speed, with results that look increasingly polished.

I wonder how much originality gets lost when everyone can make more of what already works.

I've started thinking about this as the industrialization of mediocrity.

The court record also documents that she later texted Sabatini seeking to rekindle the relationship, while trial evidence showed her repeatedly pursuing him.

The article devotes extensive space to an anonymous student and Knouse’s losing trial lawyer, who now attacks the jury after choosing to put this case before it. It gives far less scrutiny to the damaging messages, contradictions, and other evidence those jurors actually saw.

text:
now that apple put xcode inside claude code, here’s how i’d find, build and grow an iOS app with AI agents:

find it
- open appfigures or sensor tower and sort utilities by revenue
- filter for apps with a rating under 3.5
- bonus points if the top app hasn't shipped an update in 6+ months
- check the keywords they rank for in appfigures. low difficulty + high revenue is the sweet spot
- scroll the "you might also like" row on the top app's page. every app there is another market to check
- or find a startup idea on https://t.co/a5ARFnvky2 based on social sentiment

validate it
- use facundoolano/app-store-scraper to pull every review for the top 20
- give them to an agent: "cluster the 1 and 2 star reviews into the top 5 complaints and quote the users"
- pick the app where the complaints are about the product, not the price
- if people complain about the price but keep paying, that's demand. if they complain about bugs, that's your opening
- search reddit for "alternative to [app]". every thread is a list of people waiting for you

build it
- claude code + apple's new xcode plugin to build, preview and fix
- cameroncooke/XcodeBuildMCP so the agent can build, test and run the simulator on its own
- joshuayoes/ios-simulator-mcp so it can tap, swipe and screenshot like a user
- write a skill with the top 5 complaints so every feature gets checked against them
- apple's foundation models for on-device ai, so your inference cost is $0
- app intents so siri and personal agents can use your app too
- add an "import from [competitor]" button. make switching take 10 seconds

test it
- maestro tests every flow the reviewers complained about
- the agent runs them on every screen size before each build
- if the competitor's worst flow takes 6 taps, yours takes 2
- sentry for crashes, telemetrydeck for analytics
- testflight it to 20 people from those reddit threads before launch

monetize it
- revenuecat for subscriptions and mrr
- superwall to test paywalls without shipping a new build
- paywall right after the first win, never on launch
- annual as the default with a 3-day trial, weekly as the anchor
- turn on win-back offers for everyone who cancels

rank it
- your screenshots answer each complaint directly. "no ads." "works offline." "cancel anytime."
- fastlane snapshot + frameit regenerates every screenshot automatically
- a/b test them with app store connect's product page optimization
- have the agent localize your listing into 10 languages. most competitors only rank in english
- ask for a review right after a win with apple's built-in review prompt, never after an error

grow it
- find 10 creators in your niche on tiktok one. small monthly base + a bonus for every 100k views
- give each one a fresh tiktok account that only posts about your niche
- apify's tiktok scraper pulls the top 100 hooks in your niche every week. that's your hook bank
- every creator tests 3 new hooks a day in capcut. anything that loses people in the first 3 seconds gets cut
- arcads or heygen for ai ugc when you need 50 variations of a winner
- postiz to schedule everything across tiktok, reels and shorts
- faceless slideshow accounts posting 3x a day: problem, screenshot, result
- when an organic video takes off, put money behind it with tiktok spark ads instead of making new ads
- a unique apple offer code for every creator so you know exactly who drove each subscriber
- a quiz landing page on framer that ends in "download the app." web-to-app funnels convert better than cold traffic
- appsflyer to track which video, creator and ad actually turned into revenue
- apple ads on the competitor's name

i could do a whole episode on @startupideaspod if people are interested. i will never gatekeep anything im learning in real-time.

text:
Myślenie niektórych ludzi po prostu mnie rozpierdala. Naprawdę nie potraficie połączyć kilku prostych faktów?

Przypomnijmy sobie chronologię wydarzeń.

2–7 listopada – Tusk mówi o zagrożeniu sabotażem.
W tym samym czasie prewencja zostaje skierowana do pilnowania TK, a AT na granicę.
GROM twierdzi, że ćwiczenia odbywają się przy granicy.
6 listopada – Tusk w Sejmie rzuca złowieszcze: „Zobaczycie za kilka dni albo kilkadziesiąt godzin”. XD
7 listopada – na krakowskim Rynku dochodzi do ataku. Napastnik strzela do przypadkowych ludzi. Sprawca zostaje ostatecznie zatrzymany w okolicach skrzyżowania Dietla i Stradomskiej. Samochody Straży Miejskiej dowożą policjantów na Rynek.
I teraz najciekawsze. Na końcu wychodzi Kierwiński i ogłasza, że policja zareagowała natychmiast, a jej funkcjonariusze wykazali się heroiczną postawą.

Do tego pojawiają się sugestie dotyczące prawicowych sympatii sprawcy.

I tutaj mam pytanie: skąd Kierwiński nagle tyle wie? XD

Zanim śledztwo wyjaśni wszystkie okoliczności, motywy i tło ataku, już pojawiają się gotowe narracje. Skąd ta pewność? Kto to ustalił i na jakiej podstawie?

Przez lata żyliście w bańce mydlanej, opowiadając wszystkim dookoła, jak to w Polsce jest bezpiecznie, jak nie ma zamachów i jak bardzo jesteśmy odporni na takie zagrożenia.

Dzisiaj jeden człowiek pokazał, że rzeczywistość może wyglądać zupełnie inaczej.

I nie piszcie mi, że policja zareagowała, bo ostatecznie sprawca został zatrzymany. To, że doszło do zatrzymania w okolicach Dietla i Stradomskiej, nie oznacza, że od samego początku sytuacja na Rynku była pod kontrolą. Mogło dojść do znacznie większej tragedii.

A teraz czekam na jutro.

Wyjdzie Tusk i powie, że w ramach dbania o nasze bezpieczeństwo przypadkowo wojsko niemieckie pomoże w patrolowaniu ulic podczas obchodów 11 listopada 2026.

A przy okazji może jeszcze usłyszymy, że warto ograniczyć dostęp do X w Polsce, bo przecież tam informacje między zwykłymi użytkownikami rozchodzą się szybciej niż komunikaty w siedzibach służb.

Ludzie sami publikują nagrania, wymieniają się informacjami, konfrontują oficjalne komunikaty z rzeczywistością i zadają niewygodne pytania.

A to najwyraźniej nie pasuje do narracji, w której obywatel ma czekać, aż ktoś z góry wyjaśni mu, co właśnie zobaczył.

Oczywiście to ironiczny scenariusz. Ale w obecnej atmosferze coraz więcej osób zaczyna zadawać pytania o granice bezpieczeństwa, kontroli informacji i prawa obywateli do niezależnego informowania się. XD

Zamiast zaklinać rzeczywistość, zacznijcie zadawać pytania.

Czy służby były odpowiednio przygotowane? Czy zabezpieczenie było wystarczające? Czy ktoś właściwie ocenił zagrożenie?

Bo bezpieczeństwo obywateli to nie propaganda, konferencje prasowe i opowiadanie, że wszystko jest pod kontrolą.

BEZPIECZEŃSTWO WERYFIKUJE RZECZYWISTOŚĆ, A NIE RZĄDOWE OPOWIEŚCI.

author: ResearchHub
quoted_text:
Publicly funded science should work more like open source software.

Today a result is a PDF. The data often isn't shared, the code isn't public, and few studies ever get replicated.

Imagine every experiment as a repo. Data, code, and protocol, all versioned. Anyone could fork it, rerun it, and send a fix. Funders could reward replications as much as new papers.

AI makes this urgent. Agents are now making more discoveries than ever. The bottleneck becomes replication/validation. Then commercialization, which still requires moving atoms in the real world and meetings with regulators.

text:
I admit that I completely broke down today. I cried uncontrollably. I couldn’t hold myself together after witnessing what I saw with my own eyes.

Today, we went to film a journalistic report inside the displacement tents along the seashore. I swear, what we witnessed was beyond what any human being should have to endure.

I saw men crying bitterly. Men I had never seen cry when they lost their children or when their homes were destroyed. Today, I saw them crying because they were powerless to do the simplest thing: protect their children from the water and the cold.

We spoke to families who told us they had spent the entire night carrying their children in their arms after floodwater covered the floors of their tents and soaked their mattresses. They couldn’t find a single dry place to put their children. They couldn’t even give them a few hours of sleep.

I saw children no older than five, without proper clothes to protect them from the cold, without heating, and without a dry place to sleep. Children shivering inside tents that cannot keep out the rain, protect them from the wind, or provide even the most basic sense of safety.

What more must happen for this world to act? How much more suffering must people endure before someone remembers that they are human beings?

I am sick of this world. I am sick of its hypocrisy and empty slogans. To hell with a world that talks endlessly about human rights while leaving children to drown inside their tents. To hell with everyone who has witnessed this suffering and chosen silence, and to hell with the governments and institutions that have the power to act but continue to turn their backs on us.

While studying at Ashesi, Benedict Quartey ’18 worked with Dr. Ayorkor Korsah to develop RollE, an affordable, modular autonomous vehicle that allowed students and researchers to experiment with self-driving technology without expensive equipment. The project introduced him to research and helped set him on a path toward doctoral studies.

His work later expanded to speech technology for Ghanaian languages, including research resources that developers could use to build applications in Asante Twi, Akuapem Twi, Fante, and Ga.

Since building RollE at Ashesi, Quartey has continued to explore how technology can help people investigate problems and test ideas in new ways.

text:
Bitget 这次的 Anthropic IPO 打新，说实话有一种生不逢时的感觉。

11.5 日开启认购，当天晚上美股大崩盘，人心惶惶，ANT 更是从 1600 狂泻到 1386。

目前看来总认购上限 10 亿，目前仅募集到 1470 万，参与人数 366。

不吹不黑，我把数摆出来算了一下下：

一、市场现在给多少
盘前合约现在 1400 左右，对应估值约 1.4 万亿美元。10 月底还在 1.9 万亿，半个月跌了快四分之一，光是过去 24 小时就在 1342 到 1543 之间来回。

二、IPO 大概定多少
彭博 11.6 报的讨论区间是 1.2 到 1.3 万亿。Bitget 页面上写的 103 美元、估值 1.75 万亿是之前的预期，已经过时了。按 1.2 到 1.3 万亿换算，发行价大概在 71 到 77 美元。

三、算下来赚不赚
合约价比传闻定价高 7% 到 18%，但认购要加服务费：
• 公开轮 5%：按现在的价格算，大致在保本到小赚之间
• VIP 轮 12%：基本把溢价吃光了，而且上市后 3 到 5 个工作日才到账，首日卖不了

四、要想清楚的风险
• 合约价是币圈的情绪价，来得快跌得也快，不等于上市首日的价格
• 如果订单热、定价上调到 1.5 万亿，按现在的价两轮都会亏
• 美股还没站稳，延期上市也有可能
• 到手的是代币 rANT，不是股票，资金锁定不能撤

募资冷清也说明大家心里都没底。配售按比例分，人少确实能多分一点，但前提是平台真能拿到配额。

我的判断：VIP 轮性价比不高；公开轮 11.10 开，可以等临近定价、看合约价还有没有溢价再决定。溢价不到 5%，就没必要上。

以上只是个人算账，不构成投资建议。

The case for gold into Q1 2027, from the D2 desk.

Gold printed 4,070 Friday, the same tick as a year ago (4,001 on 7 Nov 2025). From that tick the next twelve weeks ran it to 5,595 (chart 1, green box). The 2006 template, mapped onto the 29 Jan top, puts about 5,000 in the second half of January 2027. Debasement++ Epoch 2 runs 100 to 300% of NAV gold delta into 19 Feb 2027 on that read. Ten points, timeline since the Trump election.

1. Cycle low 2,537 on 14 Nov 2024, nine days after the election. 5,595 on 29 Jan 2026, +121% print to print. The buyer was the official sector: Japan and China cut Treasuries for a decade while adding gold, the swap @LukeGromen has charted for years. Overseas UST holdings fell ~$70B in June.

2. 28 Feb 2026 the Iran strikes started; gold has given back 23% from the pre-war close. Oil pushed CPI to 3.7% by September and the Fed from easing to hiking. Central banks sold into us to pay for the oil. Brent: 72 pre-strikes, 126 at the April top, 98 now. The 2025 setup returns if Iran resolves and it trades in the 80s.

3. 19 Aug Bessent doubled long-end buybacks. Yields dipped a day, back above 4.7% within the week, dollar down vs every G10, gold +5%. Window closed 4 Nov with the refunding; ~$6T rolls in Q4; ten-year 4.86% now. Bessent remains Bessent.

4. The 3 Nov result does not touch the arithmetic. $38.6T at a 3.1% weighted coupon; Q4 coupon interest alone $196B. Bloomberg Economics has interest at 6.4% of GDP by 2035, above Italy, debt to GDP 131%.

5. October was the washout: almost -7%, worst October since 2008, low 3,870 on the 30th. Goldman says early to buy. CFTC managed money net longs 104,297 in the week to 3 Nov, a 21-week low, shorts at a 17-week high. The washout @MacleodFinance tracks weekly in COMEX data.

6. Democrats swept. Gold +5% on the week, BTC -2.6% since Tuesday's close (round trip in the quoted post). Whether crypto trades as a debasement hedge or a Trump trade is unclear. If the Dems go after it hard, better the old rock than digital, and yes @PeterSchiff, that point is yours. BTC and MSTR stay in the basket, smaller.

7. Saturday's data: PBOC added 830K oz in October, month 24 of the streak, buying harder as price fell. Ten-month additions 129t; official sector net 321t in Q3. WGC survey: 45% of central banks plan to buy next year, a record, the bid @JamesGRickards has argued since The New Case for Gold. Poland at 700t.

8. The bid sits in Asia. The July rebound ran in Asian hours while London and New York went sideways (chart 2). India's wedding-season demand is back on the pullback. Hong Kong central clearing for gold goes live Q1 2027.

9. The 2006 template: 22% fall in 24 trading days from the 12 May top, three fifths back a year later, new high 16 months out. This leg ran 31% and sits at day 195, so the cycle is behind the template. The difference is the buyer: 2006 had no PBOC adding every month of the fall. text:
Fortunately, I have 35 years of experience in biomedical research (anyone is welcome to check my scientific record), and I have been saying the same thing for years. I completely agree with Demis: we will cure all diseases within 10 years AND reverse aging in approximately 15 years!

I realize I am an exception among my colleagues, but what I find truly messed up is denying people, whether sick or healthy, this very real hope for the future.

Let me explain the main reason why even brilliant scientists and experts struggle to imagine how this could possibly happen. It comes down to extreme cognitive dissonance and the enormous ego of human intelligence: if WE cannot achieve something, we find it inconceivable that MACHINE intelligence could. In fact, the smarter people are, the harder it often becomes for them to accept this possibility, and the more elaborate their coping mechanisms become.

Top mathematicians have just lived through this realization, and physicists will be experiencing it soon.

Yet biologists somehow feel more secure. Not because they are smarter, but because biological systems are vastly more complex. After centuries of research by some of the greatest minds in human history, the idea that AI could solve problems in biology that have eluded us for so long, and do so within just a decade or two, seems utterly inconceivable to them.

Well, they will find out soon enough!

As someone who understands biology deeply, I know that its complexity is not insurmountable. Yes biology IS extraordinarily complex, but it is ultimately a system governed by physical laws and principles that can be decoded, which we have been doing albeit very slowly. Achieving this in a decade will require superintelligence, vastly greater computational power, and enormous amounts of biological data. That is why I believe it will take a decade or two, compared with mathematics and physics, where AI is already making extraordinary progress at a much faster pace.

The fundamental mistake is assuming that the limits of human intelligence are also the limits of intelligence itself. We have spent centuries trying to understand biology with human brains, same substrate it is made of. We are about to bring an entirely different level of intelligence to the problem, one that will eventually surpass the collective intellectual capabilities of all scientists who have ever lived.

As such, I stand 100% behind Demis and others, including Dario Amodei, who have made similar predictions. 

Mark my words: the coming revolution in biology and medicine will be unlike anything humanity has ever experienced!

text:
我们都知道模型变强之后，以前精心设计的 Agent Skill 可能成了负担，但是怎么去除不必要的 skills 很多人却不知道。

Garry Tan @garrytan 的做法很值得借鉴。他用 Eval 对比了 Opus 5.5 开启和关闭 /investigate 的表现，发现修复率没有明显差异，但每修好一个 Bug 的成本反而高了 43%，于是决定砍掉它。

我觉得这个思路应该成为 Harness Engineering 的常规操作。

比如以前为了提高 Coding Agent 的可靠性，我们设计了「先生成详细计划，再逐步排查问题」的 Workflow。

模型升级后，就可以用同一批真实任务做 A/B Eval，一组保留旧流程，一组直接让模型执行，多次测试，对比成功率、Token 消耗和执行时间。

如果旧流程已经带不来稳定的提升，甚至增加了成本，那就该考虑简化或移除。

Agent 的 Skill 和 Harness 也需要定期做减法。模型在进化，我们为旧模型设计的工作方式也应该重新验证。

text:
AI Will Kill the Production of Knowledge. Then It Will Kill Itself.

An answer can be generated in seconds. A single finding that makes that answer possible may have taken years.

Someone had to go into the field, take measurements, and collect data. Others interpreted the results and documented what they found. Ready-made answers are getting cheaper, while producing original knowledge remains costly. As it gets harder to earn a return on that work, less of it may get done.

In an experiment published in Nature, AI models trained over successive generations on the outputs of earlier models began to lose rare examples from the original data. Researchers call this model collapse.

As AI undermines the production of the original knowledge it depends on, it undermines its own future. Even tomorrow’s most powerful model can’t recover an observation no one made today.

As the collapse deepens, our screens will still be full of confident answers. The same knowledge will keep coming back dressed as a new answer.

quoted_text:
I am a professor at the @UofCalifornia. I am appalled by the conduct of one of its Regents, Scott Galloway, appointed in August by Governor Newsom.

@profgalloway is one of only 26 voting Regents entrusted with governing a university system serving hundreds of thousands of students & employing tens of thousands of faculty & staff.

Twice, first on a live Pivot episode featuring Hillary Clinton & on Prof G with Fareed Zakaria, Galloway called Elon Musk a “traitor to the West.”

He invoked Julius & Ethel Rosenberg, who were executed for espionage, and declared that Musk should be held to the same standards.

He didn’t explicitly demand Musk’s execution. But invoking the deaths of two convicted spies while calling an American citizen a traitor makes the implication hard to miss.

Musk has not been convicted of treason. Indeed, “treason against the West” isn’t even an actual crime.

Now imagine UCLA alumnus @BenShapiro, appointed a UC Regent, saying the same about George Soros.

Would the Governor defend his right to serve? Would Regent leadership shrug and call it provocative commentary? Or would there be demands for resignation?

But there’s something worse here than another of Scott’s trademark podcast rants.

He sits on the Regents’ Academic & Student Affairs Committee.

The committee’s charter says it oversees student conduct, faculty conduct, academic personnel, & campus climate, among other responsibilities.

This is not some honorary title.

The Board sets university policy, controls institutional budgets, & appoints senior university leadership.

You can unsubscribe from a podcast.

A student who finds Scott’s comments morally repugnant can’t unsub from the Regents.

UC bylaws require Regents to serve the public trust with a “high degree of ethics and candor,” including as private citizens.

Professors owe students intellectual integrity. Regents bear an even greater duty: they govern institutions that teach it.

Yet a Regent serving on the committee responsible for student & faculty conduct invokes executions while labeling a fellow citizen a traitor.

What does that say to our students?

That intellectual restraint is expected of the governed but optional for those who govern?

That standards of conduct depend on whether the target of your rhetoric is politically fashionable to despise, as long as the audience applauds?

This isn’t about defending @ElonMusk. He needs no defense from me.

Nor is it about silencing Scott. As if that were possible. He’s free to express his opinions, however reckless they may be.

But freedom of speech is not freedom from accountability, and holding a university office of public trust is not an entitlement.

There is an enormous moral chasm between exercising your right to speak recklessly and demonstrating the judgment required of one of the 26 people who govern our great public university.

The UC Board of Regents isnt a podcast sponsors can boycott. It’s a public trust.

One final irony. At @NYUStern,  Galloway teaches Brand Strategy, including a session on crisis management.

His own prescription for leadership in a crisis is unequivocal: acknowledge the problem, have leadership take responsibility, and “overcorrect.”

He’s praised the departure of corporate leaders as evidence of effective crisis management.

Now Galloway himself sits on the UC Board of Regents.

Will he hold himself to the standards he teaches, or does accountability apply only to other people’s institutions? 

Professor lecture thyself!

I believe Scott Galloway should seriously consider whether his continued service on the Board of Regents is consistent with the ethical standards and responsibilities of that office, or whether he should resign.

I welcome the opportunity to discuss these issues with Galloway directly, including what standards we should expect of those entrusted with governing the world’s best university.

Scott, you have an open invitation to join me on @Into_Impossible for an honest conversation.

text:
In 2000 I graduated college and went to work for a very well known and prestigious management consulting firm. My colleagues and I would go out to lunch every day and debate politics. We did it almost every day. There was a large group of us and I was the only conservative in it.

In 2001 I was working with many of those people on a project in Atlanta. When September 11th happened, we were on one of the top floors of a building downtown, watching the events unfold on TV.

The next day a bunch of us met up in Olympic Park. We were all confused and fearful, trying to figure out what had happened and what are travel plans were since none of us lived in Atlanta.

I sat in the park on a massive blanket with a bunch of Ivy League graduates, listening to them talk about how they hoped that the terrorist attacks would not cause people to discriminate against Muslims. The buildings were still burning. This was Wednesday. They did the Norm Macdonald post perfectly.

The park was full of people. Some had even had brought American flags. I remember vividly thinking to myself "why am I not over there with those people?"

One of my coworkers told the group that he would "call out" any TSA workers for singling out Muslims to be patted down and searched. Everyone except myself agreed with him and even cheered him on. At that point I couldn't take the foolishness anymore. I told them they were the dumbest fucking people I had ever been around and then I walked back to the Westin hotel.

I lasted seven years in that industry. I didn't particularly enjoy it and truly despised the time they make you waste, but clients liked me so my company kept promoting me. I stayed until I couldn't take it any longer. Left and never set foot in corporate America again.

That feeling I had on the blanket, being surrounded by suicidally empathetic dumb fucking people, it's the same feeling I had before the midterms, watching Democrats rally around people like Abdul El-Sayed. It's why I devoted so much time and energy to posting videos of El-Sayed telling everyone over the years, in his own words, who he really is.

I didn't make one dime off of those posts or the time spent researching. Perhaps it was a complete waste of time. Maybe so.

I'm seeing all this talk on this site now about conservatives getting paid to post. How nice for them. I have never accepted money to post. I've been offered many times from conservative companies, groups and individuals, more than ever over the past year. My answer is always the same. I told people long ago that I would never post for money, so I will never post for money. All my posts come directly from me.

Many emotions, feelings, and memories have faded over the years as I have grown older. That feeling of contempt for people ushering their own demise is still strong as ever.

author: GeoffreyHuntley
quoted_text:
Asahi Linux is moving everything from the MIT licence to GPLv2-or-later.

Asahi is the volunteer project that reverse-engineers Apple Silicon Macs so they can run Linux. In today's Linux 7.3 progress report, developer James Calligeros explains why: people have been using the permissive licence to take the team's work. "In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin."

The report points to WINE, which switched from MIT to LGPL in 2002 for the same reason: "Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it."

The same report brings real wins too. M3 Macs now install without the EXPERT flag, Thunderbolt support (USB3 and networking for now) is shipping to users, and the team got GTA IV and Fallout: New Vegas running outside the muvm VM using Google's per-process page size patches.

text:
推荐 Anthropic 刚发布的《How researchers use Claude》，文章中分析了 20 多万条科研相关的 Claude 会话，看看 AI 到底在帮研究人员做些什么。

其中 Claude Code 近一半的科研会话都在做数据分析，用于提出研究想法和假设的却只有 2.1%。

但在另一项科研人员调查中，大家反而把提出研究问题和假设看得最重要。

文章还尝试解释了背后的技术原因。

作者把科研工作拆成具体任务，发现 AI 的能力与任务是否适合 RL 高度相关。像写代码、统计分析，结果容易验证，也能快速获得反馈；而一个研究假设究竟有没有价值，往往很难立即判断。

另一个值得关注的变化来自 Claude Science。

它把蛋白质结构、药物、论文等专业数据库接入同一个 Workflow，让 Agent 能跨工具收集证据、分析问题。假设生成类任务在 Claude Science 中的占比也更高，不过这还不能证明提升完全来自工具接入。

所以 Research Agent 接下来值得投入的方向，是把文献检索、数据分析和实验验证真正串起来。

让 Agent 提出一个想法已经不难，如何让它找到可靠证据、设计验证方法，并根据结果不断修正，才是更有挑战性的部分。
